docs.title: JVector
docs.text:
JVector is a Java library for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) vector search. It builds graph indexes that combine an HNSW-style hierarchy with Vamana (the algorithm behind DiskANN), can be built concurrently and incrementally, and can be searched from disk with compressed vectors.

  • Fast to build. Construction scales with cores and can score compact codes instead of full vectors, so building needs far less memory than the vectors themselves.
  • Larger than memory. Indexes can be served from disk, with compressed codes stored next to each node's neighbors and accurate vectors used to rerank the best candidates.
  • Choice of quantizers. Product quantization (PQ), Asymmetric Scalar Hashing (ASH, experimental), binary quantization (BQ), and NVQ for reranking.
  • Native SIMD. On Java 22 and later, distance and scoring kernels run natively on x86-64 and AArch64; Java 11 and newer are supported.

docs.title: Project
docs.text: JVector is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. The source and issues are on GitHub. These pages are built from the repository's docs/ folder, so every change to them is reviewed with the code; use the edit icon on any page to propose a fix.

docs.title: ASH configuration and defaults
docs.text:
ASH has independent settings for stored codes, construction, query projection, and query execution. This reference covers library parameters and BenchYAML controls. The BenchYAML Guide defines the index YAML fields. Recipes specify their own graph and compression values.

Set JVM properties before the affected model, provider or executor is initialized. Query views and pools are cached; changing a property later does not reconfigure existing objects. CPU-count properties do not pin threads.

docs.title: Similarity
docs.text:
An ASH model is trained for one similarity, DOT_PRODUCT, EUCLIDEAN or COSINE, which AsymmetricHashing.initialize requires as its second argument, as GraphIndexBuilder does; an ASH index cannot be built without one. The model saves it, and its codes and every scorer of them use it; asking a scorer for another similarity throws IllegalArgumentException, and every ASH score function reports it in similarityFunction(), which adaptive stopping reads. You name the similarity only where a model or index is created (AsymmetricHashing.initialize, StreamingASHIndex.coldStart); the ASH build score provider, block scorers, query preparers and StreamingASHIndex.withModel take it from the model, and an ASH index's reranker rejects any other similarity. PQ and BQ keep choosing the similarity per call. CompressedVectors.similarityFunction() returns the fixed similarity, or null when each call chooses it. BenchYAML takes the similarity from the dataset's metadata (similarity_function in dataset-metadata.yml).

ASH does not require normalized vectors for any similarity. Training and encoding center each vector on its landmark and use the unit residual (x - mu) / ||x - mu||, so vector lengths are kept. Scores use the exact scale of VectorSimilarityFunction: (1 + dot) / 2 for DOT_PRODUCT and 1 / (1 + d^2) for EUCLIDEAN and (1 + cos) / 2 for COSINE.

EUCLIDEAN uses the same codes, kernels and speed as DOT_PRODUCT (ASH paper, Appendix A). Its header stores -||x - mu||^2 / 2 where a DOT_PRODUCT header stores <x, mu> - ||mu||^2, and its query term is -||q - mu||^2 / 2 in place of <q, mu>, so the kernels estimate -||q - x||^2 / 2. A EUCLIDEAN model also stores a power-of-two unit that scales vectors to about unit length, so the half-precision header holds squared distances of vectors of any length.

COSINE normalizes vectors as VectorUtil.l2normalize does when it trains and encodes, and normalizes each query in FP32 before projection and before any FP16 or INT8 conversion; it then uses the DOT_PRODUCT path, so it has the same speed and, for vectors already of unit length, the same codes and scores. Reranking with stored full-precision vectors gives exact cosine similarity. Cosine is undefined for a zero vector: a COSINE model or index throws IllegalArgumentException for a zero vector when it trains, encodes, inserts or searches, as l2normalize does, so callers must reject zero vectors first.

Indexing:

// The similarity is fixed here and saved with the model.
AsymmetricHashing ash = AsymmetricHashing.initialize(vectors, VectorSimilarityFunction.EUCLIDEAN,
        AsymmetricHashing.ITQ, encodedBits, 1, bitsPerDimension, executor);
ASHVectors codes = ash.encodeAll(vectors, executor);
// Graph construction scores by the model's similarity; another one is rejected.
var builder = new GraphIndexBuilder(BuildScoreProvider.ashBuildScoreProvider(codes),
        vectors.dimension(), 32, 100, 1.2f, 1.2f, true);
var graph = builder.build(vectors);

Scoring:

VectorSimilarityFunction similarity = codes.similarityFunction(); // EUCLIDEAN
var approximate = codes.scoreFunctionFor(query, similarity);
var reranker = vectors.rerankerFor(query, similarity);
try (var searcher = new GraphSearcher(graph)) {
    var result = searcher.search(new DefaultSearchScoreProvider(approximate, reranker), 10, 50, 0f, 0f, Bits.ALL);
}

A fused index reads the similarity from its saved model: view.approximateScoreFunctionFor(query, similarity) must be given the same one. StreamingASHIndex takes the similarity when it is created and trains every model for it.

docs.title: Stored codes and training
docs.text:
BenchYAML puts these under compression[].parameters with type: ASH. Construction compression controls graph scoring. Search compression selects the codes stored with a fused ASH graph.

Parameter Default / requirement Optional values and definition optimizer Required ITQ (1): iterative-quantization transform. RANDOM (2): random transform. encodedBits Exactly one of this and compressionRatio Total stored bits including the 40-bit / five-byte header. The positive payload encodedBits - 40 must be divisible by bitsPerDimension. compressionRatio Alternative to encodedBits BenchYAML accepts 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. Resolves a payload near the requested FP32-to-code ratio, with a minimum 64-bit payload and whole projected dimensions; inspect the printed resolved size. bitsPerDimension (b) 1 Integer 1 through 9, all supported by fused ASH. 1, 2 and 4 have the most optimized kernels (see below). Stored-code precision is independent of query-projection arithmetic. landmarkCount (C) 1 Integer 1 through 256 for the quantizer. Symmetric graph-construction scoring currently requires C=1. Projected dimension (d) Derived, not a separate YAML field d = (encodedBits - 40) / b, with 1 <= d <= D for input dimension D. Increasing d or b increases code size.

For an exact payload, use encodedBits = 40 + d*b. For example, a 256-D input projected to 128 dimensions at four bits uses encodedBits: 552. Include the header when comparing memory budgets with other quantizers.

docs.title: Choosing the projected dimension for speed
docs.text:
For the fastest construction and search, use b = 1, 2 or 4 and make d a multiple of 64. The native kernels then process whole 64-bit words and whole SIMD vectors, with no leftover dimensions:

  • Construction compares stored codes with each other. At 1 bit, the kernel works in words of 64 dimensions. At 2 bits, it works in words of 32 dimensions. At 4 bits, it works in vectors of up to 128 dimensions.
  • Search builds per-query lookup tables in 16-byte chunks of code and projects queries 32 output dimensions at a time.

Other values of d are correct and handled in one extra masked step, so the penalty is small. In the measurements below, a 2-bit code at d = 380 costs about 20-30% more per construction comparison than at d = 384, and search QPS differs by about 1.5%. When a byte budget lands just short of an aligned d, prefer the aligned value. For example, with a 384-D input and a 100-byte budget, d = 384 at 2 bits (101 bytes, no dimension reduction) is a better choice than d = 380 (100 bytes).

The other widths, b = 3 and 5 through 9, store each dimension as an unsigned b-bit field. Search scores their graph neighborhoods with the projected query rounded to INT8 and integer dot products (VNNI on x86 processors that have it), so make d a multiple of 8. Their other asymmetric scoring uses the same 4-bit query tables as 2 and 4 bits. Construction still compares their codes with a portable per-dimension path, so building is slower than at 1, 2 or 4 bits; native code-to-code kernels for these widths are left for future work.

Construction comparison cost, in ns per code pair, on one pinned core with the native provider, on an Intel Xeon 6985P-C and on an AWS m6id.4xlarge (Ice Lake).

b d Xeon 6985P-C m6id.4xlarge 2 192 9.3 16.7 2 380 16.6 30.0 2 384 13.8 22.5 4 190 15.2 24.0 4 192 14.5 24.1 4 384 18.4 28.5

Training and base encoding retain their FP32 projection path; some training statistics and factorizations use FP64 internally. Query precision does not change the trained model, base encoding, stored-code layout or index format.

docs.title: Graph construction
docs.text:
BenchYAML selects construction scoring through compression[].scoring on an ASH construction entry. Omission uses the JVM policy, which defaults to symmetric-all. For example, this JVM property selects mixed scoring:

-Djvector.bench.ashConstruction=symmetric
Property value Insertion search Existing-node / diversity scoring symmetric-all (default) Encoded vector against encoded vectors; no dense insertion-query projection Symmetric encoded scoring symmetric Original vector used as an asymmetric query Symmetric encoded scoring symmetric-scalar Original vector used as an asymmetric query Scalar symmetric scoring; diagnostic control asymmetric Original vector used as an asymmetric query Original vector used as an asymmetric query; diagnostic control asymmetric-cached Original vector used as an asymmetric query Cached asymmetric query state per node; diagnostic control with extra memory use

jvector.bench.ashConstruction controls BenchYAML/Grid, not every library builder. For library integration, obtain a provider using BuildScoreProvider.ashBuildScoreProvider(encoded). Use builder.addGraphNode(node, provider.searchProviderFor(node)) for fully symmetric insertion. The overload taking an original vector retains asymmetric query preparation. Both policies use the same stored ASH vectors; application queries continue to use asymmetric scoring.

Construction policy can change the graph, recall and QPS. Use fresh indexes when comparing modes: the graph cache key does not include this JVM property, so changing it does not invalidate an existing cached graph.

docs.title: Encoding while vectors arrive
docs.text: To build a graph while its vectors stream in with a fixed model, ash.vectorsBuilder(capacity) encodes batches from any number of threads into distinct ordinals. Its live() view scores codes while they fill in, so a graph can be built over them at the same time; score a code only after its batch is encoded. build(size) returns the finished, immutable ASHVectors. Ordinals never encoded keep the all-zero code. For an index whose model changes while it grows, StreamingASHIndex uses MutableASHVectors, which re-encodes its pages for a new model one at a time.

docs.title: In-memory code layout
docs.text:
ASHVectors keeps one copy of the codes, in compact pages. Each vector's code body sits back to back with the others: sign words at 1 bit, sign-magnitude projection codes at 2 and 4 bits, and offset-binary fields at the other widths (dimension j is the unsigned field at bits [j*b, (j+1)*b), with value field - (2^b - 1)/2). Every stored offset includes the landmark term -scale * <A mu_c, code>, so asymmetric scoring needs only Aq. Bodies have no per-vector object, array or padding. Scale, offset and landmark are decoded once into three parallel arrays. Every scorer, symmetric and asymmetric, reads the codes in place, and the encoder writes straight into the pages.

Retained memory per vector is the serialized size plus 4 bytes, because the two binary16 header fields are held as floats: for example 101 bytes on disk and 105 bytes in memory for 768-D at 32x. Pages hold up to 256 KiB, which keeps them below G1's smallest humongous-object threshold so the collector never rounds them up to whole regions. ASHVectors.get(i) returns an allocated copy; copyTo(i, dest) fills reusable storage. Optional caches built for block scoring (blockScorerFor with a block size) hold a second, interleaved copy and are charged in ramBytesUsed() when created; graph construction and search do not build them.

docs.title: Query projection and scoring
BenchYAML precision selection
docs.text: Set queryProjection in the parameters map of an ASH compression entry. See ASH query parameters for values and JVM precedence. ASH CSV rows record ash_query_projection_requested and ash_query_projection_effective; the latter is read from the prepared view, with fp16+fp32 indicating observed automatic FP32 range fallback. Non-ASH rows have blank precision columns; an unused projection has blank effective precision. See the precision guide.

docs.title: Providers, CPU budgets and serialization
docs.text: Setting Default Optional values and definition jvector.vectorization_provider Automatic selection native, panama, default (scalar). Supported Java 22+ runtimes prefer native, with existing fallbacks. Explicit native requires successful loading. jvector.enable_native_vectorization true true / false; automatic native selection. Explicit provider selection overrides it. Deprecated jvector.experimental.enable_native_vectorization is a lower-precedence alias. jvector.physical_core_count OS topology detection bounded by available processors; fallback heuristic Positive thread budget for JVector's bounded pool and queued workers. Construction and queries can use separate budgets/processes; see Thread budgets. -XX:ActiveProcessorCount JVM/container detection Positive processor count exposed to the JVM; coordinate with allocated physical cores. Does not set affinity. --add-modules=jdk.incubator.vector Not added by the application Enables the Vector API module needed by SIMD providers on supported runtimes. --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED JVM native-access policy Native access for classpath deployments. Named-module deployments should enable the relevant module. -Xms, -Xmx JVM ergonomics Initial / maximum heap; account for resident input, model and construction memory. -ea, -da Assertions normally disabled Enable / disable Java assertions; independent of numerical precision.

docs.title: Thread budgets
docs.text: Graph insertion mostly waits on memory, so a second hardware thread per core fills those stalls: give construction every hardware thread, for example -Djvector.physical_core_count=16 -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=16 on 8 cores with two threads each, or pass a pool of that size to the builder. Builds of millions of vectors gain the most; recall and the built graph's search speed do not change. Compute-bound search runs best with one worker per physical core. Search that waits on storage needs more queries in flight than cores; see Building and serving larger-than-memory indexes.

docs.title: BLAS threads
docs.text:
ASH training is the only BLAS and LAPACK user. JVector sets the native BLAS thread count for its own calls, so a host does not need to configure MKL or OpenBLAS: training uses one BLAS thread, or as many as the executor passed to AsymmetricHashing.initialize(..., ForkJoinPool executor). Queries never call BLAS. With the native provider, MKL applies the count per calling thread (MKL_Set_Num_Threads_Local). OpenBLAS has only a process-wide count (openblas_set_num_threads; its openblas_set_num_threads_local also sets the process-wide count), so JVector sets it for the duration of training, and trainings running at the same time on other threads share the first one's count until the last finishes. Other providers leave BLAS threading to MKL_NUM_THREADS, OMP_NUM_THREADS and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS. io.github.jbellis.jvector.util.BlasThreads applies the same limit to a host's own BLAS work.

BenchYAML trains in its construction pool, so BLAS uses construction.workers threads (all physical cores by default). Set MKL_DYNAMIC=FALSE so MKL uses the count it is given. The ASH versus PQ study scripts also set the thread variables, to one for queries and the core budget for construction, as in the published runs. OS affinity (numactl --physcpubind) and memory placement (--membind, --interleave) are deployment choices.

docs.title: Graph and search parameters in BenchYAML
docs.text: Use the BenchYAML Guide for index type, graph parameters, writer selection, compression, and reranking.

docs.title: Query delivery and measurement controls
docs.text:
Set BenchYAML query delivery in the search section (queryExecution, requestsPerWorker) and the ASH batch limit in the ASH search parameters. Database integrations select their own admission policy and executors. See Integrating ASH queries into a database.

Setting Default Optional values / definition jvector.bench.queryThreads 0 Direct caller count: 0 uses common pool, 1 is serial, larger positive values use a dedicated caller pool. Does not set queued worker count. jvector.bench.verifyConcurrentResults false true / false; validate concurrent results against reference results. jvector.bench.runConfig jvector-examples/yaml-configs/run-config.yml Run YAML path for measured benchmarks, console and CSV fields. jvector.bench.sourceRef Unset Source identity for provenance; no numerical effect.

Run YAML benchmarks, console and logging select computed/reported throughput, recall, latency and visit counts, and measurement sets warmup, timed passes and the page cache state; see Run configuration. Construction separately reports quantizer training, encoding, NVQ training and graph/write. The throughput benchmark can also report per-query response times, page reads per query and, for queued execution, mean batch size. Unloaded latency and loaded response time describe different measurements. Independent build/query JVM repetitions are launch choices, not model defaults; preserve individual CSVs.

The ASH versus PQ case script (run-ash-pq-benchmark.sh) accepts JVECTOR_BENCH_DATA_DIR (required: where datasets are downloaded and reused), JVECTOR_BENCH_BUILD_SMT, JVECTOR_BENCH_ADAPTIVE, JVECTOR_BENCH_OVERQUERY, JVECTOR_BENCH_HEAP (128g) and JVECTOR_BENCH_NUMA_POLICY (bind:0; alternatively interleave:<nodes>). These defaults belong to the script, not the library. See Reproducing ASH versus PQ for launch and artifact details.

Implementation references: YAML compression parsing, ASH model, construction modes, and run configuration.

docs.title: ASH PCA correctness
docs.text:
PCA first computes FP64 covariance with DSYRK and its eigendecomposition with DSYEVD. This avoids computing and discarding a full tall left-singular-vector matrix. The input is read-only. Finite values, covariance trace, eigenvalue energy, the retained tail, the retained/discarded spectral gap and selected eigenpair residuals are validated before the leading directions are accepted.

Covariance squares the condition number. A retained eigenvalue or cutoff gap at the scale of accumulated FP64 error causes fallback to direct DGESDD. Zero energy, wide input and eigenvalue nonconvergence also use direct SVD. Its full right basis preserves null-space completion for underdetermined training. Invalid input, invalid native arguments and invalid workspace sizes are reported; allocation failures are not swallowed. Model and graph formats are unchanged.

Tests compare subspace projectors with an independent direct SVD, including repeated eigenvalues inside the retained subspace, ties at its boundary, ill-conditioned and rank-deficient matrices, wide inputs and input preservation.

docs.title: Why PCA avoids the QR SVD driver
docs.text:
Some LAPACK builds return incorrect results from the multi-threaded, optimal-workspace QR SVD path (DGESVD). With MKL 2020.4, a finite, well-formed 15,360 × 768 training matrix produced either DGESVD info=767 (QR nonconvergence; see the LAPACK contract) or a successful return with a 1.7% spectral-energy error. The same matrix was accurate to about 1e-13 with DGESDD, with DGESVD on minimum workspace, or with one thread.

PCA therefore never calls DGESVD. The covariance path above is the primary method, and the divide-and-conquer DGESDD driver, also used by ITQ orthogonalization, is the fallback. Tall inputs overwrite a scratch copy with the unused left vectors; wide inputs request full right vectors so projections can include null-space directions when training has fewer rows than dimensions. There are no CPU-, vendor-, bit-width- or JDK-specific branches or thread-count workarounds.

Saved models are not rewritten. Retrain the ASH compressor and rebuild its graph to adopt the current PCA.

docs.title: ASH performance
docs.text: This page compares fused ASH and fused PQ graph indexes on three large datasets, at matched code sizes: both store the same bytes per vector, including ASH's five-byte header. These datasets are not public; Reproducing ASH versus PQ explains how to run the same comparison on public 1M datasets on your own hardware.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: ASH wins total construction in 6/6 configurations, recall in 12/12 cases and QPS in 22/24 cases. The sum of all six construction times is 48.5% lower with ASH. The better value in each comparison is in bold.

docs.title: Total construction seconds (lower wins)
docs.text: Dataset Compression PQ ASH ASH change Faster MPNet 10M 32x (b=2) 343.7 238.1 −30.7% ASH MPNet 10M 16x (b=4) 568.9 301.2 −47.1% ASH Cohere 10M 32x (b=2) 478.0 263.3 −44.9% ASH Cohere 10M 16x (b=4) 771.2 335.8 −56.5% ASH CAP 6M 32x (b=2) 295.6 190.2 −35.6% ASH CAP 6M 16x (b=4) 630.7 261.8 −58.5% ASH Sum: six configurations 3,088.1 1,590.5 −48.5% ASH

docs.title: Setup and method
docs.text:
Machine. One Intel Xeon 6985P-C socket at 2.30 GHz base: 48 physical cores, 2 threads per core (96 hardware threads), 504 MiB L3. 354 GiB RAM in two NUMA nodes of about 177 GiB each. Debian 12, Linux 6.1. Transparent huge pages: enabled=always, defrag=madvise.

Storage. Datasets, model caches and indexes are on local NVMe SSDs in Linux md RAID 10 (512 KiB chunk, two near-copies), formatted XFS. The page cache was not dropped between runs.

JVM. OpenJDK 22.0.2 (Eclipse Temurin). Flags: --add-modules=jdk.incubator.vector --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -da -Xms2g -Xmx128g -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=<cores>. No collector is selected, so the JVM uses its default: G1 for the 8- and 48-core runs and Serial for the 1-core runs, because ActiveProcessorCount=1. JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS are empty.

JVector system properties. -Djvector.vectorization_provider=native -Djvector.parallel_writer=true -Djvector.physical_core_count=<cores> -Djvector.bench.queryThreads=<4 × cores> -Djvector.bench.verifyConcurrentResults=true, with timed throughput passes of at least 3 s (measurement.throughput.minSeconds: 3.0 in the study's run configurations). ASH construction scoring is symmetric-all, the default; no other ASH properties are set.

Native thread pools. MKL_NUM_THREADS, OMP_NUM_THREADS, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS and GOTO_NUM_THREADS equal the core count for construction and 1 for queries; MKL_DYNAMIC=FALSE.

CPU and memory placement. Each JVM starts under numactl. Construction uses one hardware thread on each of the 48 physical cores, with memory interleaved across both NUMA nodes. Queries use 1 or 8 physical cores on node 0, with memory bound to node 0.

Datasets. All use dot-product similarity on normalized vectors, 10,000 queries and exact top-100 ground truth. MPNet 10M: 9,997,697 base vectors × 768 dimensions. Cohere 10M (English v3): 10,000,000 × 1,024. CAP 6M (gte-Qwen2-1.5B case law): 6,070,488 × 1,536.

Index parameters. On-disk index format 7, fused graph, parallel writer. Degree (M) 32, efConstruction 100, neighbor overflow 1.2, alpha 1.2, hierarchy and final refinement on. ASH: ITQ optimizer, one landmark (C=1), symmetric-all construction scoring, and b = 2 or 4 bits per projected dimension over D/2 projected dimensions. Code size per vector, including the five-byte header: MPNet 101 / 197 bytes, Cohere 133 / 261 bytes and CAP 197 / 389 bytes for b = 2 / 4. PQ uses the same number of bytes as 8-bit subspaces with 256 centroids. Reranking uses NVQ vectors stored in the graph.

Query parameters. Top 10 returned. Overquery 1.0 and 2.0 (rerank 1x and 2x) rescore 10 and 20 candidates with NVQ. Search pruning off. ASH uses queued execution with a maximum batch of 8 and automatic query projection, which resolves to INT8 on this CPU (AVX-512 VNNI): one ASH worker per core (1 or 8), queue capacity 8 per core, fed by 4 × cores caller threads (4 or 32); the mean batch size is 8.0. PQ uses direct execution with 4 × cores caller threads. Concurrent results are verified against single-threaded results.

Measurement protocol. Each configuration was built twice from empty caches. Construction time is quantizer training, vector encoding, NVQ training, and graph construction and writing; dataset loading and setup are excluded. Each construction figure is the mean of the two builds:

Configuration ASH build 1 (s) ASH build 2 (s) MPNet 10M 32x (b=2) 227.3 249.0 MPNet 10M 16x (b=4) 317.6 284.8 Cohere 10M 32x (b=2) 291.2 235.3 Cohere 10M 16x (b=4) 348.2 323.4 CAP 6M 32x (b=2) 192.6 187.8 CAP 6M 16x (b=4) 260.7 262.9

Query JVMs reuse the first build's index, one JVM for 1 core and one for 8 cores. QPS is the mean of three timed samples of at least three seconds each; each JVM runs about 90,000 rerank-1x queries in total. Recall@10 is the fraction of the exact top 10 returned. Jobs ran one at a time, with no other benchmark process on the machine. PQ was measured in an earlier run on the same machine, JDK, placement, input files and graph parameters, with PQ codes sized to the same stored bytes per vector as ASH.

Single-core variation. Single-core QPS varies between graphs built from the same settings. On an earlier MPNet 10M 32x graph, ASH measured 10,414 / 7,838 QPS on one core (rerank 1x / 2x). Three further runs of the current code and of the earlier code on the reported graph averaged 9,229 / 7,460 and 9,124 / 7,334 QPS with identical recall, so the code performs the same; on this graph, ASH's single-core figures for that case are below PQ's 9,349 / 7,540.

ASH memory. Encoded ASH vectors are stored back to back in shared pages and scored in place, without per-vector objects. Measured on 2M MPNet vectors as live heap with and without the encoded vectors (Serial and G1 agree within 1%), ASH retains 109 bytes per vector at b = 2 and 205 at b = 4, compared with 189 and 285 for the earlier per-vector storage: 42% and 28% less. The codes occupy 101 and 197 bytes per vector on disk; the remaining 8 bytes hold the header scale and offset as floats and a per-vector construction term. The library's own accounting (ramBytesUsed) reports the same 109 and 205 bytes.

docs.title: Reproducing ASH versus PQ
docs.text: This study compares fused ASH and fused PQ graph indexes at matched code sizes: both store the same bytes per vector, including ASH's five-byte header. It runs on five public 1M datasets, which BenchYAML downloads from the public JVector dataset catalog, and uses only packaged JVector code and io.github.jbellis.jvector.example.BenchYAML. Results are BenchYAML's own output: CSV files and the tables it prints.

docs.title: Two ways to run it
docs.text:
Every case comes in two forms with the same index settings:

  • One JVM per measurement (studies/ash-vs-pq), run by run-ash-pq-study.py. One JVM builds and saves the index, then a fresh JVM measures each query core budget and overquery. Each JVM sees only its CPU budget (-XX:ActiveProcessorCount and a CPU list), so a 1-core measurement really has one core, including for garbage collection and JIT compilation, and no measurement inherits JIT, heap or cache state from construction or from an earlier measurement. Use this form for comparisons you report.
  • One JVM per case (studies/ash-vs-pq-single-jvm), run by benchyaml-play.sh. One JVM builds the index, then queries it once with 8 search workers at overquery 1. It is quicker and closer to an application that builds and serves in one process, but its queries run in the JVM that just built the index, sharing its heap, JIT state and threads. Use it for quick end-to-end checks, and compare its results only with each other.

docs.title: Build the checkout
docs.text:
Use JDK 22 or later on Linux, with numactl and lscpu. Follow the native prerequisites, including the compiler, Meson, Ninja and CMake. Native packaging fetches the pinned oneDNN source and includes the ASH add-on. ASH training also uses the installed BLAS/LAPACK provider; note which one you have, since a Java fallback trains more slowly.

export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk-22
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
mvn -B -pl jvector-examples -am -DskipTests package -Dnative.onednn=true

This writes jvector-examples/target/jvector-examples-<version>-jar-with-dependencies.jar. Build once and keep the checkout and JAR fixed throughout a comparison. The scripts require a clean checkout so each run records an exact commit, and they require the native vector provider, so a failed native build cannot silently become a scalar measurement.

docs.title: Datasets and index settings
docs.text:
Dataset Recipe prefix Base vectors Dimensions Queries Code bytes per vector Ada002 1M ada002 982,790 1536 10,000 197 Cohere English v3 1M cohere 1,000,000 1024 10,000 133 DPR-Gemma 1M dprgemma 999,762 768 10,000 101 OpenAI-1536 1M openai1536 999,000 1536 1,000 197 OpenAI-3072 1M openai3072 999,000 3072 1,000 389

All use dot-product similarity with the dataset's own top-100 ground truth. The first run downloads each dataset into the data directory you name; later runs reuse it.

ASH uses one landmark, an ITQ-trained transform to D/2 dimensions, and 2 bits per projected dimension. PQ uses as many 8-bit subspaces as ASH's code bytes, 256 centroids, no centering and non-anisotropic training.

Both use an on-disk index (format 7) with fused graph features, NVQ reranking, degree 32, efConstruction=100, neighbor overflow 1.2, hierarchy, final refinement and the parallel writer, and return the top 10 at overquery 1 and 2. ASH queries use queued execution with a maximum batch of 8, automatic query projection and adaptive stopping. PQ queries use direct execution.

Each algorithm is built at its fastest thread setting. On the machines we measured, ASH construction was fastest on both hardware threads of every core (SMT) and PQ construction on one thread per core; check this on your own hardware with --build-smt.

docs.title: Run the study (one JVM per measurement)
docs.text:
python3 jvector-examples/run-ash-pq-study.py \
  --data /data/vectors --output /data/jvector-bench/ash-vs-pq

For each dataset and algorithm, this builds the index in one JVM, then measures overquery 1 and 2 with 1 and with 8 physical cores, each in a fresh JVM: 2 construction and 8 query JVMs per dataset. Placement comes from lscpu: construction uses every physical core with memory interleaved across all NUMA nodes, and queries use the first physical cores of one node, with memory on that node. Options:

  • --datasets and --algorithms select a subset.
  • --build-smt lists the algorithms built with SMT (default ash).
  • --no-ash-adaptive searches ASH without adaptive stopping.
  • --query-cores and --overqueries change the query budgets and overqueries.
  • --repetitions repeats each query JVM, for run-to-run variation.
  • --dry-run prints the JVM launches without running them.

Rerunning the same command after an interruption reuses indexes that were already built. Do not run anything else on the machine during a study.

docs.title: One JVM by hand
docs.text:
run-ash-pq-benchmark.sh runs one JVM of the study; the study script calls it for every launch. It checks that the CPU list names exactly the requested physical cores, so two hardware threads of one core cannot count as two cores.

export JVECTOR_BENCH_DATA_DIR=/data/vectors
CASE=/data/jvector-bench/cohere-2bit-ash

# Construction on 48 physical cores using both threads of each (pick CPUs from lscpu).
JVECTOR_BENCH_BUILD_SMT=1 JVECTOR_BENCH_NUMA_POLICY=interleave:0,1 \
  bash jvector-examples/run-ash-pq-benchmark.sh cohere-2bit-ash.yml construction 48 0-95 "$CASE"

# Queries reuse the saved model and graph, each in a fresh JVM.
JVECTOR_BENCH_ADAPTIVE=1 JVECTOR_BENCH_OVERQUERY=1.0 \
  bash jvector-examples/run-ash-pq-benchmark.sh cohere-2bit-ash.yml queued 1 0 "$CASE"
JVECTOR_BENCH_ADAPTIVE=1 JVECTOR_BENCH_OVERQUERY=1.0 \
  bash jvector-examples/run-ash-pq-benchmark.sh cohere-2bit-ash.yml queued 8 0-7 "$CASE"

For the matching PQ case, use cohere-2bit-pq.yml, direct instead of queued, no SMT or adaptive settings, and its own case directory. The comments at the top of the script list every option.

docs.title: Run a case in one JVM
docs.text:
benchyaml-play.sh rebuilds the checkout, then runs one recipe in a single JVM on one hardware thread of each physical core. Copy bench-profiles/example.env to bench-profiles/local/profile.env and set the JDK, a working directory and the data directory (see the benchmark launcher).

BENCH_RUN_CONFIG=jvector-examples/yaml-configs/ash-pq/run-single-jvm.yml BENCH_ADAPTIVE=true \
  jvector-examples/benchyaml-play.sh \
  jvector-examples/yaml-configs/index-parameters/studies/ash-vs-pq-single-jvm/cohere-2bit-ash.yml

For PQ, run cohere-2bit-pq.yml without BENCH_ADAPTIVE. These recipes differ from the study's in four lines: construction.workers: max, search.workers: [8], overquery [1.0] and useSavedIndexIfExists: No. Queries are measured as in the study. Keep one search case per JVM: a second case would repeat queries the first already ran, so its queries would no longer be cold.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
The run configurations in yaml-configs/ash-pq select what BenchYAML measures and records.

  • Construction: BenchYAML's training, encoding, NVQ and graph-write timers. Dataset loading and download are excluded.
  • Queries (warm index, cold queries): the index stays in the page cache, the JVM warms up on base vectors until JIT compilation settles, then each held-out query runs once. That single pass is the throughput measurement; recall and visit counts come from later passes in the same JVM. Direct execution uses 4 × cores caller threads; queued execution uses at most one worker per core and a maximum batch of 8.
  • Recall: recall@10 against the dataset's ground truth, the same for every mode. Concurrent results are checked against single-threaded searches.

BenchYAML writes its CSV files under each case directory's logging folder and prints its tables. The scripts also keep, under runs, the source commit, JAR checksum, index and run YAML, Java version, CPU topology, console output, exit code and a command.sh that reruns the exact Java command.

Hardware, OS scheduling and parallel graph construction cause run-to-run variation, so reproducing the study means the same protocol and comparable results, not identical numbers.

docs.title: Published results
docs.text: ASH performance reports results on 6M and 10M datasets that are not in the public catalog, measured with an earlier version of this protocol.

docs.title: Choosing ASH query-projection precision
docs.text: Query-projection precision is independent of ASH's code parameters b and d. Selecting INT8 projection does not change the stored two-bit or four-bit ASH codes. Training and base-vector encoding retain their existing FP32 behavior.

docs.title: Recommended setting
docs.text:
These recommendations concern CPU query throughput and latency. Validate recall on your data before deploying FP16 or INT8.

Use the default, auto, on every processor. What it selects depends on the instructions the processor supports:

Processor support auto selects Notes x86-64 with AVX-512 VNNI and AVX-512 FP16 INT8, native kernel, 512-bit tiles Faster than FP16 projection. Use fp16 where recall at low overquery matters more than throughput. x86-64 with AVX-512 VNNI, without AVX-512 FP16 INT8, native kernel, 256-bit tiles FP16 projection is unavailable. x86-64 with AVX-VNNI, without AVX-512 INT8 through the oneDNN add-on Without the add-on, auto uses FP32. x86-64 without VNNI FP32 AArch64 FP32

To require INT8 and fail if it is unavailable, rather than fall back:

-Djvector.ash.queryProjection=int8

docs.title: Available settings
docs.text:
Set the precision per model in code with AsymmetricHashing.setQueryOptions(ASHQueryProjection, maxBatchSize), or for every model in the JVM with jvector.ash.queryProjection. Either must take effect before the model's first query:

Setting Behavior auto (default) Use INT8 where an integer dot-product backend is available (x86-64 VNNI); otherwise try optimized FP16, with the existing FP32 fallback if FP16 is unavailable or outside its supported range. fp32 Use the existing FP32 projection. fp16 Require optimized FP16 projection with FP32 accumulation and output. Report an error if unavailable or outside the supported range. int8 Require optimized INT8 projection with signed 32-bit integer accumulation and FP32 output. Report an error if unavailable; never silently substitute FP16 or FP32.

auto selects INT8 first because it was the fastest projection on every CPU measured: 1.03-1.10x FP16 on a CPU with AVX-512 FP16 and AMX, and 1.2-1.5x FP32 on AVX-512 VNNI CPUs without FP16, across nine 1M datasets. The query is quantized to two INT8 digits with one scale: a coarse digit and its rounding remainder, times 254. Nearly all INT8 projection error came from rounding the query; with the second digit, exhaustive recall matches FP32 projection, while the matrix keeps one INT8 digit per row.

On AVX-512 VNNI CPUs, INT8 uses JVector's exact-integer Highway kernel for single queries and batches, in the native library itself: 512-bit tiles on CPUs that also have AVX-512 FP16, and 256-bit tiles on other AVX-512 VNNI CPUs, where 512-bit integer dot products slowed the graph search that follows them. The oneDNN add-on serves INT8 on CPUs with AVX-VNNI but not AVX-512, and chooses the CPU implementation within FP16 at runtime. Setting the environment variable JVECTOR_ASH_INT8_ONEDNN makes INT8 use the add-on everywhere, for example to compare its AMX kernels; both compute the same integers, so the results are identical. Explicit FP16 and INT8 settings fail clearly if the required backend is unavailable, including when a virtual machine does not expose the needed hardware features. setQueryOptions checks its precision when called; a precision from the jvector.ash.queryProjection property is checked at the model's first query, because training, encoding and compaction never depend on query settings. To check before building anything, call ASHQueryProjection.FP16.isSupported() (or requireSupported(), which throws with the reason and what to use instead).

The model caches its query-projection view on first use. Changing the property afterwards does not reconfigure an existing view, and setQueryOptions throws once the view exists.

docs.title: BenchYAML runs
docs.text:
Set queryProjection in the parameters map of an ASH compression entry. The BenchYAML Guide defines the accepted values. An explicit -Djvector.ash.queryProjection=... overrides YAML. The default is auto. Use one projection mode per JVM.

experiments.csv adds two columns for ASH cases:

  • ash_query_projection_requested: the selected setting after JVM/YAML precedence.
  • ash_query_projection_effective: the prepared projection's actual precision. auto can resolve to int8, fp16 or fp32; fp16+fp32 means the automatic FP16 view has used its FP32 range fallback.

The columns are blank for non-ASH cases. Effective precision is blank if no query projection was initialized. Reporting reads the existing view after measurement; it does not prepare another view or infer precision from the CPU.

docs.title: Effect on graph construction
docs.text:
BenchYAML defaults to symmetric-all construction: insertion and diversity use encoded symmetric scoring, without dense query projection for insertion. Query precision therefore affects application queries, not insertion under this default.

Select scoring: mixed on the ASH construction entry to use asymmetric insertion and symmetric diversity scoring. Query projection then applies during insertion. Library callers explicitly choose an encoded node score provider or an original-vector insertion overload for their graph builders. See ASH configuration and defaults.

Neither construction mode changes training or base-encoding precision. To measure query-projection effects independently, query the same saved graph under each precision in separate JVM runs.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: FP16 requires the native vector provider, a CPU with AVX-512 FP16, and the oneDNN add-on. INT8 requires the native vector provider, and the add-on only on CPUs without AVX-512 VNNI. Published release JARs include the add-on; source builds add it with -Dnative.onednn=true, which also needs CMake. See the native development guide for build commands, supported runtime behavior, diagnostics and tests.

docs.title: Validate a selection
docs.text: Use DistancesASH to check projection throughput and numerical behavior. Use standard BenchYAML configurations to measure graph QPS, recall and latency at the application's physical-core budget. Compare query precisions on the same graph; measure construction separately when insertion precision changes. A projection-throughput gain does not imply the same graph-query speedup.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Processor instruction sets.
  • oneDNN CPU runtime dispatch.
  • oneDNN INT8 arithmetic.

The repository pins its oneDNN version in jvector-native/src/main/onednn/subprojects/onednn.wrap.

docs.title: ASH query batching: maintainer design
docs.text: Database integrators should use the caller integration guide. They do not need to know or configure the coordination described here.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Projecting several queries in one matrix multiply costs less per query than projecting them one at a time. When synchronous searches on different threads need a projection at the same time, ASH can combine them into one batch on one of those caller threads. It creates no executor, worker, timer or thread pool.

The combiner, CallerBatchProcessor, is generic: it knows nothing about ASH, FFM or oneDNN, and can serve other computations that benefit from combining independent caller work.

docs.title: Setting
docs.text: The only setting is the maximum batch: AsymmetricHashing.setQueryOptions per model, or the jvector.ash.queryBatchSize property as the default (8; 1 turns batching off).

docs.title: Capacity and the light-traffic path
docs.text:
Capacity follows the CPU budget. With C the smaller of the JVM processor limit and the physical-core budget, the combiner has C direct slots and max(1, floor(C / 4)) combining contexts. The recommended caller worker count is 4C.

While nothing is queued, a caller takes a direct slot and projects its own query immediately, so light traffic pays no batching cost. Only when overlap uses up the direct slots do callers queue. A combining caller takes the requests already waiting, up to the maximum batch, without waiting for a full batch, and requests are served in arrival order.

docs.title: Failures and fallback
docs.text:
A failed batch fails every query in it and frees its capacity, so later calls proceed. Reentry into the same processor is rejected. A projection without a batch kernel, or an older native library without the batch entry point, uses single-query projection. FP16 falls back to single-query projection if the native batch reports the operation unsupported; explicit INT8 reports an error instead of changing precision.

Each model counts its combiner and query projection once in ramBytesUsed(). Per-thread request records and scratch belong to the caller's budget.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text: Use BenchYAML for graph measurements. Compare batch size 1 with the default under the same affinity, CPU budget, caller count, data and warmup, at isolated, saturated and intermediate arrival rates, reporting recall and latency.

docs.title: Integrating ASH queries into a database
docs.text:
The database selects the physical-core budget C for search. Queries may be submitted independently without blocking a producer thread for every outstanding request. JVector prepares currently waiting compatible queries together, then executes each graph search independently. It never waits for a timer to fill a batch. An isolated request starts as soon as its execution capacity is available.

The existing synchronous GraphSearcher API remains available. The prepared-query and bounded-execution APIs are optional and do not change index formats, write ordering, FP32 encoding/training, or the automatic query-projection precision policy.

See Choosing ASH query-projection precision for processor-family recommendations and projection settings. The ASH configuration reference lists model parameters, construction modes, runtime flags and their defaults. The BenchYAML Guide describes projection and query delivery settings. The precision guide explains the requested and effective precision columns in experiments.csv.

docs.title: Recommended asynchronous allocation
docs.text:
Use these defaults for the search CPU budget assigned by the database when the index is resident in memory, so search is limited by CPU. For an index served from storage, see Indexes served from storage.

  • At most C execution workers, shared across the indexes competing for those cores. Producers do not need a worker thread for every submitted query.
  • Maximum preparation batch 8 and admission 8C. These are fixed defaults, not settings to tune for particular datasets. Admission includes pending, preparing and executing requests; completion callbacks are excluded.
  • One immutable model representation per loaded model, with reusable prepared state and exclusive search state for each active request.
Physical search cores C Maximum execution workers Request admission 1 1 8 2 2 16 4 4 32 8 8 64 16 16 128 32 32 256 48 48 384

The integration needs to select only C. Do not expose internal batching policy as database configuration. Larger explicit batches remain supported by the numerical API; this recommendation does not impose an eight-row API limit. The defaults bound memory and waiting but cannot guarantee a time limit under arbitrary overload. Reject or backpressure arrivals when admission is exhausted.

Choose physical cores, not both SMT siblings counted separately. Reserve a separate budget for construction, compaction and other database work. Tell JVector the allocation before initialization using jvector.physical_core_count; use -XX:ActiveProcessorCount consistently when appropriate. Neither property pins threads. Use the database's scheduler, OS affinity or container controls, and place query execution and index memory together on NUMA systems.

docs.title: Indexes served from storage
docs.text:
When the index is larger than memory, each search spends most of its time waiting for node reads, one after another, and the CPU is mostly idle. Then:

  • Run more searches at once than there are cores, so other searches proceed while some wait on reads. Throughput rises with workers until the device reaches its random-read limit; past that, added workers only add latency.
  • Admit one request per worker (admission = workers). Requests waiting behind a busy worker add their whole wait to latency and add no throughput.
  • Use a maximum preparation batch of 1. Projection batching saves microseconds of CPU, and holding queries for a batch costs more than that.
  • Set the query options on the model in code with AsymmetricHashing.setQueryOptions(precision, 1) if synchronous searches share the model, so they do not combine either.

Building and serving larger-than-memory indexes shows how to choose the worker count from the device's read rate and the reads each query makes.

For an integration retaining only synchronous searches, the caller recommendation is 4C bounded caller threads, with the same physical CPU budget. That does not mean an asynchronous integration needs 4C execution workers. Reproducing ASH versus PQ measures both execution modes separately.

docs.title: Library responsibilities and host responsibilities
docs.text:
ImmutableGraphIndex.queryPreparer() returns an optional QueryPreparer. Cache it with the loaded model. newState() creates reusable PreparedQuery buffers. prepare and prepareBatch snapshot FP32 query inputs, compute the projection and scoring data, and retain no traversal state. ASH uses its selected native query representation; encoding and training remain FP32. Unsupported providers retain their existing fallback behavior.

BatchingExecutor<T> is a reusable two-stage executor, independent of ASH and graph types. Its operation supplies a compatibility key, preparation, execution and completion. A key is an immutable identity for the numerical model, not a dataset name or mutable query buffer. Use null when preparation cannot benefit from batching, as with the current PQ query path. Distinct keys never share a preparation call. Mixed-model requests retain FIFO pending order; grouping only collects compatible requests currently adjacent at the front.

The host owns the executor and maps its request objects to these operations:

int searchCores = databaseSearchBudget;
int maximumBatch = 8;
int admission = Math.multiplyExact(searchCores, maximumBatch);
var searches = new BatchingExecutor<Request>(searchCores, admission, maximumBatch,
                                            databaseSearchExecutor, operation);
if (!searches.trySubmit(request)) {
    // The host still owns this request: reject or apply bounded backpressure.
}

The supplied executor must schedule asynchronously and explicitly reject work it cannot accept. Do not use direct execution, caller-runs fallback or silent discard. The service validates known unsuitable thread-pool policies. It submits at most C reusable drain tasks and releases their execution capacity when idle; it does not permanently park C tasks in the database's pool. A dedicated host pool may use an array-backed work queue to avoid a queue-node allocation for each task submission. Do not submit synchronous waiters to a pool whose entire capacity they would occupy while waiting for this same pool to run searches.

The execution operation borrows an exclusive GraphSearcher/view and binds the prepared state through ScoringView.scoreProviderFor(prepared, true). It then uses the existing search, filtering and reranking API. Models without a preparer use ordinary scoring. Numerical batches call the native batch kernel directly, without a second scheduling layer. The preparing worker executes the first search and publishes the others, allowing parallel traversal without waiting for the whole batch to finish.

docs.title: Input, result and resource ownership
docs.text:
An accepted request owns stable input data until preparation completes; keeping it stable through completion is the simplest contract. Source APIs that reuse a scratch vector must copy into request-owned reusable storage before fetching the next vector. A batch must not consist of several references to one source buffer that is overwritten on each fetch. The database may queue many independent requests from one producer, provided each request's inputs have this lifetime.

Each active traversal exclusively owns its searcher, view and mutable scoring state. PreparedQuery owns the query snapshot and numerical buffers; its ramBytesUsed() excludes shared model weights. Do not prepare it again until every search and resumable iterator borrowing it has finished. Publishing it to another thread requires a normal queue/executor handoff. Generation checks detect reuse of a prepared state that is still bound to a scoring provider.

Completion returns each result or error through that request's callback. Use the database's request identifier/promise/response destination to correlate it; results need not return on the original worker or finish in submission order. Completion callbacks must return promptly and must not wait for other work that needs the same execution budget. Admission is released before completion so callbacks can recycle a bounded request record safely.

For a completed top-K SearchResult, request state can be recycled once the callback has copied or transferred its result. A resumable iterator instead retains an exclusive search session: keep its searcher, view and prepared state leased until iteration finishes or closes. Do not return a worker's reusable searcher to the pool while such an iterator is live. Budget retained sessions and application-held results separately from the executor's admission count.

This executor schedules read-only query work. It does not reorder additions, deletions, flushes or publication of indexes. Retain the database's existing ordering, visibility and view-consistency rules for those operations.

A request timeout can stop the client waiting; it does not cancel a native call or release borrowed buffers. Drain accepted work before closing model/index resources. Interruption is preserved by close, which waits for callbacks too. Close the batching service before shutting down its host executor; forcibly discarding already accepted host tasks violates the execution contract.

Preparation, search and explicit dispatch failures are delivered once to each accepted request. A throwing completion callback is contained: inspect completionFailureCount() and firstCompletionFailure() for monitoring. Later submissions remain usable; graceful close reports retained callback failures after draining. Call close from the lifecycle owner, not a service operation or callback. Pool only bounded request/state storage, and include per-request scratch, host task queues and retained sessions in the integration's memory budget.

docs.title: Deployment and measurement
docs.text:
Build/package native dependencies through the repository's oneDNN instructions. Enable Vector API modules and native access as described in the provider guide. The preferred query implementation runs on the host workers without a nested native thread pool; avoid adding native worker counts on top of that CPU budget.

Validate production-like CPU/NUMA placement and actual traffic. Isolated queries must launch without deliberate batching delay; sustained backlog should create larger batches; intermediate arrivals should neither require a different configuration nor an unbounded queue. Include preparation, traversal, reranking, admission and dispatch in the metrics where they occur. Compare distributions, serious stalls and achieved QPS, with unchanged recall and explicit overload behavior. Use the checked-in BenchYAML recipe for reproducible library comparisons; its unloaded latency and bounded-backlog response samples are different metrics.

docs.title: Batched input vector access
docs.text:
File-backed input vectors can be supplied without loading the entire dataset into Java heap. RandomAccessVectorValues remains the basic contract. Its optional BatchedVectorValues extension lets algorithms request ranges or arbitrary selections while the source schedules bounded asynchronous I/O.

This API concerns the input vector source. It does not select the stored graph's reader, writer, layout, or direct-I/O backend.

docs.title: Runnable hello-world examples
docs.text:
From the repository root, using the JDK required by the examples module (currently JDK 23), run. The jdk20 profile enables the Java vector provider and avoids requiring a native-library build for these examples:

mvn -Pjdk20 -pl jvector-examples -am compile exec:exec@hello-batched-vectors
mvn -Pjdk20 -pl jvector-examples -am compile exec:exec@hello-batched-quantization

By default, both examples use e5-small-v2-100k from JVector's existing public dataset catalog. This is a real embedding dataset; its cleaned base contains 99,443 vectors with 384 dimensions. The catalog loader downloads only the base file on first use and reuses its cache thereafter. It honors catalog cache settings, including DATASET_CACHE_DIR; there is no eager heap preload and no synthetic data generation. The first invocation needs network access to the catalog and uncached base file.

  • HelloBatchedVectors shows a full range scan, arbitrary selection with duplicates, and copying a borrowed vector.
  • HelloBatchedQuantization trains a PQ codebook and encodes the full base file with PQ and NVQ through their usual APIs.

Pass your own fixed-dimension .fvecs file using -DvectorFile:

mvn -Pjdk20 -pl jvector-examples -am compile exec:exec@hello-batched-vectors \
    -DvectorFile=/path/to/ada_002_100k_base.fvecs
mvn -Pjdk20 -pl jvector-examples -am compile exec:exec@hello-batched-quantization \
    -DvectorFile=/path/to/ada_002_100k_base.fvecs

Alternatively, run either class's main in your IDE with the file path as its single argument. The quantization example needs at least 256 vectors. Caller-supplied files and downloaded catalog files are never deleted or rewritten by these examples. Values are read as stored; the source does not normalize, deduplicate, or scrub them.

docs.title: Open a file
docs.text:
FvecFileVectorValues associates a file with the capability interface:

try (var source = FvecFileVectorValues.open(Path.of("vectors.fvecs"))) {
    System.out.println(source.size());
    System.out.println(source.dimension());
}

The file must remain immutable while open. The source uses positional channel reads, not memory mapping, and uses the OS page cache. Each fvecs record contains a little-endian dimension integer followed by that many float32 coordinates; every record must have the same dimension. I/O failures during consumption propagate as UncheckedIOException.

docs.title: Dataset streaming and caches
docs.text: Prepare the input through the existing dataset catalog/download cache, then open its local .fvecs path with FvecFileVectorValues. The examples use loadBaseVectorFile, which honors catalog cache settings and DATASET_CACHE_DIR without materializing the base vectors. Downloads must finish before the source is opened; cursors stream a stable local file, not an in-progress remote download.

docs.title: Purpose and benchmark opt-in
docs.text:
The input file need not be fully preloaded for quantizer training (samples or full scans for statistics), batch encoding, or streaming FP/NVQ serialization. Training samples are temporary working memory; returned models do not retain those samples. Encoded vectors and graph structures keep their existing memory requirements.

BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML preserve resident loading by default. To opt in, set this root field in the index-parameter YAML used by either runner:

useDatasetPrefetching: true

Omitted or false preserves the resident path. The existing VM option -Djvector.dataset_loader=buffered explicitly overrides the YAML flag; preload overrides the flag in the other direction. Neither runner changes a user's YAML files.

The harness uses file input for bulk consumption in quantized construction and existing disk storage. Uncompressed construction, or a search configuration that requires raw input rather than stored vectors/codes, still uses resident input. The VM option does not bypass this resident-input routing. If an explicit buffered request requires resident input, the harness logs the reason for using preload. A mixed configuration requiring resident input remains resident; split those cases into separate configurations to measure dataset prefetching independently. This is source routing, not a restriction on the vector-access API.

Grid consumes each input batch through training/encoding and inline serialization; the original insertion vector is supplied from that batch, while peer scoring uses resident quantized codes. Query scoring is unchanged from main. Raw-input exact-query configurations retain resident input; quantized query paths continue to use their existing codes and stored reranking vectors. Compaction algorithms and query scoring are unchanged. AutoBenchYAML's separate legacy compaction-query validation still uses resident original vectors; that pass retains its existing memory requirement. The current compactor processes saved partition indexes, not the original input file. Any future original-input training, encoding or serialization step can use the same bulk hooks.

The source retains bounded reusable read buffers during consumption. It does not change persistent dataset, index or quantizer caches. File preparation remains outside construction timing; input consumption is included in the corresponding library calls. Queries and ground truth remain resident. Files must be complete and immutable, and buffered loading requires NO_SCRUB metadata. Existing direct calls to DataSets.loadDataSet(name) still preload. Application-provided RAVVs need no changes; future quantizers opt into VectorAccess for their bulk input needs.

Use a distinct AutoBenchYAML output/checkpoint file for each loading mode so earlier completed results are not reused as a different mode. The harness closes its input source after the configuration finishes.

docs.title: Random ordinals: fetch an arbitrary selection
docs.text:
Use a selection when the algorithm knows several requested ordinals ahead of time, for example a random training sample. The ordinal list can be unsorted and can contain duplicates. In this small example, every ordinal exists in the default 100k dataset:

int[] ordinals = {42, 7, 90_000, 42};
List<VectorFloat<?>> retained = new ArrayList<>();
try (var cursor = VectorAccess.openSelection(source, ordinals, 0, ordinals.length)) {
    while (cursor.next()) {
        // File cursor storage is reused: copy vectors kept for later computation.
        retained.add(cursor.vector().copy());
        System.out.println("Loaded ordinal " + cursor.ordinal());
    }
}
// retained is in order 42, 7, 90000, 42 and remains valid after cursor closure.

For a training sample, VectorAccess.copySelected(source, ordinals, executor) performs this materialization in parallel, with source-aware scheduling and the same order/duplicate guarantees. The algorithm selects the ordinals; the source only retrieves them. For a single unpredictable point request, the existing getVector(ordinal) API remains available; copy a shared result before retaining it.

docs.title: Scan ordinals: process the file in order
docs.text:
Use a range for a full pass, such as computing statistics or encoding vectors. Consume each borrowed vector before advancing; no copy is needed in this example:

int scanned = 0;
double firstCoordinateSum = 0;
try (var cursor = VectorAccess.openRange(source, 0, source.size())) {
    while (cursor.next()) {
        firstCoordinateSum += cursor.vector().get(0);
        scanned++;
    }
}
System.out.printf("Scanned %d vectors; sum = %f%n", scanned, firstCoordinateSum);

For a partition, openRange(source, 10, 20) reads ordinals 10 through 19. openRange(startInclusive, endExclusive) uses an exclusive end; equal endpoints are an empty range, including openRange(size, size). Selection arguments instead use an array slice: openSelection(ordinals, offset, count). Keep the selection array unchanged until its cursor closes.

VectorAccess selects the optional batching capability or falls back to ordinary point access. Algorithms should normally use these utilities rather than inspecting the concrete file-source type. The runnable HelloBatchedVectors example demonstrates both patterns, including a full scan of the real catalog dataset.

docs.title: Use with quantization and indexes
docs.text:
The algorithm chooses its vectors and performs computation. VectorAccess handles capability selection and fallback. The source owns file format, scheduling, I/O workers, buffering, and read-ahead.

PQ chooses its training sample as before and materializes it with:

List<VectorFloat<?>> training = VectorAccess.copySelected(source, ordinals, executor);

For capable sources, the utility schedules selected reads in storage order, then restores the original sample order and duplicates. PQ's sample policy and centroid learning are unchanged. The point-access fallback retains the existing parallel path and avoids copying non-shared resident vectors.

PQ, NVQ, and binary quantization bulk encoding use VectorAccess.forEach; NVQ's mean computation uses a range cursor and preserves its accumulation order. Existing calls to ProductQuantization.compute, encodeAll, and NVQuantization.compute accept the file source directly, as shown in the runnable quantization example.

For a new quantizer, use the full-scan overload without generating all ordinals:

VectorAccess.forEach(source, executor, (ordinal, vector) -> {
    // Encode or consume the borrowed vector here; copy it only if retaining it.
    encoded[ordinal] = compressor.encode(vector);
});

Use copySelected for retained training samples, openRange for an ordered sequential reduction, and the mapped forEach overload when output positions refer to different input ordinals. These utilities work with existing sources without buffered hooks. Full-precision graph construction retains its existing resident source in the harness. The optional bulk hooks are not a substitute for resident raw vectors in comparison-heavy construction. A caller can still use the ordinary point-access API; no library-wide policy is imposed. The source does not change distance metrics, quantizer parameters, graph pruning, or hierarchy. Algorithm restrictions still apply, such as FusedPQ requiring 256 clusters and anisotropic PQ requiring normalized training vectors.

Other quantizers and indexes can adopt the same utilities independently. Existing integrations can continue supplying ordinary RandomAccessVectorValues; they do not have to implement batching. No algorithm-specific policy belongs in the file source, and alternative sources can implement the same interface.

docs.title: Configure bounded read-ahead
docs.text:
Most callers use open(path). Immutable named options customize individual limits:

var options = FvecFileVectorValues.Options.defaults()
        .withMaxBufferBytes(32L << 20)
        .withBatchVectors(64)
        .withReadAhead(3);
try (var source = FvecFileVectorValues.open(path, options)) {
    // Use VectorAccess or ordinary point access.
}

The default I/O worker count follows PhysicalCoreExecutor, the compute sizing used by Grid and BenchYAML. It adapts to the machine and honors -Djvector.physical_core_count; there is no fixed core count. Blocking file reads for range and selection cursors run on a separate source-owned pool. Unpredictable point reads execute on the requesting thread using exclusively leased channels; point and asynchronous reads share the I/O concurrency limit. withIoThreads(count) remains available for explicit benchmark tuning. The quantization example uses the shared compute pool and does not shut it down.

Other defaults are at most 64 vectors per batch and three batches of read-ahead. Payload capacity is capped at min(1% of file bytes, 64 MiB), with one record as the minimum. A configured maximum is also capped at 1% of the file. Copies and cursors share the budget, including queued, in-flight and ready payloads, point-read buffers. Read-ahead zero disables speculative batches. Selected reads fetch requested records without reading the gaps between sparse samples.

This is an I/O payload budget, not a total-process memory limit. Retained training vectors, encoded outputs, graph data, scratch vectors, JVM/channel internals and the OS page cache consume additional memory. statistics() reports logical source reads and payload allocation, not physical device I/O.

docs.title: Ownership and closure
docs.text:
• A cursor has one consumer. Independent cursors can run concurrently.
  • A failed advance invalidates the cursor. Its value and ordinal are unavailable; open a new cursor to retry. Other views remain usable if the source is still open.
  • A shared cursor vector is borrowed until the next advance or close. Call .copy() before retaining it. Non-shared resident sources allow retention without copying.
  • Point-access views have their own scratch vector and are single-consumer. Use copy() or threadLocalSupplier() for concurrent point access.
  • Close cursors with try-with-resources, stop consumers, then close the root source.
  • Copies share the root's storage and I/O executor. Closing a copy affects that view only; closing the root invalidates all copies and releases the shared resources.
  • If point reads are still running when the root closes, close waits for each read in progress to finish; later point reads fail with IllegalStateException.
  • Direct payload buffers become eligible for JVM reclamation after references are released; closure does not promise immediate native-memory reclamation.

docs.title: Measure input loading
docs.text: The vector prefetching benchmark compares the exact buffered source with full preload and demand-only reads, timing sample retrieval, training and full-set encoding separately. It runs from the command line or IntelliJ.

docs.title: How to run benchmarks
docs.text:
JVector runs dataset benchmarks with BenchYAML. See the BenchYAML Guide for the construction and search fields, and Results for what each console and CSV field reports.

For a first run, benchmark one small public dataset from the repository root: 

mvn compile exec:exec@bench -pl jvector-examples -am -DbenchArgs=cohere-english-v3-100k
It downloads the dataset on first use (about 430 MB), builds and searches 100,000 vectors with the default index parameters and run configuration, and prints one table of throughput, nodes visited and recall for each overquery, in about a minute.

To run a benchmark - Decide which dataset(s) you want to benchmark. A dataset consists of - The vectors to be indexed, usually called the "base" or "target" vectors - The query vectors - The "ground truth" results that are used to compute accuracy metrics - The similarity metric used compute the ground truth (dot product, cosine similarity or L2 distance) - Configure the parameters combinations for which you want to run the benchmark. This includes index construction parameters, quantization parameters and search parameters.

JVector supports datasets in the fvecs/ivecs format. These consist of three files, for example base.fvecs, queries.fvecs and neighbors.ivecs containing the base vectors, query vectors, and ground truth. (fvecs and ivecs file formats are described here)

The general procedure for running benchmarks is mentioned below. The following sections describe the process in more detail. - Specify the dataset names to benchmark in datasets.yml. - Certain datasets will be downloaded automatically. If using a different dataset, make sure the dataset files are downloaded and made available (refer the section on Custom datasets). - Adjust the benchmark parameters in default.yml. This will affect the parameters for all datasets benchmarked. You can specify custom parameters for a specific dataset by creating a file called <your-dataset-name>.yml in the index-parameters subfolder. - Decide on the kind of measurements and logging you want and configure them in run-config.yml.

You can run the configured benchmark with maven: 

mvn clean compile exec:exec@bench -pl jvector-examples -am

docs.title: Specifying dataset(s)
docs.text:
The datasets you want to benchmark should be specified in jvector-examples/yaml-configs/datasets.yml. You'll notice this file already contains some entries; these are datasets that bench can automatically download and test with minimal additional configuration. Running bench without arguments and without changing this file will cause ALL the datasets to be benchmarked one by one (this is probably not what you want).

To benchmark a single dataset, comment out the entries corresponding to all other datasets. (Or provide command line arguments as described in Running bench from the command line)

Datasets are grouped into categories. The categories can be arbitrarily chosen for convenience and are not currently considered by the benchmarking system.

Dataset similarity functions are configured in jvector-examples/yaml-configs/dataset-metadata.yml.

Example datasets.yml:

category0:
  - my-dataset-a
  - my-dataset-b
some-other-category:
  - another-dataset-a
  - another-dataset-b

docs.title: default.yml / \<dataset-name>.yml
docs.text:
jvector-examples/yaml-configs/index-parameters/default.yml specifies the default index construction and search parameters to be used by bench for all datasets.

You can specify a custom set of a parameters for any given dataset by creating a file called <dataset-name>.yml, with <dataset-name> replaced by the actual name of the dataset. This is the same as the identifier used in datasets.yml. The format of this file is exactly the same as default.yml. The name must match exactly, including case, and the file's dataset: field must name the same dataset; BenchYAML stops with an error otherwise. Place the file directly in index-parameters, not a subfolder. Subfolders hold example pipelines that you run by path.

See the BenchYAML Guide for the field reference and an example index configuration.

Most parameters can be specified as an array. For these parameters, a separate benchmark is run for each value of the parameter. If multiple parameters are specified as arrays, a benchmark is run for each combination (i.e. taking the Cartesian product). For example: 

construction:
  outDegree: [32, 64]
  efConstruction: [100, 200]
will build and benchmark four graphs, one for each combination of M and ef in {(32, 100), (64, 100), (32, 200), (64, 200)}. This is particularly useful when running a Grid search to identify the best performing parameters.

docs.title: run-config.yml
docs.text:
This file contains configurations for - Specifying the measurements you want to report, like QPS, latency and recall - Specifying how they are measured, such as warmup, timed passes and the page cache state - Specifying where to output these measurements, i.e. to the console, or to a file, or both.

The configurations in this file are "run-level", meaning that they are shared across all the datasets being benchmarked. Select another file with -Djvector.bench.runConfig=<path>.

See Run configuration for every option, run-config.yml for the default, and run-config-larger-than-memory.yml for measuring an index served from storage.

docs.title: Running bench from the command line
docs.text:
Once configured to your liking, you can run the benchmark through maven: 

mvn compile exec:exec@bench -pl jvector-examples -am

To benchmark a subset of the datasets in datasets.yml, you can provide a space-separated list of regexes as arguments. 

# matches `glove-25-angular`, `glove-50-angular`, `nytimes-256-angular` etc
mvn compile exec:exec@bench -pl jvector-examples -am -DbenchArgs="glove nytimes"

docs.title: Custom Datasets
docs.text:
Datasets are configured via YAML catalog files under jvector-examples/yaml-configs/dataset-catalogs/. The loader recursively discovers all .yaml/.yml files in that directory tree. See jvector-examples/yaml-configs/dataset-catalogs/local-catalog.yaml for the full format reference.

To add a custom fvecs/ivecs dataset:

  1. Add a .yaml file to the YAML catalog directory, mapping your dataset name to its files: 
    _defaults:
  cache_dir: ${DATASET_CACHE_DIR:-dataset_cache}

my-dataset:
  base: my_base_vectors.fvecs
  query: my_query_vectors.fvecs
  gt: my_ground_truth.ivecs
  2. Place your fvecs/ivecs files at the paths you specified in the YAML (or specify a cache_dir / base_url to fetch them from a remote source).
  3. Add the dataset's similarity function to jvector-examples/yaml-configs/dataset-metadata.yml: 
    my-dataset:
  similarity_function: COSINE
  load_behavior: NO_SCRUB
  4. Add the dataset name to jvector-examples/yaml-configs/datasets.yml so BenchYAML can find it: 
    custom:
  - my-dataset

For remote datasets, use base_url to specify where files should be downloaded from. The ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} syntax is supported for environment variable expansion. See the example config for details.

docs.title: Final index serialization
docs.text: For an on-disk index, set construction.writerMode to sequential or parallel in the index parameters. Both writers serialize the completed graph after cleanup. The parallel writer defaults to 64 records per batch. See the BenchYAML Guide for configuration and Deferred batch serialization for writer details.

docs.title: Fused PQ and ASH comparison
docs.text: Reproducing ASH versus PQ provides byte-matched recipes for five public 1M datasets, scripts that run one case or a whole study, and the measurement protocol. ASH performance reports results on larger datasets.

docs.title: BenchYAML Guide
docs.text: BenchYAML uses dataset configuration to build an index and measure search. Each case produces one index. Construction scoring determines the graph topology, search scoring determines how queries traverse that graph, and reranking optionally rescores the candidates.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text:
• Index parameters describe construction and search for a dataset. Running BenchYAML with a dataset name loads index-parameters/<dataset>.yml, named exactly like the dataset and declaring it, or default.yml when the dataset has no file. Subdirectories hold example pipelines, such as in-memory graphs and in-memory builds flushed to fused on-disk graphs, and published studies. Run them by passing their paths to BenchYAML.
  • Dataset catalogs locate the base vectors, query vectors, and ground truth. Dataset metadata supplies the similarity function. Vector types come from the dataset. A dataset marked is_int8: true holds signed int8 vectors (unsigned .bvecs data such as SIFT1B must be converted first). Its cases use type: onDisk, compression None, reranking.type: None and fusedGraph: [No], as the int8 files in index-parameters do.
  • Run configuration selects which measurements to compute, how to measure them, and which to display or log; see Run configuration.

Each index-parameter file sets yamlSchemaVersion: 3, the current onDiskIndexVersion, and its dataset name. An optional top-level useDatasetPrefetching: true streams base vectors in order during construction instead of loading them all into memory; see Batched input vector access.

See How to run benchmarks for dataset setup and commands.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
Choose inMemory or onDisk for the case. To measure both index forms, use separate cases with matching graph settings. The graph settings and fusedGraph are lists of sweep values. useSavedIndexIfExists is a scalar. Each compression list entry has a type and its own settings.

Field Values Description type inMemory, onDisk inMemory keeps the graph in memory for search. onDisk serializes the completed graph and reopens it for search. streaming Yes, No Optional scalar. Yes builds the index as a live index is built, inserting vectors as they arrive; see Streaming builds. Defaults to No. coldStartSize Integers ≥ 0 Required with streaming: Yes, which it sweeps. 0 starts the index with the construction compressor's model.
