A positive count starts it cold; see Streaming builds. trainWhileStreaming Yes, No Optional with streaming: Yes, swept. Yes lets a cold index train its first model, with the construction compressor's optimizer, once its sample holds 20 × the dimension vectors. No fixes a random projection after coldStartSize vectors instead. Defaults to No. writerMode sequential, parallel Selects the writer after graph cleanup for onDisk. Defaults to parallel. pageAlignment Power of two from 512 to 1048576 Optional, onDisk only. Places base-layer node records so none crosses a page boundary of this size, typically 4096; see Page-aligned records. Omitted, records are packed back to back. Part of the saved-index identity. useSavedIndexIfExists Yes, No Controls reuse of a compatible index, inMemory or onDisk, batch or streaming. Yes saves each built index, with the traversal codes it stores, in the working directory's index_cache and reuses it on later runs; an inMemory index is reloaded into memory. A cache hit skips fresh construction and serialization measurements. Saved indexes are never deleted automatically, so starting-point configurations use No; recipes that query an index from a later JVM, such as the ASH/PQ comparison, use Yes. workers Positive integer or max Optional. Threads for quantizer training, encoding, graph insertion and the parallel writer. max is the platform's physical core count, which is also the default. outDegree Positive integers Maximum final neighborhood degree, also called M. upperLayerDegree Positive integers Optional, schema 3, with addHierarchy: [Yes]. Maximum degree of the layers above the base layer; with it, outDegree is the base layer's degree. Omit for outDegree on every layer. Each value is one more build. efConstruction Positive integers Search width used to find candidates during insertion. neighborOverflow Finite numbers ≥ 1.0 Temporary neighborhood capacity relative to final degree. Java float suffixes such as 1.2f are accepted. addHierarchy Yes, No Builds upper graph layers. refineFinalGraph Yes, No Refines the graph during final cleanup. fusedGraph Yes, No Applies to onDisk. Yes stores ASH or PQ neighbor codes alongside the graph records. search.compression selects the codec. compression[].type None, ASH, PQ, BQ Selects the representation for construction scoring. None uses source vectors. compression[].parameters Quantizer parameters Supplies training and encoding settings for this entry. compression[].scoring symmetric, asymmetric, mixed Optional for ASH construction. symmetric scores encoded vectors during insertion and pruning. asymmetric scores source queries against codes for both operations. mixed uses asymmetric insertion and symmetric pruning. reranking.type None, FP32, NVQ FP32 rescores candidates with source vectors. NVQ rescores them with NVQ codes. None or omission skips reranking where the scorer and layout allow it.

docs.title: Streaming builds
docs.text:
A streaming case adds the base vectors one at a time, in file order, from one thread per construction worker, to an index that keeps no copy of the vectors, as a database's live index would. The case needs a single ASH compression entry. Searches use the codes the index built, whatever search.compression says, with the search case's query settings.

  • Warm start. With coldStartSize: [0] the index starts with the construction compressor's model and encodes each vector as it arrives. Train that model on a window with the ASH trainingStart and trainingCount parameters to stand in for a model inherited from an earlier index.
  • Cold start. With a positive coldStartSize the index first builds and searches its graph with exact scores, as an uncompressed index does. When its first model is ready, trained with trainWhileStreaming: [Yes] or a random projection without it, the index encodes the vectors it holds, rescores the graph's edges with ASH scores and continues with ASH. While the first model trains, inserts run on at most half the logical CPUs, so the training gets the CPU it needs.
  • The flush. At the end, the build readies the index as a flush does: every vector ends on the newest model.

inMemory streaming indexes rerank from the source vectors, so reranking is FP32 or None. onDisk streaming indexes are then written and reopened for search, with fusedGraph: [No]: the index's codes are stored beside it, and NVQ reranking is centered with the mean the index kept as vectors arrived, so writing reads each vector once. The console reports the streaming timeline, the insertion rate, how long fixing the first model held inserts and the memory the index holds. Build time covers insertion, the flush preparation and graph cleanup, plus writing for onDisk. With useSavedIndexIfExists: Yes, a saved streaming index is reused, with its codes, only by a case with the same streaming settings and insert threads, so later JVMs can query it, for example with fewer cores.

ASH construction uses symmetric scoring by default. When scoring is omitted, the configured ASH construction policy applies. See ASH configuration and defaults for the JVM setting.

An onDisk index that does not fuse its ASH codes (fusedGraph: [No]) writes the build's codes beside the index file during the flush, as a deployed index would, and a search with the same ASH settings loads them when it opens the index instead of encoding the base vectors again. Indexes cached before codes were stored, PQ and BQ codes, and searches with other ASH settings still encode. Results defines the build-phase and code timings.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Search uses the index selected by construction.type. Changes to stored features define separate index cases. Search sweeps such as topKOverquery use the index for their case. When CSV logging is enabled, the row also records the index type, writer mode, reranker, ASH construction mode, and query delivery settings including the number of callers or workers. A run with mixed delivery policies reports thread counts per case in the CSV.

Field Values Description topKOverquery Map of positive integer K to lists of finite multipliers ≥ 1 Required for search. The integer part of K × multiplier is the candidate budget. Return up to K results, with a second scoring pass when configured. useSearchPruning List of Yes and No values Enables traversal pruning for supported scorers and similarity functions. workers List of positive integers or max Optional sweep. Direct search uses this many calling threads; queued search uses this many workers to prepare and execute queries. Each value queries the same index, so [1, 8] reports 1 and 8 workers from one build. Later search cases repeat queries that earlier cases already ran, so for cold-query measurements use one search case per JVM. Omitted, the JVM-wide settings apply. queryExecution direct, queued direct runs each search on a calling thread. queued sends searches to a fixed pool of workers through a bounded queue and, for ASH, prepares waiting queries together, with fused codes or with codes stored beside the index or held in memory. Applies to every compression entry. Defaults to direct. requestsPerWorker Positive integer Optional, queued only. Queries admitted per worker, counting the one it is searching; the queue holds this many times the worker count. Defaults to the larger of 8 and the ASH maxBatchSize. Use 1 when search waits on storage, so queries do not queue behind busy workers. compression[].type None, ASH, PQ, BQ Selects the traversal representation. None scores source vectors. compression[].parameters Quantizer parameters Supplies encoding settings for traversal. Reuse matching construction models and codes where possible.

For a fused disk case, Grid writes the selected search codes over the completed topology. Matching ASH or PQ settings reuse the construction model and codes. With a non-fused layout, compressed traversal uses a separate in-memory code store. With source-vector disk search and no reranker, the inline source vectors are the sole vector feature.

docs.title: ASH query parameters
docs.text:
Place queryProjection in the parameters map of an ASH compression entry. Place maxBatchSize in that map on an ASH search entry; it requires search.queryExecution: queued.

Field Values Description queryProjection auto, fp32, fp16, int8 Optional. auto is the default and selects INT8 where an integer dot-product backend exists, then FP16 where supported, with FP32 fallback. fp32 selects FP32 projection. fp16 and int8 require their selected paths. The mode applies to ASH search and asymmetric construction scoring. Explicit ASH settings in one JVM must agree. Entries that omit it inherit the JVM mode, which defaults to auto. The jvector.ash.queryProjection JVM property overrides YAML. maxBatchSize Positive integer Caps the number of queued queries whose projections are prepared together. Defaults to 8. Batching saves CPU when search is compute-bound; when search waits on storage, 1 avoids holding queries for a batch.

FP16 projection uses FP32 accumulation and output. INT8 projection uses integer accumulation and FP32 output. Fully symmetric construction scores encoded vectors directly. See the ASH precision guide for provider and hardware requirements.

docs.title: Validate the index and scorer
docs.text:
Grid validates the selected scorer, layout, similarity function, and precision before training or construction. Disk writer, page alignment, cache, and fused layout settings apply to onDisk cases. Fused disk search requires ASH or PQ search compression.

With reranking.type: None or an omitted reranker, search returns up to K results ordered by traversal score, including compressed scores where supported. If the selected scorer or layout requires a reranker, Grid throws an exception during configuration validation. The fused ASH and PQ scorer setup requires an FP32 or NVQ scoring feature.

Grid rejects settings that do not apply to the case. Search type None scores with full-precision vectors, so it requires reranking.type: None. Explicit precision requests require support on the selected provider and machine.

docs.title: Run configuration
docs.text:
The run YAML applies to every index configuration in an invocation. Select it with -Djvector.bench.runConfig=<path>. Its sections, in order:

Section Purpose benchmarks The benchmarks to compute and the stats from each: throughput (AVG, MEDIAN, MAX queries per second), latency (AVG, STD, P999 for one query at a time), count (visited, expanded, expanded base layer nodes per query) and accuracy (recall, MAP). measurement Optional. How the benchmarks run; see below. console The benchmark stats and named metrics to print. logging Optional. The directory, run identifier, stats and metrics for experiments.csv.

measurement settings, each optional:

Field Values Description evictIndex true, false Cold index: drops each on-disk index file from the page cache before its first search, so search reads it from storage. Pages the open index has already read stay cached. Linux and JDK 22+ only. Defaults to false. throughput.warmup random, base, none Warmup queries. random uses random vectors; base uses base vectors sampled from the dataset, which follow the data without favoring the measured queries. Defaults to random. throughput.warmupPasses Integer ≥ 0 Warmup passes over the query count. Defaults to 3. throughput.untilCompiled true, false Continues warming, up to 10 passes, until a pass adds little JIT compilation, so timed passes run compiled code. Defaults to false. throughput.passes Integer ≥ 1 Timed passes; the throughput stats summarize them. With 1 and minSeconds: 0, each held-out query runs once (cold queries) in the first search case. Defaults to 3. throughput.minSeconds Number ≥ 0 A timed pass repeats the queries until it has run this long; 0 runs them once. Defaults to 1.0.

Named metrics under console.metrics and logging.metrics come in the categories system, disk, construction and execution. Results defines each one.

The default run configuration prints one short table for a first run. The larger-than-memory run configuration measures queries that read the index from storage.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Each search case prints one console row per overquery and, with logging, appends one row to experiments.csv in the run directory. The console shows the selected fields under their headers; the CSV starts with fixed columns, then one column per selected field, named by its key. A field a case does not produce is left blank.

docs.title: Fixed CSV columns
docs.text: Column Meaning schema_version Version of the CSV layout. run_id, run_uuid The run's directory name (from logging.runId) and a unique id for it. system_id A hash of the machine and JVM description in the run's system information, for joining runs from one system. dataset_name The dataset. M, efConstruction, neighborOverflow, addHierarchy, refineFinalGraph The graph construction parameters. M is outDegree. feature_set The features stored in the index, such as [NVQ_VECTORS, FUSED_ASH]. build_compressor, search_compressor The compressors used for construction and for search traversal. usePruning, topK, overquery The search settings of the row. rerankK Candidates kept for reranking, topK × overquery rounded down. ash_query_projection_requested, ash_query_projection_effective The requested ASH query projection precision and the one in effect; blank without ASH search. index_type, writer_mode, reranking_type, ash_construction_mode Schema 3 only: construction.type, writerMode, reranking.type and the ASH construction scoring mode. query_execution, query_threads, max_batch_size Schema 3 only: direct or queued, the query workers (queued) or caller threads (direct), and the ASH query batch limit.

docs.title: Benchmark fields
docs.text:
Selected under benchmarks. In the console, (of N) under a throughput header is the number of timed passes.

Selector CSV key Console header Meaning throughput: AVG search.throughput.avg_qps Avg QPS Mean queries per second over the timed passes. search.throughput.stddev_qps, search.throughput.cv_pct ± Std Dev, CV % Spread of QPS across passes, as a standard deviation and as a percentage of the mean. Only with more than one pass. throughput: MEDIAN search.throughput.median_qps Median QPS Median QPS over the timed passes. throughput: MAX search.throughput.max_qps, search.throughput.min_qps Max QPS, Min QPS Fastest and slowest timed pass. latency: AVG, STD, P999 search.latency.mean_ms, std_ms, p999_ms Mean, STD, p999 Latency (ms) Time of one query run on its own, one at a time: mean, standard deviation and 99.9th percentile. count: visited search.count.avg_visited Avg Visited Nodes scored per query. count: expanded search.count.avg_expanded Avg Expanded Nodes whose neighbors were explored, per query. count: expanded base layer search.count.avg_expanded_base_layer Avg Expanded Base Layer The same, in the base layer only. accuracy: recall search.accuracy.recall_at_{topK} Recall@{topK} Fraction of each query's true topK neighbors among its topK results, averaged over queries. accuracy: MAP search.accuracy.map_at_{topK} MAP@{topK} Mean average precision of the topK results.

docs.title: Named metrics
docs.text:
Selected under metrics, by category.

Category: field CSV key Console header Meaning system: max_heap_mb search.system.max_heap_mb Max heap usage (MB) The larger of the heap in use before and after the case's queries; not a sampled peak. system: max_offheap_mb search.system.max_offheap_mb Max offheap usage (MB) The same for direct and mapped buffers. disk: file_count, total_file_size_mb search.disk.file_count, search.disk.total_file_size_mb File count, Total file size (MB) Files in the work and saved-index directories after the queries, and their total size. construction: index_build_time_s construction.index_build_time_s Index build time (s) Building and writing the index; blank when every index came from the index cache. construction: graph_build_time_s construction.graph_build_time_s Graph build time (s) onDisk: graph construction and cleanup. construction: flush_time_s construction.flush_time_s Flush time (s) onDisk: writing the completed graph, its features and any stored codes. Graph build plus flush equals the index build time. construction: reopen_time_s construction.reopen_time_s Reopen time (s) onDisk: opening the written index files. construction: codes_write_time_s construction.codes_write_time_s Codes write time (s) The part of the flush spent writing the ASH codes stored beside a non-fused index. construction: codes_file_size_mb construction.codes_file_size_mb Codes file size (MB) Size of the stored codes file, when the search uses it. construction: index_quant_time_s construction.index_quant_time_s.{type}.compute_time_s, .encoding_time_s Idx {type} compute (s), Idx {type} encoding (s) Training the quantizer and encoding the vectors for construction, per quantizer type: PQ, BQ, ASH or NVQ. Compute time is blank when the model was loaded from the compressor cache. construction: search_quant_time_s search.search_quant_time_s.{type}.compute_time_s, .encoding_time_s Search {type} compute (s), Search {type} encoding (s) The same for the search traversal codes of an index that does not fuse them. search.search_quant_time_s.ASH.load_time_s Search ASH load (s) Loading the ASH codes stored with the index, in place of training and encoding; a row has this or the encoding time, not both. execution: response_mean_ms, response_p50_ms, response_p95_ms, response_p99_ms, response_p999_ms search.execution.response_* Loaded mean, p50, p95, p99, p99.9 (ms) Each query's time in the throughput benchmark's timed passes: with queued execution from submission to completion, with direct execution the search itself. execution: mean_batch_size search.execution.mean_batch_size Mean batch Queries prepared together, on average, by queued ASH execution. execution: page_reads_per_query search.execution.page_reads_per_query Page reads (per query) Linux only: the process's major page faults per query in the timed passes, which counts pages read from storage.

docs.title: Quantizer parameters
docs.text:
The fields below belong to the parameters map of their compression entry. D is the dataset dimension.

Quantizer and field Values Description ASH optimizer ITQ, RANDOM Training transform. Required for a new model. ASH compressionRatio 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 Nominal FP32-to-code ratio. The parser rounds to whole projected dimensions and uses a minimum payload. Specify either compressionRatio or encodedBits. ASH encodedBits Positive integer bit budget Includes a 40-bit header. The payload must be divisible by bitsPerDimension and yield 1 through D projected dimensions. ASH bitsPerDimension 1–9, in memory and fused. 1, 2 and 4 have the fastest kernels. Bits per projected dimension in the stored codes. Defaults to 1. ASH landmarkCount 1–256 Number of landmarks. Defaults to 1. The model is trained for the dataset's similarity. Symmetric and mixed construction require one landmark. ASH trainingStart, trainingCount Base ordinals inside the dataset Optional. Trains the model only on trainingCount base vectors starting at trainingStart (default 0), as an index that has seen only its first vectors would. All base vectors are still encoded. Omitted, training samples the whole set. A windowed model gets its own cache entries, and its codes are always re-encoded rather than loaded. PQ m Integer from 1 through D Number of subspaces. Specify either m or mFactor. PQ mFactor Positive integer yielding a valid m Chooses the subspace count by integer division of D by mFactor. PQ k Integer from 1 through 256 Centroids per subspace. Defaults to 256. Training requires at least k vectors. Fused PQ requires 256. PQ centerData "Yes", "No" Centers data before encoding. Omission enables centering for Euclidean similarity only. Quote these values in the YAML parameter map. PQ anisotropicThreshold −1.0 ≤ value < 1.0 Controls anisotropic training on unit-normalized input. The default −1 disables anisotropic weighting. BQ parameters Omitted Uses sign codes and Hamming scoring to approximate cosine similarity.

NVQ reranking uses the built-in encoder settings. BenchYAML chooses the subvector count and uses eight bits per dimension.

docs.title: Example index parameters
docs.text:
These sections describe source-vector graph construction followed by fused ASH disk search with NVQ reranking on a 768-dimensional dot-product dataset.

construction:
  type: onDisk
  writerMode: parallel
  useSavedIndexIfExists: No
  outDegree: [32]
  efConstruction: [100]
  neighborOverflow: [1.2]
  addHierarchy: [Yes]
  refineFinalGraph: [Yes]
  fusedGraph: [Yes]
  compression:
    - type: None
  reranking:
    type: NVQ

search:
  topKOverquery:
    10: [1.0, 2.0]
  useSearchPruning: [No]
  queryExecution: queued
  compression:
    - type: ASH
      parameters:
        optimizer: ITQ
        encodedBits: 808
        bitsPerDimension: 2
        landmarkCount: 1
        queryProjection: fp16
        maxBatchSize: 8

For a source-vector memory case, select inMemory, use None compression in both sections, and omit the disk settings. Use reranking.type: None to measure search with traversal scores alone. For an index larger than memory, see the larger-than-memory example.

docs.title: Related guides
docs.text:
• How to run benchmarks covers dataset setup and invocation.
  • Fused PQ and ASH comparison specifies the matched compression budgets, machine setup, and measurement procedure.
  • ASH configuration and defaults covers model and runtime settings.
  • Building and serving larger-than-memory indexes covers sizing, page alignment and query settings for indexes served from disk.
  • Deferred batch serialization explains writer batching and feature production.

docs.title: Binary quantization (BQ)
docs.text: Binary quantization keeps one bit per dimension: the sign of each component. Scores are Hamming distances between bit strings, which approximate cosine similarity. It needs no training and is the cheapest code to compute and compare, but also the coarsest.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Very high-dimensional embeddings, where even one bit per dimension leaves enough information to steer the graph search, and cheap construction and traversal matter most.
  • Cosine similarity, or vectors normalized to unit length. BQ ignores the similarity function and always scores by Hamming distance, so it is a poor fit for unnormalized dot products and Euclidean distance.
  • Always with reranking (FP32 or NVQ), and usually with a larger rerank depth than PQ or ASH need.

For most data, ASH at 1 bit per projected dimension, or PQ, is more accurate at the same or smaller size; measure on your data.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
var bq = new BinaryQuantization(vectors.dimension());
var codes = (BQVectors) bq.encodeAll(vectors);

// construction scored with BQ codes
var buildScores = BuildScoreProvider.bqBuildScoreProvider(codes);

// search: BQ traversal, reranked with full vectors
var asf = codes.scoreFunctionFor(query, similarity);
var reranker = vectors.rerankerFor(query, similarity);
var result = searcher.search(new DefaultSearchScoreProvider(asf, reranker), topK, rerankK,
                             0.0f, 0.0f, Bits.ALL);

BQ codes are kept in memory beside the graph; there is no fused BQ layout. The in-memory BQ example configuration runs this pipeline in BenchYAML.

docs.title: Size
docs.text: 8 × ⌈dimension / 64⌉ bytes per vector: 128 bytes for 1,024 dimensions (32× smaller than FP32).

docs.title: Building and installing JVector
docs.text:
This guide covers two ways to get JVector: using a release from Maven Central, and building it from source for a particular platform and vector backend. ASH requires release 4.1.0-rc.1 or later.

  • Vector backends
  • Using a release from Maven Central
  • Building from source
  • Checking which backend is in use

docs.title: Vector backends
docs.text:
JVector picks one of three vectorization providers when it starts:

Provider Java runtime Platforms Notes Native 22 and newer Linux x86-64 (SSE4.2 or newer), Linux AArch64 Fastest. Kernels built with Google Highway; the best instruction-set tier is chosen at startup. Required for INT8 and FP16 ASH query projection. Panama 20 and newer Any Uses the incubating Java Vector API. Used on macOS, Windows and other platforms, and on Linux when native code is unavailable. Scalar 11 and newer Any Plain Java. Used on Java 11 to 19.

Native is preferred on Java 22 and newer when the native library loads; otherwise JVector falls back to Panama, then scalar. SIMD and native acceleration lists the properties that override this choice.

The optional oneDNN add-on is a second native library that ASH uses for FP16 query projection, for INT8 on processors with AVX-VNNI but not AVX-512, and for batched FP32 encoding. Without it, ASH falls back to the Highway or Java kernels for those operations. See Choosing ASH query-projection precision.

docs.title: Using a release from Maven Central
docs.text:
JVector is published as one multi-release jar, io.github.jbellis:jvector.

Maven:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.jbellis</groupId>
  <artifactId>jvector</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.0-rc.1</version>
</dependency>

Gradle (Kotlin DSL):

implementation("io.github.jbellis:jvector:4.1.0-rc.1")

docs.title: What the jar contains
docs.text:
• The core library, compiled for Java 11.
  • The Panama provider, used on Java 20 and newer (META-INF/versions/20).
  • The native provider, used on Java 22 and newer (META-INF/versions/22), with native libraries for Linux x86-64 and Linux AArch64, and the oneDNN add-on for both.

There is nothing else to install: the native libraries load from the jar, and oneDNN is built in rather than linked against a system libdnnl. ASH training uses the system BLAS and LAPACK (MKL or OpenBLAS) when installed and a slower Java implementation otherwise; see BLAS threads.

docs.title: JVM options
docs.text:
Java runtime Options Provider 11 to 19 none Scalar 20 and 21 --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector Panama 22 and newer --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED Native on Linux, else Panama

Without --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector, Java 20 and newer use the scalar provider. Do not pass it on Java 11 to 15, which do not have that module. On Java 22 and newer, --enable-native-access avoids the JVM's native-access warning; if native access is denied, JVector falls back to Panama. If your application runs as named modules, grant native access to the module that contains JVector instead of ALL-UNNAMED.

If you repackage JVector into a single "uber" jar, keep the Multi-Release: true manifest entry and the META-INF/versions directories; otherwise the Panama and native providers are lost or, on older runtimes, can fail to load.

docs.title: Common requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 22 or newer to run the build, whatever runtime you target.
  • Maven 3.8 or newer, and Git.

Clone the repository and build from its root:

git clone https://github.com/datastax/jvector.git
cd jvector
mvn -DskipTests install

install places the jar in your local Maven repository as version 4.1.0-SNAPSHOT (or whatever version the checkout declares), ready to use as a dependency. Use package instead to build without installing; the jar is jvector-multirelease/target/jvector-<version>.jar.

docs.title: Builds by target
docs.text:
Target Additional requirements Command Linux x86-64 or AArch64, native GCC 12 or newer (11 or newer on AArch64), Meson, Ninja mvn -DskipTests install Linux, native with oneDNN (recommended for ASH) As above, plus CMake 3.13 or newer; adds a few minutes to the first build mvn -DskipTests install -Dnative.onednn=true Linux, both architectures As above, plus a cross-compiler (g++-aarch64-linux-gnu on x86-64) mvn -DskipTests install -Dnative.crossarch Linux, both architectures with oneDNN (what a release contains) All of the above mvn -DskipTests install -Dnative.crossarch -Dnative.onednn=true macOS and other platforms None mvn -DskipTests install (no native library is built; JVector uses Panama or scalar)

On Linux the native library is part of every build, so Meson and Ninja are required there. On Ubuntu, bash build_native_lib.sh --auto-install-deps (in jvector-native/src/main/native/src) installs the toolchain and builds the library. Debug builds, manual Meson builds, compiler notes and ISA tiers are covered in the native library README.

A jar built on one Linux architecture contains only that architecture's native library unless you add -Dnative.crossarch. A jar built on macOS contains no native library and runs with Panama or scalar everywhere.

docs.title: Building and running the examples
docs.text:
mvn -pl jvector-examples -am -DskipTests package -Dnative.onednn=true

On macOS, drop -Dnative.onednn=true. The Getting started section and the examples README show how to run each program.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text: Building and testing lists the test commands, including the scalar tests on a Java 11 runtime.

docs.title: Checking which backend is in use
docs.text:
JVector logs its choice at startup, for example:

INFO: Native Vector API enabled. Using NativeVectorizationProvider.
INFO: Highway ISA tier: avx3_spr, Env variable JVECTOR_MAX_ISA: (not set)

On Java 20 and 21, or wherever native code is unavailable, it logs Using PanamaVectorizationProvider. From code, VectorizationProvider.getInstance() returns the provider in use.

docs.title: Choosing an index
docs.text:
A JVector index is a graph plus up to two kinds of vector data:

  • Traversal codes score candidates while the search walks the graph. They are compact and approximate: full vectors, or codes from PQ, ASH or BQ.
  • Reranking vectors rescore the best candidates at the end: full-precision (FP32) vectors or NVQ codes.

Choosing an index means choosing where the graph lives, which traversal codes to use, where those codes are stored, and what reranks.

docs.title: Step 1: memory or disk
docs.text:
Your situation Start with A small collection whose full vectors fit comfortably in memory, or low-dimensional data where quantization saves little In-memory graph, full vectors, no quantization Vectors fit in memory but you want faster traversal In-memory graph, ASH or PQ traversal, FP32 rerank The index must persist, or vectors do not fit in memory On-disk index, fused ASH or PQ traversal, NVQ rerank The index is many times larger than memory The same, with page-aligned records; see Larger-than-memory indexes

The on-disk layout with fused codes and NVQ reranking is the default in the benchmark tools and the usual starting point for a database. The example configurations give one ready-to-run file per layout.

docs.title: Step 2: the traversal quantizer
docs.text:
Quantizer Choose it when Notes PQ You want the stable, widely deployed default Any similarity; optional anisotropic weighting; fused PQ requires 256 clusters per subspace ASH (experimental) You want the best accuracy for a given code size, or faster builds Any similarity (chosen when the model is trained); fused or in memory; API may change between releases BQ Dimension is very high, vectors are normalized, and a coarse first pass is enough One bit per dimension, scored by Hamming distance as an approximation of cosine similarity; not fused None The collection is small or low-dimensional Scores full vectors; no training

On large datasets at the same code size, fused ASH builds faster than fused PQ and reaches higher recall at a given throughput; see ASH performance. PQ remains the choice when API stability matters most.

The code size sets the accuracy and memory trade-off. A 32× compression (for example, 128 bytes for a 1,024-dimension FP32 vector) is a common starting point; see Memory and disk sizing.

docs.title: Step 3: fused or separate codes
docs.text:
Layout How it works Best for Fused Each node's on-disk record carries its neighbors' codes, so a search reads the codes with the graph Indexes that should not hold codes in memory; fewest reads per query Separate Codes are kept in memory (or in a file beside the index) and the graph holds only neighbor ids Smaller files; streaming indexes that keep their codes beside the flushed index

Fused codes repeat each node's code in every record that links to it, so a fused index is larger on disk (degree × code size per node). Reranking vectors have a similar choice: inline in each record, or separated into their own block. Fused and separated layouts compares all of these in detail. Fused ASH, stored ASH codes and page-aligned records need on-disk format version 7, which JVector 4.0.x cannot read; see UPGRADING.md.

docs.title: Step 4: reranking
docs.text:
Reranker Size per vector Use it when NVQ About a quarter of FP32 (dimension + 60 bytes with two subvectors) On-disk indexes: high accuracy at a fraction of the read size FP32 4 × dimension bytes Exact final scores, or in-memory indexes that already hold the vectors None 0 Full-vector traversal, or when approximate scores are good enough

Rerank more candidates to raise recall; see Tuning.

docs.title: Similarity
docs.text: JVector supports DOT_PRODUCT, COSINE and EUCLIDEAN. An ASH model is trained for one similarity and saved with it; ASH does not require normalized vectors. See ASH similarity. Int8 indexes use ByteVectorSimilarityFunction, with the same three functions. Under COSINE, ASH and int8 indexes both reject a zero vector with IllegalArgumentException when it is added or used as a query.

docs.title: Graph Index Compaction
docs.text: OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor merges multiple on-disk HNSW graph indexes into a single compacted index. This is useful in write-heavy workloads where data is continuously ingested into small segment indexes that accumulate over time; periodically compacting those segments into one larger index improves search throughput and recall without rebuilding from scratch.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
source[0].index  ─┐
source[1].index  ─┤──► OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor ──► compacted.index
source[N].index  ─┘

Each source is an OnDiskGraphIndex with an associated FixedBitSet marking which of its nodes are live (not deleted). The compactor merges all live nodes into a single graph, assigns the output ordinals (dense over the live nodes, grouped by region), and retrains the Product Quantization codebook for outputs that carry one.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
List<OnDiskGraphIndex> sources = List.of(index0, index1, index2);

// Mark all nodes live (no deletions)
List<FixedBitSet> liveNodes = sources.stream()
    .map(s -> { var bs = new FixedBitSet(s.size()); bs.set(0, s.size()); return bs; })
    .collect(toList());

var compactor = new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(
    sources, liveNodes,
    VectorSimilarityFunction.COSINE,
    /* executor= */ null                  // null = use by default shared threadpool in compactor
);

compactor.compact(Path.of("compacted.index"));

// Where every source node landed, one mapper per source: oldToNew(i) is the output ordinal of
// source node i, or OrdinalMapper.OMITTED for a deleted node.
List<OrdinalMapper> mapping = compactor.ordinalMappers();

docs.title: Output ordinals
docs.text: The compactor assigns the output ordinals; the caller does not choose them. Live nodes are numbered 0 .. live - 1, sources in ascending-size order, and within a source by the region of the merged hierarchy each node descends to, so nodes that are close in vector space get adjacent ordinals: records are written sequentially, every cell's members are contiguous (the cell join below relies on this), and consecutive nodes explore the same neighbourhood of every target. Callers that keep external references to nodes (a row id to ordinal table, for instance) translate them through ordinalMappers() after compact returns.

docs.title: Output format version
docs.text: The sources may be of any on-disk format version the reader supports (2 to 6); the compactor detects each source's version from its file. The output is written at OnDiskGraphIndex.CURRENT_VERSION unless withVersion(int) asks for another one, so by default a compaction also upgrades old sources. An output that carries fused PQ needs version 6, and one with upper layers version 4 or above; a version that cannot hold the output is rejected when compact starts. A sharded compaction writes every shard at the version of the compactor the session was opened on. A compressed sidecar written beside the graph (compact(graphPath, compressedPath)) serializes its merged compressor at the same version, so the two files always share one; a PQ with an anisotropic threshold needs version 3 or above.

docs.title: Handling Deleted Nodes
docs.text:
Deleted nodes are excluded from the output by marking them as false in the corresponding FixedBitSet; they get no output ordinal (ordinalMappers() reports OrdinalMapper.OMITTED for them).

// Example: every 5th node is deleted
FixedBitSet live = new FixedBitSet(source.size());
for (int i = 0; i < source.size(); i++) {
    if (i % 5 != 0) {
        live.set(i);
    }
}

docs.title: Compacting into several outputs (sharding)
docs.text:
A compaction that splits its output, such as one writing each token range to its own file, can run as N separate compactions, one per output, each over all the sources with only that output's nodes marked live. That repeats per output what does not depend on the output: every one of them trains the codebooks again, on its own slice. A sharded compaction session does it once: the compactor is built over everything that may be written, and each shard is merged by its own compactShard call, with that shard's nodes as the live set. The codebooks are trained by the first shard that needs them, on the live nodes of every shard together, and reused by the rest.

// liveNodes: the live nodes of ALL the shards together
var compactor = new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, VectorSimilarityFunction.COSINE, null);
var session = compactor.sharded();

// shardNLiveNodes: per source, the nodes of shard N, a subset of liveNodes
List<OrdinalMapper> shard0 = session.compactShard(shard0LiveNodes, output0);   // shard0.get(s).oldToNew(n): ordinal of source s's node n in output0, or OMITTED
List<OrdinalMapper> shard1 = session.compactShard(shard1LiveNodes, output1);   // every shard has its own mapping

Shards may become known one at a time (each output is closed as its rows arrive); the session does nothing until the first call. Sources that ship a compressed sidecar use the compactShard overload that also takes the compressed path. Each shard is otherwise an ordinary merge of its own nodes: its upper layers, cells, ordinals and merge store are its own, and its cost follows its node count. Since a shard holds a small part of every source, each source is sparse in it; see "Sparse sources" below.

Measured on two 1M-node sources (1024 dimensions, cosine, degree 32) split into M shards by a hash of the row, total wall time and recall@10 over all shards (8 cores):

M one compaction per shard, retained same-source edges only one session, same-source join off one session rebuild of every shard 4 454 s, 0.781 566 s, 0.825 876 s, 0.836 16 981 s, 0.823 300 s, 0.821 567 s, 0.894 946 s, 0.903 64 1203 s, 0.875 335 s, 0.875 627 s, 0.945 886 s, 0.947

Training once removes the growth with M (the two codebooks take 43 s once instead of about 14 s per shard at M = 64); the same-source join costs about as much again as the rest of the merge and brings the recall to within a point of a rebuild.

docs.title: Ordinal assignment
docs.text: Each source assigns its own local ordinals. The compactor merges the upper layers first (see "Hierarchical Levels"), then builds the output mapping: sources in ascending-size order, and within a source by the level-1 node of the merged hierarchy each node descends to (an exact greedy descent through the merged upper layers, refined by a width-8 beam over level 1, keyed by a breadth-first walk position over the merged level-1 graph). When no source has an upper layer there are no cells, and level 0 falls back to the graph search.

docs.title: PQ Retraining
docs.text: If the sources carry PQ (FusedPQ, or a compressed sidecar), the compactor retrains the Product Quantization codebook on the combined dataset and re-encodes every live node for the output. This is done by PQRetrainer, which performs balanced proportional sampling across all sources (up to ProductQuantization.MAX_PQ_TRAINING_SET_SIZE vectors total, at least 1000 per source). The merge itself does not run on these codes: whatever the sources carry, it runs on the vectors (see "The merge store" below), so the input type determines the output format and nothing else.

docs.title: Neighbor Selection (per node)
docs.text:
For each live node at each graph level, the compactor gathers a candidate neighbor pool and then applies diversity selection:

1. Gather from same source (gatherFromSameSource)\ Iterate the node's existing neighbors in its source index. Filter out deleted nodes. Score each with the similarity function. No graph search — neighbors are already precomputed.

2. Gather from other sources (gatherFromOtherSource)\ Keep the top searchTopK candidates per larger target, scored exactly: at level 0 through the cell join described below, at the upper levels through a graph search of the target. The graph search also stands in at level 0 for a node without a cell; when the target carries PQ codes the traversal scores through them and the top candidates are rescored exactly, otherwise the traversal is exact.

searchTopK  = max(2,  ceil(degree / numSources) * 4)
  • Level 0 uses pair-asymmetric cross-linking. Sources are processed smallest first, one source at a time. A node gathers candidates only from the sources larger than its own, through the cell join. Every candidate is also offered back to the node it found, with its exact score: since similarity is symmetric, the offer is exactly the candidate that node's own scan of the smaller source would have produced. Each node holds up to 16 offer slots, kept in a banded, spill-to-disk buffer so peak memory is independent of node count. When a source's turn comes, its nodes union the offers they received with their retained same-source edges and their own candidates before diversity selection. The largest source gathers nothing itself; a node of it that received no offers keeps its retained edges unchanged and skips selection entirely.
  • Level L > 0: the compactor first descends greedily from the source's entry point through each level above L (one searchOneLayer call with topK=1 per level, feeding the result into the next via setEntryPointsFromPreviousLayer()), then performs the full beam search at level L. This mirrors standard HNSW construction and gives a much better starting point than jumping directly to level L from the global entry node.

Sparse sources: the same-source join\ Step 1 keeps only the live neighbours, and nothing replaces the dead ones. That is the right economy while most of a source is live, since the source's own graph already holds its same-source edges. It fails when a source's live nodes are a minority, which is every source of a shard (a shard of M keeps 1/M of each): a node then keeps degree × live fraction of its same-source edges, and the output is close to bipartite between the sources. So in a sharded compaction a source with fewer than half of its nodes live is also searched for the node's own neighbours, exactly as another source is: at level 0 it is one more target of the cell walk (the largest source, which otherwise scans nothing, scans itself), at the upper levels and in merges without cells one more graph search. The node itself and the neighbours it retained are dropped from the result, and no reverse offers are made within a source, since every node of it runs the same scan. An ordinary compact never joins a source with itself, however many of its nodes are deleted: its cost and output are unchanged by this.

3. Diversity selection (Vamana-style)\ Candidates are sorted by exact score (descending). The compactor selects up to maxDegree diverse neighbors using an adaptive alpha. At level 0 the pairwise comparisons between a candidate and the already-selected neighbours run on vectors decoded from the wide code (below), and the candidate's pruning threshold is recomputed against the node from the same decoded vector, so both sides of the inequality carry the same quantization bias; the ordering itself always uses the exact scores.

for alpha in [1.0, 1.2]:
    for each candidate c (highest score first):
        if c is already selected: skip
        if ∀ selected neighbor j: similarity(c, j) ≤ score(c) × alpha:
            select c
    if |selected| == maxDegree: stop

docs.title: Cell join
docs.text: With an upper layer in any source, level-0 candidates come from a scan rather than a search. The output ordinals group every source's nodes by the level-1 node of the merged hierarchy they descend to, their cell — every source's level-1 nodes are cells, so the partition is as fine as the merged index's own level 1; each source's nodes of a cell form a contiguous ordinal range, so their vectors are contiguous in the merge store (the inverted lists of an IVF index whose centroids are the merged level-1 nodes). Level 0 is processed in ranges of consecutive ordinals: for each node of a range a width-64 beam over the merged level-1 graph, seeded at the node's own cell, picks its probe cells (at most 4,096 members per larger source, best cells first; the beam is wide because the merged cells are small, and it must rank enough of them to fill the budget); the range's (cell, node) pairs are then inverted so that each probed cell of each larger source is streamed once and every vector in it is scored against all the range's nodes that probe it (eight queries per pass, the queries kept in L1), keeping each node's best searchTopK by exact score. Survivors enter the unchanged pipeline (reverse offers, diversity, write). Nodes without a cell, and merges where no source has an upper layer, use the graph search.

docs.title: The merge store
docs.text: Before level 0 is written, every live vector is copied once into a scratch region of the output file at its output ordinal (4 × dimension bytes per node; truncated away when the merge finishes). The cell scan streams it, and survivors, retained edges and offered candidates take their vectors from it, so no source record is read for a candidate during level 0 and every score the output is written from is exact. Outputs that carry PQ (FusedPQ, or a sidecar) get a second cache from the same pass holding the retrained codes by output ordinal: record writes copy neighbour codes from it instead of re-encoding per edge, and for sidecar sources (compact(graphPath, compressedPath)) it becomes the merged compressed vectors file.

docs.title: Wide code
docs.text: The compactor also trains a product quantization with four dimensions per subspace (max(8, dimension / 4) subspaces of 256 centroids, capped at the dimension: 192 bytes per node at 768 dimensions) and encodes every live node into a third cache in the same pass. It serves one purpose: the pairwise diversity comparisons at level 0, where a candidate's vector is decoded from its code rather than read from the merge store, so a node's selection touches one row per candidate instead of one per (candidate, neighbour) pair. Candidate scores against the node stay exact. The coarser code also collapses near-duplicates onto one code, which the diversity rule then prunes, so the degree is spent on distinct neighbours; a finer two-dimensional code kept them apart and merged to lower recall.

docs.title: Hierarchical Levels
docs.text:
Level 0 (base layer) stores inline vectors, FusedPQ codes, and the neighbor list. Upper levels store only the neighbor list (plus PQ codes at level 1 for cross-level searching).

The upper layers are merged before level 0: for each live upper-layer node the compactor keeps its retained same-source edges, adds candidates from a greedy descent and a beam search in every other source's upper layers, and diversity-selects the result. The merged lists are held in memory (a few per cent of the nodes) until the ordinals exist, and the merged level 1 — every source's level-1 nodes with their merged edges — is the cell hierarchy the ordinal assignment and the cell join run on. Its adjacency and the levels above it stay on the heap; the level-1 vectors (about 3 % of the dataset) are written once to a file beside the output and read through a read-only mapping, so they are page cache rather than a fixed heap cost. They are written after level 0.

Processing is batched per source and run in parallel across sources using a ForkJoinPool. A backpressure window keeps at most taskWindowSize batches in-flight at once, bounding memory use.

docs.title: Entry Node
docs.text: The output's max level is the highest level that still has a live node: a merged level that came out empty (a shard, or a heavily deleted source, can miss every node of the sources' top levels) is dropped. The entry node of the compacted graph is: 1. The designated entry node of the first source that reaches the output's max level, if it is live. 2. Otherwise, the first live node found at that level, scanning those sources in order.

docs.title: Benchmarking
docs.text: Use CompactorBenchmark (in benchmarks-jmh) to measure compaction performance. See benchmarks-jmh/src/main/java/io/github/jbellis/jvector/bench/CompactorBenchmark.md for full instructions.

docs.title: Default: partition and compact in one run
docs.text:
Adjust -Xmx to fit the dataset in memory (e.g., 220g for large datasets).

java -Xmx220g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector \
  -cp benchmarks-jmh/target/compactor-benchmark.jar \
  io.github.jbellis.jvector.bench.CompactorBenchmark \
  -p workloadMode=PARTITION_AND_COMPACT \
  -p datasetNames=<dataset> \
  -p numPartitions=4 \
  -p splitDistribution=UNIFORM \
  -p indexPrecision=FUSEDPQ \
  -wi 0 -i 1 -f 1

docs.title: Measuring the heap memory footprint
docs.text:
To measure compaction's true heap footprint — without the dataset occupying heap — run the two steps separately.

Note: measureRecall defaults to true. With the default, even COMPACT mode loads the dataset's query vectors and ground truth and runs a search after compacting, which adds heap usage. Set -p measureRecall=false so the heap reflects only the compactor itself.

Step 1: build partitions (dataset in memory, large heap required)

java -Xmx220g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector \
  -cp benchmarks-jmh/target/compactor-benchmark.jar \
  io.github.jbellis.jvector.bench.CompactorBenchmark \
  -p workloadMode=PARTITION \
  -p datasetNames=<dataset> \
  -p numPartitions=4 \
  -p splitDistribution=UNIFORM \
  -p indexPrecision=FUSEDPQ \
  -wi 0 -i 1 -f 1

Step 2: compact only (dataset not loaded; use a small heap to measure the compactor's footprint)

java -Xmx5g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector \
  -cp benchmarks-jmh/target/compactor-benchmark.jar \
  io.github.jbellis.jvector.bench.CompactorBenchmark \
  -p workloadMode=COMPACT \
  -p measureRecall=false \
  -p datasetNames=<dataset> \
  -p numPartitions=4 \
  -p splitDistribution=UNIFORM \
  -p indexPrecision=FUSEDPQ \
  -wi 0 -i 1 -f 1

COMPACT with measureRecall=false skips dataset loading entirely, so -Xmx5g is sufficient even for large datasets. This confirms that the compactor itself — not the dataset — drives heap usage.

Key workloadMode values:

Mode Description PARTITION_AND_COMPACT (default) Build partitions, compact them PARTITION Build N partition indexes and exit; use before COMPACT COMPACT Compact existing partitions BUILD Build one index over the full dataset

Results are written as JSONL to target/benchmark-results/compactor-*/compactor-results.jsonl. The durationMs field records only the compaction time (not dataset loading or JVM startup). When measureRecall=true, each result also includes recall, avgSearchLatencyMs, and p99SearchLatencyMs from searching the compacted graph.

Comparison against build-from-scratch (results averaged over three runs).

  • Build from scratch: build with PQ, search using FusedPQ with FP reranking.
  • Compaction: build source partitions with PQ, compact using FusedPQ with FP rescoring, search using FusedPQ with FP reranking. Source partitions are based on a Fibonacci distribution with 4 partitions.
Dataset Dim Build from Scratch Compaction Delta cap-6M 768 0.626 0.619 -0.008 cap-1M 768 0.656 0.656 0.000 gecko-100k 768 0.690 0.701 +0.011 e5-small-v2-100k 384 0.572 0.586 +0.014 ada002-1M 1536 0.687 0.703 +0.016 e5-base-v2-100k 768 0.676 0.692 +0.016 cohere-english-v3-10M 1024 0.544 0.561 +0.017 e5-large-v2-100k 1024 0.686 0.703 +0.017 ada002-100k 1536 0.751 0.769 +0.018 cohere-english-v3-1M 1024 0.593 0.612 +0.019

docs.title: Heap memory footprint
docs.text: All datasets above can be compacted under COMPACT with measureRecall=false and -Xmx5g. In addition, compaction successfully scales to a dataset with 2560 dimensions and 10M vectors under the same heap constraint.

docs.title: Deferred batch serialization
docs.text: The parallel graph writer can serialize complete layer-zero records into bounded worker buffers. Each record contains its ordinal, inline features, neighbor count, and adjacency list. By default, a worker writes up to 64 complete records together. The final partial batch is written without adding records or padding to the format. This preserves the V6 layout and existing readers.

docs.title: Production sources
docs.text: The library writer does not depend on Grid, BenchYAML, dataset preloading, or

docs.title: 744's buffered-access API. It accepts the existing
docs.text:
Map<FeatureId, IntFunction<Feature.State>>: callers supply feature states for the requested original ordinals from their own source. That source can be resident vectors, a database's flush/compaction source, or another source; it must support concurrent supplier calls and remain available through final serialization. The writer does not require the original dataset to be fully resident.

Complete-record batching also applies when all input vectors are preloaded. Its benefits come from deferring per-insertion feature writes and grouping final writes, independently of how input vectors are loaded. Buffered range access is an optional Grid integration, not a prerequisite for the core writer.

docs.title: Caller migration: early writes versus deferred batches
docs.text:
Use the parallel writer when deferring NVQ/FP encoding to final serialization. A sequential final writer performs that encoding on one thread and can regress construction time. Sequential callers should retain encoding during insertion and writeFeaturesInline.

Both examples assume the same trained nvq, graph builder, node count, writerWorkers, and output path. The builder's construction scoring is unchanged; its peer vectors are supplied separately. vectorForOrdinal is the application's lookup of an original input vector, not a harness loader.

docs.title: Old: write each inline feature during insertion
docs.text:
try (var writer = new OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter.Builder(builder.getGraph(), outputPath)
        .withParallelWorkerThreads(writerWorkers)
        .withMapper(new OrdinalMapper.IdentityMapper(count - 1))
        .with(new NVQ(nvq))
        .build()) {
    for (int ordinal = 0; ordinal < count; ordinal++) {
        var vector = vectorForOrdinal.apply(ordinal);
        builder.addGraphNode(ordinal, vector);
        writer.writeFeaturesInline(ordinal, Feature.singleState(
                FeatureId.NVQ_VECTORS, new NVQ.State(nvq.encode(vector))));
    }
    builder.cleanup();
    writer.write(Map.of()); // Preserve the earlier feature writes; add adjacency.
}

docs.title: New: supply the features when writing the completed graph
docs.text:
for (int ordinal = 0; ordinal < count; ordinal++) {
    builder.addGraphNode(ordinal, vectorForOrdinal.apply(ordinal));
}
builder.cleanup();

try (var writer = new OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter.Builder(builder.getGraph(), outputPath)
        .withParallelWorkerThreads(writerWorkers)
        .withMapper(new OrdinalMapper.IdentityMapper(count - 1))
        .with(new NVQ(nvq))
        .build()) {
    writer.write(Feature.singleStateFactory(FeatureId.NVQ_VECTORS,
            ordinal -> new NVQ.State(nvq.encode(vectorForOrdinal.apply(ordinal)))));
}

The second call supplies NVQ payloads during final serialization, together with adjacency, in batches of up to 64 complete records. No writeFeaturesInline pass is needed. The same pattern works for FP using InlineVectors and InlineVectors.State, or another supported inline feature. Supply every configured inline feature to obtain complete-record batching, including fused PQ if configured.

Final suppliers run concurrently. vectorForOrdinal must remain available through write and provide independent borrowed vectors per worker, or stable vectors. For an existing RandomAccessVectorValues, threadLocalSupplier() supplies those independent views; it does not require buffered hooks. A caller can instead return already encoded feature states from its own storage, without retaining original FP vectors for this write.

Integrations that already call write with every inline feature supplier receive batching when using the parallel writer. Integrations that write features early must move those calls to final suppliers to use the deferred path. The incremental API remains compatible: a one-pass source whose values cannot be obtained again must retain encoded states for final writing or continue using incremental writes.

docs.title: Batch size and memory
docs.text:
The default is 64 records. To override it, call withParallelBatchSize(records) before with(...) on either OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter.Builder or RandomAccessOnDiskGraphIndexWriter.Builder. The value must be positive. Each active worker holds one buffer of recordSize * records bytes; feature encoders and vector sources have their own memory costs. No dataset-sized output buffer is allocated.

The unified RandomAccessOnDiskGraphIndexWriter.Builder retains its existing parallel/sequential selection. Setting the batch size does not enable parallel writing, and is ignored by the sequential writer. A caller-supplied executor remains caller-owned and must outlive the write.

docs.title: Dataset prefetching in Grid
docs.text:
For a parallel write, Grid supplies NVQ or FP32 features after cleanup. Final serialization suppliers consume worker-local ranges through VectorAccess.openRange. Sources implementing the buffered-access capability use that implementation; ordinary sources retain the ordinary-access fallback. Borrowed vectors are consumed before advancing a cursor, and ranges are released after the workers finish.

This integrates with #744's optional useDatasetPrefetching setting. It does not change construction scoring, quantization parameters, or the query path. Production integrations can opt into deferred serialization by supplying their features at the final write; their existing vector-source and incremental-write APIs remain valid.

docs.title: Running the benchmark writer paths
docs.text:
Select construction.writerMode in the BenchYAML index parameters. The default is parallel. Both writer modes serialize the graph after cleanup.

Grid sizes its writer pool from PhysicalCoreExecutor; no machine-specific worker count is embedded in this change. Dataset prefetching is a separate optional setting in the index YAML. An ordinary preloaded dataset can use the same deferred writer.

This default applies only to the benchmark entry points. The library's unified writer builder retains its existing sequential default, and application callers still explicitly choose parallel writing. Code calling Grid directly can select its writer through GraphIndexBuilderConfig.getInstance().setParallelBuild(...).

docs.title: Fused and separated layouts
docs.text:
An on-disk JVector index stores up to two kinds of vector data next to the graph, and each can be placed in more than one way:

  • Traversal codes (ASH or PQ) can be fused into the graph or kept separate.
  • Reranking vectors (FP32 or NVQ) can be inline in each node's record or separated into their own block.

These choices decide what must be in memory, how large the index file is, and how much a query reads from disk. They do not change the graph itself, so the same graph can be written either way.

docs.title: Traversal codes: fused or separate
docs.text:
Fused Separate Where the codes live In each node's record, next to its neighbor list: the codes of that node's neighbors One code per vector, held in memory (PQVectors, ASHVectors), optionally saved to a file beside the index Memory for codes None beyond the page cache Every code: vector count × code bytes Index size on disk Adds degree × code bytes per node Adds nothing to the graph; a codes file adds code bytes per node Reads per expanded node One record gives the neighbors and their codes One record for the neighbors; codes come from memory Writer feature FusedASH, FusedPQ (FeatureId.FUSED_ASH, FUSED_PQ) None in the graph; write codes with CompressedVectors.write and load them with ASHVectors.load or PQVectors.load Limits Fused ASH: 1–9 bits per dimension, fastest at 1, 2 and 4; fused PQ: 256 clusters per subspace; needs an FP32 or NVQ reranker in the graph Works with ASH, PQ and BQ

Choose fused when memory is the constraint: the codes cost no memory, and each disk read during traversal brings the codes it needs. This is the default in the benchmark tools.

Choose separate when the codes fit in memory and disk space or write volume matters more: the index file is much smaller, because each code is stored once instead of once per incoming edge, and traversal scores neighbors from memory without reading their codes from disk. Streaming indexes (StreamingASHIndex) already hold one code per vector, so they are usually flushed this way; BenchYAML's streaming cases write those codes beside the flushed index and load them when the index is opened.

As a rough guide, fused codes add degree × code bytes to every record. At degree 32 with 128-byte codes that is 4 KB per node, more than the rest of a typical record; see Memory and disk sizing.

docs.title: Reranking vectors: inline or separated
docs.text:
Inline Separated Where the vectors live In each node's record (InlineVectors, NVQ) In one contiguous block of the index file, after the node records (SeparatedVectors, SeparatedNVQ) Node record size Graph + codes + reranking vector Graph + codes only Reading a reranking vector Comes with the node's record A separate read at a fixed offset in the vector block

Inline is the common choice and what the examples use: a record read for any reason also brings its reranking vector, and page-aligned records keep each read to one page.

Separated keeps node records small, so traversal touches less data per node and more of the graph fits in the page cache; each reranked candidate then costs one read from the vector block. Consider it when records are large (high dimension, FP32 reranking) and the rerank depth is small compared with the nodes a search expands. Measure both on your data before committing.

Fused ASH, stored ASH codes and page-aligned records require on-disk format version 7, which JVector 4.0.x cannot read; see UPGRADING.md.

docs.title: Common layouts
docs.text:
Layout In memory On disk per node Notes Fused ASH or PQ + inline NVQ Graph's upper layers Neighbors, neighbors' codes, NVQ vector Default for indexes served from disk; see Larger-than-memory indexes Separate ASH or PQ codes + inline NVQ All codes Neighbors, NVQ vector Smallest file with accurate reranking; codes must fit in memory Separate codes + inline FP32 All codes Neighbors, full vector Exact final scores; largest records Separate codes + separated NVQ or FP32 All codes Neighbors only, plus the vector block Smallest traversal reads

See Choosing an index for picking the quantizer and reranker, and the example configurations for ready-to-run fused and separate layouts.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
JVector is published to Maven Central as io.github.jbellis:jvector:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.jbellis</groupId>
  <artifactId>jvector</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.0-rc.1</version>
</dependency>

With Gradle: implementation("io.github.jbellis:jvector:4.1.0-rc.1"). The library runs on Java 11 and newer; ASH requires 4.1.0-rc.1 or later.

docs.title: Enable SIMD
docs.text:
Run your application with these JVM options so JVector can use the Vector API and its native kernels:

--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector
--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED

On Java 22 and later JVector prefers its native library (bundled for Linux x86-64 and AArch64), on Java 20 and 21 it uses the Panama Vector API, and older runtimes use plain Java. Building and installing explains each backend and how to check which one is in use.

docs.title: Build and search an index
docs.text:
This builds an in-memory graph over a set of vectors and finds the ten nearest neighbors of a query:

RandomAccessVectorValues vectors = ...;           // your vectors
VectorSimilarityFunction similarity = VectorSimilarityFunction.DOT_PRODUCT;
VectorFloat<?> query = ...;

try (var builder = GraphIndexBuilder.builder(vectors, similarity, 32)   // max degree
             .withBeamWidth(100)
             .withNeighborOverflow(1.2f)
             .withAlpha(1.2f)
             .build();
     var graph = builder.build(vectors)) {
    SearchResult result = GraphSearcher.search(query, 10, vectors, similarity, graph, Bits.ALL);
    for (var match : result.getNodes()) {
        System.out.printf("vector %d  score %.6f%n", match.node, match.score);
    }
}

The complete program is HelloVectorWorld. It downloads a small public dataset on first use; the examples README shows how to build and run it and the other hello-world programs, including HelloASHWorld, which writes a compressed on-disk index and searches it.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Tutorial 1: the building blocks (vectors, graphs, searchers).
  2. Tutorial 2: writing an index to disk and searching it.
  3. Tutorial 3: compressed vectors and reranking for indexes larger than memory.
  4. Int8Example: building, writing and searching an index of signed int8 vectors (mvn compile exec:exec@tutorial -Dtutorial=int8 -pl jvector-examples -am).
  5. Choosing an index and Tuning for production settings.

docs.title: Graph construction
docs.text: JVector builds a Vamana-style graph (the algorithm behind DiskANN): each new node searches the graph for its nearest neighbors, keeps a diverse subset of them, and links back to them. On top of that base layer it can add an HNSW-style hierarchy. Construction is concurrent and incremental: many threads can insert at once, and a graph can keep growing after it is first searched.

docs.title: Ways to build
docs.text:
Approach API Use it when Batch builder.build(vectors) All vectors are available up front; inserts them in parallel and cleans up Incremental builder.addGraphNode(node, ...) from any number of threads, then builder.cleanup() Vectors arrive over time, or you control the threads; markNodeDeleted and cleanup remove nodes Streaming ASH StreamingASHIndex A database's live index: build and search while vectors arrive, holding only the graph and ASH codes, and move to newer ASH models without rebuilding Merge OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor Combine several on-disk indexes into one; see Compaction Continue a graph GraphIndexBuilder.builder(scoreProvider, dimension, existingGraph) Add to a graph that was built or loaded earlier

cleanup() must run before a graph is written or handed to readers: it removes deleted nodes, optionally refines the graph (below) and trims every neighbor list back to the maximum degree.

StreamingASHIndex can start with a trained model or cold. A cold index records the vectors it is given and answers searches by scoring them exactly, while it keeps a uniform sample. Once enough have arrived it trains its first model on the sample (or fixes a random projection), then inserts the recorded vectors into its graph while new inserts continue; inserts never wait for training. Later models re-encode the codes page by page; the graph is never rebuilt.

docs.title: What construction scores with
docs.text:
Every insertion is a search, so the representation used for scoring sets much of the build's speed and memory.

Scoring Provider Memory Notes Full vectors BuildScoreProvider.randomAccessScoreProvider (or builder(vectors, similarity, M)) The vectors, unless read from a file-backed source Exact scores; simplest Int8 vectors BuildScoreProvider.byteVectorScoreProvider (or builder(byteVectors, ByteVectorSimilarityFunction, M)) The signed int8 vectors, one byte per dimension Exact scores; no compression. Write the index with the InlineByteVectors feature (format version 7) PQ codes BuildScoreProvider.pqBuildScoreProvider PQ codes Builds under a memory limit; see Tutorial 3 BQ codes BuildScoreProvider.bqBuildScoreProvider BQ codes Cheapest scoring, coarsest graph ASH codes, symmetric BuildScoreProvider.ashBuildScoreProvider, inserting with provider.searchProviderFor(node) ASH codes Compares stored codes with each other; needs neither the source vectors nor query projection during insertion. The fastest ASH option ASH codes, asymmetric ashBuildScoreProvider, inserting with the original vector ASH codes, plus each inserted vector while it is inserted Scores the original vector against codes

ASH graph construction lists every ASH scoring policy, and Larger-than-memory indexes shows a complete symmetric build that streams vectors from a file.

docs.title: Hierarchical or flat
docs.text:
Hierarchical (default) Flat Layers A base layer with every node, plus upper layers holding a random, shrinking sample of nodes, as in HNSW The base layer only Where a search starts The top layer's entry node; each layer narrows the start for the next One fixed entry node (the first node inserted) Final refinement Available (refineFinalGraph) Not run: refinement applies only to graphs with upper layers On disk Upper layers are loaded into memory; the base layer can stay on disk Nothing extra to load

Each node's top layer is drawn at random, so the number of nodes in each upper layer falls by about a factor of the degree per layer, and the upper layers add little memory. Searches start closer to the query's region, so they usually take fewer steps. Keep the hierarchy unless you have measured that a flat graph does as well on your data.

Hierarchy and refinement are set JVM-wide through GraphIndexBuilderConfig (also exposed over JMX), or per builder through the deprecated constructors that take addHierarchy and refineFinalGraph. In BenchYAML they are addHierarchy and refineFinalGraph, and upperLayerDegree sets a different maximum degree for the upper layers; in the API, GraphIndexBuilder.builder(scoreProvider, dimension, maxDegrees) takes one degree per layer.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Degree, beam width, neighbor overflow and alpha trade build time and size against recall; see Tuning construction and search.

docs.title: Building and serving larger-than-memory indexes
docs.text:
An index is larger than memory when its on-disk graph does not fit in the memory left for the operating system's page cache. Construction then has to avoid holding the source vectors, and each query reads graph nodes from storage. This guide covers sizing, construction, the record layout on disk, and query settings for that case. It applies to any on-disk graph; the examples use fused ASH traversal codes with NVQ reranking, the layout that keeps the most of a search on one node read.

The larger-than-memory BenchYAML example runs the same pipeline.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
Disk. Each base-layer node is one record:

Part Bytes Node id 4 Fused ASH codes degree × code bytes, where code bytes = encodedBits / 8 NVQ vector 4 + the sum over subvectors of (subvector dimensions + 28); dimensions + 60 with two subvectors Full-precision vector, if stored inline 4 × dimensions Neighbor count and neighbor list 4 × (degree + 1)

Page alignment can add padding (see below). Upper graph layers and the header add little. Multiply the record size by the vector count for the index size.

Memory for construction. Symmetric ASH construction keeps the graph's neighbor lists and every node's ASH code in memory, not the source vectors. At degree 32 with neighbor overflow 1.2, the neighbor lists take about 430 bytes per node on the Java heap; add the code bytes per node. Size -Xmx with headroom above that, and leave the rest of memory to the page cache.

Memory for queries. Searches read node records through the page cache. The more of the index the cache holds, the fewer reads reach the device, so query throughput rises with memory even when the index does not fit.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
Construction streams the source vectors in order, trains ASH, encodes every vector, builds the graph by comparing codes, and writes the index in one parallel pass:

var pool = PhysicalCoreExecutor.pool();
int b = 2, d = 368;                                   // choose b and d with the record size in mind
var ash = AsymmetricHashing.initialize(vectors, VectorSimilarityFunction.DOT_PRODUCT, AsymmetricHashing.ITQ,
        AsymmetricHashing.HEADER_BITS + b * d, 1, b, pool);
var mean = new VectorMean(vectors.size(), vectors.dimension());
var codes = ash.encodeAll(mean.duringScan(vectors), pool);
var nvq = NVQuantization.create(mean.mean(), 2);

var scores = BuildScoreProvider.ashBuildScoreProvider(codes);
try (var builder = new GraphIndexBuilder(scores, vectors.dimension(), 32, 100, 1.2f, 1.2f, true, true)) {
    pool.submit(() -> IntStream.range(0, vectors.size()).parallel()
            .forEach(node -> builder.addGraphNode(node, scores.searchProviderFor(node)))).join();
    builder.cleanup();

    var source = vectors.threadLocalSupplier();
    try (var views = ExplicitThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> builder.getGraph().getView());
         var writer = new OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter.Builder(builder.getGraph(), path)
                 .withParallelWorkerThreads(PhysicalCoreExecutor.getPhysicalCoreCount())
                 .withMapper(new OrdinalMapper.IdentityMapper(vectors.size() - 1))
                 .with(new FusedASH(32, ash)).with(new NVQ(nvq))
                 .withPageAlignment(4096)
                 .build()) {
        System.out.println(writer.describeRecordLayout());
        writer.write(Map.of(
                FeatureId.FUSED_ASH, node -> new FusedASH.State(views.get(), codes, node),
                FeatureId.NVQ_VECTORS, node -> new NVQ.State(nvq.encode(source.get().getVector(node)))));
    }
}
  • Streaming input. Open the base vectors as a file-backed source (FvecFileVectorValues) so they are read on demand. Scans such as encoding use contiguous ranges with bounded read-ahead; see Batched input vector access.
  • Symmetric scoring. ashBuildScoreProvider scores stored codes against each other, so insertion needs neither source vectors nor query projection.
  • Deferred features. The parallel writer asks for the NVQ vectors while it writes each record, so they are encoded during the write instead of being held for every node; see Deferred batch serialization.
  • Threads. Graph insertion mostly waits on memory and gains from a second hardware thread per core; see Thread budgets.

docs.title: Page-aligned records
docs.text:
A query reads one record per node it expands. When a record crosses a page boundary, that read costs two page reads from the device instead of one. withPageAlignment(pageBytes) on any graph writer builder places records so none crosses a page boundary:

  • Records that fit in a page are packed as many per page as fit, with the remainder of each page left empty.
  • A record larger than a page starts on a page and is padded to whole pages, but only when its last page would be at least half full. Otherwise the padding would cost most of a page per record while saving a small fraction of a page read, and the index is written unaligned.
  • The header is padded to whole pages, so the first record starts on a page boundary. Pages are counted from the start of the file, so an index written after other data in the same file lines up too.

describeRecordLayout() on the writer reports the record size, the placement and the padding, or why a requested alignment was not applied. Alignment needs format version 7, changes no search results, and is opt-in; without it records are packed back to back as before. Use the page size of the storage stack, normally 4096.

Alignment pays most when a record nearly fills a whole number of pages. A record just over a page boundary gains little and costs nearly a page of padding; reduce it below the boundary instead, with fewer ASH bits or a lower degree. For example, at 768 dimensions with degree 32 and NVQ with two subvectors, 776 encoded bits (368 dimensions at 2 bits) give a 4,068-byte record that fits one 4 KB page, while 808 bits (384 dimensions) give 4,196 bytes, just over it.

Compaction does not yet accept page-aligned indexes.

docs.title: Serving queries
docs.text:
A query from disk makes one dependent read after another: it reads a node, chooses the next, then reads again. Its latency is roughly the page reads per query times the device's read latency, and the CPU is mostly idle. Throughput is then limited by the device's random-read rate:

queries per second ≈ device random reads per second ÷ page reads per query

For example, a device rated at 268,000 random 4 KiB reads per second serving queries that make 100 page reads each tops out near 2,700 queries per second, however many cores are available. Page alignment, memory for the page cache, a lower degree, and less overquery all reduce page reads per query.

Settings for search that waits on storage:

  • Searches in flight. Run more searches at once than there are cores, so others proceed while some wait on reads. Throughput rises with searches in flight until the device reaches its read limit; past that, more searches only add latency. Measure a range such as 1, 2, 4 and 8 searches per core.
  • Admission. Admit one request per worker. A request waiting behind a busy worker adds that wait to its latency and adds no throughput.
  • Batching. Use a maximum batch of 1. Preparing several ASH queries together saves microseconds of CPU; holding queries for a batch costs more.
  • Precision and batch size in code. Set them on the model right after opening the index, before the first query:
var ash = ((FusedASH) index.getFeatures().get(FeatureId.FUSED_ASH)).getASH();
ash.setQueryOptions(ASHQueryProjection.AUTO, 1);

Integrating ASH queries into a database covers bounded admission and executor ownership; ASH configuration and defaults lists the JVM settings.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
Two independent conditions decide what a measurement shows:

  • Cold queries: held-out queries, each presented once to a JVM whose JIT compilation has already settled on other inputs. A query set that repeats finds the pages its earlier passes cached and runs at memory speed, which a service does not see for new queries.
  • Cold index: the index starts outside the page cache, so search reads it from storage. Warmup then caches the pages it touches, so it should use inputs that favor no measured query, such as a sample of base vectors.
