  • Recall within ~0.006 of main

docs.title: This PR is a fix for an issue in how file sizes were calculated by the JVector test harness, i.e. BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML.
Problem 1: The index cache directory accumulates across runs
docs.text: In Grid.runOneGraph (and runAllAndCollectResults), BenchmarkDiagnostics monitors two directories: diagnostics.startMonitoring("testDirectory", workDirectory); diagnostics.startMonitoring("indexCache", Paths.get(indexCacheDir)); // "index_cache/" getTotalBytes() sums both. The index_cache/ directory is persistent — it is never wiped between runs. So the reported disk figure grows monotonically across the run, regardless of which configuration is under test. The delta between a fused-PQ run and a non-fused-PQ run is invisible.

docs.title: Problem 2: Even within a single run, the snapshot captures all feature sets, not just one
docs.text:
When multiple feature sets are built in the same runOneGraph call, the directory total covers all of them. You can't attribute disk usage to a specific configuration from that number.

There is even a TODO in the code acknowledging this at line 233: // TODO this does not capture disk usage for cached indexes. Need to update

docs.title: The fix
docs.text:
Rather than directory-level monitoring, measure the specific graph file for each feature set directly after it is written. In buildOnDisk, the path for each feature set's graph file is already computed:

if (handles.containsKey(features)) { graphPath = handles.get(features).writePath(); } else { graphPath = outputDir.resolve("graph" + n++); }

After the build completes, Files.size(graphPath) gives the exact on-disk size for that specific configuration. This value should be returned from buildOnDisk (as part of a result map keyed by feature set) and then included in the BenchResult params or metrics map alongside the other per-configuration numbers.

docs.title: 694.enhancement
docs.text:
Add FloatArray interface to allow easy float[] vector extraction from MemorySegmentVectorFloat and ArrayVectorFloat instances. It solves the problem that we have to: - use explicit typecast to known types (float[], MemorySegment) to figure out what kind of the holder object VectorFloat has - deal with reflection (MemorySegment available in JDK-22 but OpenSearch baseline is JDK-21) or per-element access semantics which is inefficient

The suggestion is to introduce new FloatArray interface to have a fast track float[] array conversion for VectorFloats that support it. The change is 100% non-breaking.

Closes https://github.com/datastax/jvector/issues/696

docs.title: Runtime Configuration for Graph Index Builder (JMX by default, pluggable backend)
docs.text:
Description Introduces GraphIndexBuilderConfig, a managed singleton that exposes GraphIndexBuilder construction parameters as runtime-tunable attributes. Before this change, options such as addHierarchy, refineFinalGraph, and parallelBuild could only be set at the construction call site and required a code change or application restart to modify. With this change, all parameters — graph topology flags, write path selection, build-time compression type, and PQ compression tuning — can be inspected and updated live, without restarting the JVM.

Changes take effect the next time a GraphIndexBuilder is constructed; they do not affect indexes that are already being built or have already been built.

Architecture

GraphIndexBuilderConfig implements GraphIndexBuilderSettings, a plain domain interface with no dependency on JMX or any other transport, and registers itself with ManagementRegistry (package io.github.jbellis.jvector.management). The registry hands the registration to whichever ManagementBackend is active for the JVM. By default, that's JMX: the io.github.jbellis.jvector.management.jmx.JmxManagementBackend wraps GraphIndexBuilderConfig in a javax.management.StandardMBean and registers it with the platform MBeanServer under the object name io.github.jbellis.jvector:type=GraphIndexBuilderConfig — behaviorally identical to prior releases, so JConsole/jmxterm usage below is unchanged. All attributes are stored as volatile fields so writes from a management-backend thread are immediately visible to application threads without additional synchronization. Registration is best-effort throughout this stack: a failure (for example, in a restricted JVM environment) logs a warning but does not disrupt normal operation — the singleton continues to supply its default values.

The management backend is selectable per JVM via the jvector.management.backend system property:

Value Behavior (unset) or jmx JMX (default) — identical to the behavior described below. none No external exposure. GraphIndexBuilderConfig remains fully usable programmatically; nothing is registered with any transport. Use this where JMX is disallowed. a fully-qualified class name A custom io.github.jbellis.jvector.management.spi.ManagementBackend implementation, loaded reflectively (must have a public no-arg constructor).

See docs/admin-service-interfaces.md for the full design.

Managed Attributes

Graph topology

Attribute Type Default Description AddHierarchy boolean true When true, builds HNSW-style hierarchy layers on top of the base Vamana graph. false produces a flat level-0 (plain Vamana) index, which uses less memory and may build faster on small datasets. RefineFinalGraph boolean true When true, runs a second diversity-refinement pass over each node's edges after the initial build. Improves recall at the cost of additional build time.

Write path

Attribute Type Default Description ParallelBuild boolean false When true, serializes level-0 node records concurrently via OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter. Both writers produce an identical on-disk format; switching this flag does not require re-indexing existing data.

Build-time compression

Attribute Type Default Description BuildCompressionType String "NONE" Compression used for scoring during graph construction. Valid values: "NONE" (full-precision), "PQ" (Product Quantization), "BQ" (Binary Quantization).

PQ build compression parameters — consulted only when BuildCompressionType is "PQ"

Attribute Type Default Description PqMFactor int 8 Subspace divisor: the number of PQ subspaces m is computed as dimension / mFactor. Must be a positive integer that evenly divides the vector dimension. PqK int 256 Number of centroids per PQ subspace. Must be positive; conventionally a power of two (256 is the standard value). PqCenterData boolean false When true, globally centers the dataset before PQ cluster training. Recommended for Euclidean similarity; typically not needed for cosine or dot-product. PqAnisotropicThreshold float -1.0 Anisotropic loss threshold for PQ encoding. -1.0 disables anisotropic weighting; positive values bias the quantizer toward directions that matter most for inner-product search.

How to Enable

GraphIndexBuilderConfig is initialized automatically on first access and registers its MBean with the platform MBeanServer. No application code changes are required to activate JMX management — connecting a JMX client to a running JVector process is sufficient.

Programmatic access — read or set values directly from application code:

import io.github.jbellis.jvector.management.GraphIndexBuilderConfig;

GraphIndexBuilderConfig config = GraphIndexBuilderConfig.getInstance();

// Read current values
boolean addHierarchy            = config.isAddHierarchy();
boolean refineFinal             = config.isRefineFinalGraph();
boolean parallelBuild           = config.isParallelBuild();
String  buildCompressionType    = config.getBuildCompressionType(); // "NONE", "PQ", or "BQ"
int     pqMFactor               = config.getPqMFactor();
int     pqK                     = config.getPqK();
boolean pqCenterData            = config.isPqCenterData();
float   pqAnisotropicThreshold  = config.getPqAnisotropicThreshold();

// Update at runtime (affects all subsequent GraphIndexBuilder constructions)
config.setAddHierarchy(false);
config.setParallelBuild(true);

// Switch to PQ build-time compression with custom parameters
config.setBuildCompressionType("PQ");
config.setPqMFactor(4);        // dimension / 4 subspaces
config.setPqK(256);
config.setPqCenterData(true);  // recommended for Euclidean similarity

Non-deprecated constructor — GraphIndexBuilder constructors that do not accept explicit boolean flags read from GraphIndexBuilderConfig at construction time:

// Reads addHierarchy and refineFinalGraph from JMX config
var builder = new GraphIndexBuilder(scoreProvider, dimension, M, beamWidth,
                                    neighborOverflow, alpha);

Constructors that accept explicit flags continue to honor the caller-supplied values and do not consult the singleton, enabling call-site overrides when needed.

Using JConsole

JConsole is the standard JMX browser included with every JDK installation.

  1. Launch JConsole
jconsole

In the connection dialog, select the target JVM process by name or PID and click Connect. If connecting to a remote process, use <host>:<jmxPort> after enabling remote JMX on the target JVM:

-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port=9999
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=false
  1. Navigate to the MBean

Select the MBeans tab. In the left-hand tree expand:

io.github.jbellis.jvector
  └── GraphIndexBuilderConfig
        └── Attributes
  1. Read an attribute

Click on Attributes. The right-hand panel lists all attributes with their current values:

AddHierarchy              true
RefineFinalGraph          true
ParallelBuild             false
BuildCompressionType      NONE
PqMFactor                 8
PqK                       256
PqCenterData              false
PqAnisotropicThreshold    -1.0
  1. Set an attribute

Double-click the value cell next to the attribute you want to change, type the new value (true or false), and press Enter. The change takes effect immediately; the next GraphIndexBuilder constructed in that JVM will use the new value.

Attribute changes are also logged at INFO level by JVector:

INFO  GraphIndexBuilderConfig - JMX: addHierarchy changed true → false

Using jmxterm (command-line alternative)

# Connect to the target JVM by PID
java -jar jmxterm.jar
open <pid>

# Navigate to the MBean
bean io.github.jbellis.jvector:type=GraphIndexBuilderConfig

# Read all attributes
info -b

# Read a specific attribute
get AddHierarchy
get BuildCompressionType

# Set graph topology flags
set AddHierarchy false
set ParallelBuild true

# Switch to PQ build-time compression
set BuildCompressionType PQ
set PqMFactor 4
set PqK 256
set PqCenterData true
set PqAnisotropicThreshold -1.0

Notes

  • The GraphIndexBuilderConfig class is annotated @Experimental. The attribute set and object name may change in a future release.
  • JMX is the default management backend but not the only one: set -Djvector.management.backend=none to disable external exposure entirely (the config remains usable programmatically), or point it at a fully-qualified class name to supply a custom io.github.jbellis.jvector.management.spi.ManagementBackend. See docs/admin-service-interfaces.md.
  • JMX attribute changes are global — they apply to all GraphIndexBuilder instances created after the change in the same JVM. Per-graph overrides are not supported in this release; callers that need per-graph control should pass values explicitly to the appropriate constructor.
  • The parallelBuild attribute requires OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter to be on the classpath (it is part of jvector-base). Both writers produce an identical on-disk format; switching this flag does not require re-indexing existing data.
  • The PQ parameters (PqMFactor, PqK, PqCenterData, PqAnisotropicThreshold) are only consulted when BuildCompressionType is "PQ". Setting them while BuildCompressionType is "NONE" or "BQ" has no effect on the current build but the values are retained and will apply if BuildCompressionType is later changed to "PQ".
  • setBuildCompressionType accepts values case-insensitively ("none", "None", and "NONE" are all valid) and normalizes to the canonical name on storage. It validates immediately and throws IllegalArgumentException for unrecognised strings, so JMX clients receive an error at set time rather than silently at build time.

docs.title: 706.enhancement
docs.text: Resolves #705

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This branch eliminates scattered version-comparison branching (if version >= X, if version < Y, version == Z) from the on-disk graph index read/write path and replaces it with a Strategy + Factory pattern: each supported format version (2–6) gets its own GraphIndexFormat implementation, and GraphIndexFormatFactory centralizes version→format dispatch and detection.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
New abstraction (graph/disk package): - GraphIndexFormat — strategy interface covering header/footer read+write, feature ordering, and full sequential/random-access write orchestration for a single format version. - AbstractGraphIndexFormat — shared default implementation; versions override only what's actually different for them. - GraphIndexFormatV2..GraphIndexFormatV6 — one small class per version, built on a natural inheritance chain (V4 extends V3, V5 extends V4 + footer, V6 extends V5 + feature reordering + fused-PQ support). - GraphIndexFormatFactory — forVersion(int), detectVersion(reader) (magic-number sniffing), getCurrentVersion(). - WriteContext — bundles the ~7 parameters that used to be threaded individually through every serializer method.

Migrated call sites: - AbstractGraphIndexWriter (and its OnDiskSequentialGraphIndexWriter / RandomAccessOnDiskGraphIndexWriter subclasses) now delegate all format-specific work to the resolved GraphIndexFormat instead of branching on version inline. Feature-support validation (Builder.build(), fused-PQ gating) now asks the format (supportsFeature) instead of hardcoding version thresholds. - Header / CommonHeader now delegate header size/read/write and common-header size/read/write to the per-version format, removing the version >= 3 / >= 4 / >= 6 chains that used to live in both classes. - OnDiskGraphIndex load/footer dispatch goes through GraphIndexFormat.loadOnDiskIndex, removing the inline version >= 5 && useFooter branch; the two remaining fused-PQ-layout checks now ask - CompactWriter (streaming N:1 compaction writer) validates once, at construction, that fused PQ is actually supported by the target format; the three per-call version == 6 checks in its hot paths were simplified to the already-existing fusedPQEnabled flag, since this writer only ever targets the current version. No added per-record overhead.

Fixed along the way: - A regression where the writer/reader split silently dropped eager in-memory cache priming (getInMemoryLayers/getInMemoryFeatures) for non-footer format versions — caught by a ramBytesUsed() test failure, fixed by centralizing construction + priming in OnDiskGraphIndex.construct(). - allFeatures() / nonFusedFeatures() helpers now return explicit, frozen EnumSet.of(...) listings instead of deriving from EnumSet.allOf(...) / complementOf(...), so a future FeatureId addition can't silently change what an already-shipped version claims to support.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• New TestGraphIndexFormatFactory: version→format dispatch, unsupported-version rejection, per-version characteristics (supportsMultiLayer, usesFooter, getSupportedFeatures), and magic-number version detection.
  • New TestOnDiskGraphIndex.testVersionRoundTrip: explicit write/read round trips for versions 3, 4, and 5 (single-layer and, for 4/5, multi-layer), in addition to the existing version-2 and current-version (6) coverage.
  • Full jvector-tests suite passes (208 tests, 0 failures).

docs.title: 708.enhancement
docs.text:
This pull request adds comprehensive native C++ unit tests and benchmarks for the SIMD kernel dispatcher and vector similarity functions, and integrates them into the build and CI pipeline. The most important changes are:

Testing and Benchmarking Enhancements:

  • Adds a new test_simd_kernels executable using Google Test, with tests for ISA detection and SIMD kernel correctness, and integrates it into the Meson build and GitHub Actions CI workflow.
  • Adds a new bench_simd_kernels executable using Google Benchmark to micro-benchmark cosine_f32, dot_product_f32, and euclidean_f32 functions at realistic embedding dimensions.

Build System and Code Organization:

  • Moves the core SIMD kernel and dispatcher source files into a src/ subdirectory and updates the Meson build rules and include paths accordingly. The native code layout has been reorganized in preparation for modularizing it into a standalone library, improving structure and maintainability.

CI Improvements:

  • Updates the GitHub Actions workflow to install libgtest-dev, build, and run the new native C++ tests for all relevant ISA tiers, ensuring dispatcher correctness across hardware.

docs.title: Skip jextract binding generation by default
docs.text:
Description

Modifies the process by which maven builds the native SIMD library so that bindings are not generated by default. This change only impacts you if you build jvector from source.

Motivation

The existing build process re-generates the bindings on each build as long as jextract is in the path. This can cause issues since the jextract version on the system may not match the jextract version used to generate the checked-in bindings. This not only creates noise in the git working tree, but can also cause build errors since newer jextract releases may use language features from newer JDKs.

Usage notes

  • jextract_vector_simd.sh is split into two scripts, build_native_lib.sh and jextract_generate_bindings.sh. Bindings are not generated by default during the build process.
  • To force binding generation, set the maven property native.jextract.skip to false at runtime or in the pom. Alternatively, run jextract_generate_bindings.sh directly.
  • If you have multiple jextract versions installed, or if jextract is not installed, you can set the environment variable JEXTRACT_BIN to the full path of the executable.

Example: 

JEXTRACT_BIN="/opt/jextract-22/bin/jextract" mvn compile -pl jvector-native -Dnative.jextract.skip=false

docs.title: 730.fix
docs.text:
This PR is a bug fix for the issue reported by the Cassandra team (https://github.com/riptano/cndb/issues/19259) that results in the first 128k vectors copied during compaction being invisible to GraphIndex.View, causing recall scores to plummet after compaction.

When rescore() is called the nodes specified for rescoring are never marked as completed, so they are hidden from the subsequent Views. This PR adds a call to markComplete() for each node added during the call to rescore(). The workaround for this issue implemented by the Cassandra team marks added nodes complete in a batched fashion after rescoring but is otherwise equivalent. It is detailed at https://github.com/datastax/cassandra/pull/2617.

docs.title: New Features
docs.text:
Added optional batched vector access and a bounded file source for quantizer training, encoding and existing full-precision/NVQ disk serialization. Capable algorithms can consume samples or full scans without requiring an upfront preload of the original base dataset; existing vector sources remain supported.

BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML support useDatasetPrefetching: true in their index configuration. The flag defaults to false, preserving resident loading and scoring. Comparison-heavy uncompressed configurations retain resident input. The existing jvector.dataset_loader VM option overrides the flag, while configurations requiring resident raw vectors still preload; an explicit buffered request logs the reason for that fallback.

See batched vector access for ownership, resource limits, examples and the benchmark opt-in. Encoded vectors, training working memory and graph structures retain their existing memory requirements.

Google Highway native SIMD is no longer experimental and is preferred by default on supported Java 22+ runtimes. jvector.enable_native_vectorization is the supported flag; the former name remains a deprecated compatibility alias.

Successful native selection uses MemorySegmentVectorFloat instead of ArrayVectorFloat. Consumers should use VectorFloat, or FloatArray.array() when array access is needed; direct casts and assumptions about get()'s backing storage must be updated. copyFrom supports both built-in float vector types. Disable automatic native selection with -Djvector.enable_native_vectorization=false to retain the previous provider choice. Native operations require provider-created vectors; copying between storage types does not make mixed-storage arithmetic valid.

Pass --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED for classpath deployments. Missing native access can produce JVM warnings; denied native access, an unsupported ABI, a missing ABI query, or missing required library symbols cause automatic selection to fall back to the Java provider. Explicitly forcing native fails during initialization.

Java requires ABI 1 and checks the native library's explicit supported set before calling kernels. Compatible native releases keep the same ABI ID. Libraries that predate the ABI query are rejected; the bundled library supports ABI 1.

docs.title: Native SIMD Acceleration on AArch64 (NEON, SVE, SVE2)
docs.text:
PR: #723

Description

This PR extends JVector's native Highway SIMD backend to AArch64 (64-bit ARM), bringing the same native acceleration that x86-64 users already have to ARM-based servers and development machines (e.g. AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon under Linux, Ampere Altra).

AArch64 support was previously absent from the native layer — ARM hosts silently fell back to the Panama Vector API path. The native binary now ships three AArch64 ISA tiers, all compiled as vector-length-agnostic (scalable) code:

Tier Highway target Notes NEON HWY_NEON Baseline; all AArch64 CPUs SVE HWY_SVE Scalable Vector Extension SVE2 HWY_SVE2 SVE2 + i8mm + bf16

SVE and SVE2 are compiled as VL-agnostic (scalable) code, so the same binary runs correctly on any SVE/SVE2-capable CPU regardless of its physical vector length. NEON operates on fixed 128-bit vectors. At JVM startup, the best available tier is selected automatically via CPU feature detection — identical to the existing CPUID-based dispatch on x86-64.

The following changes were made:

  • NativeVectorizationProvider — the hard-coded x86_64 architecture check is extended to include aarch64, so the provider is offered on ARM Linux hosts.
  • jvector_arch.h — new header introducing JV_ARCH_X86_64 / JV_ARCH_AARCH64 preprocessor macros; all arch-specific code is guarded with #if/#elif/#endif.
  • jvector_cpu_features.h — AArch64 feature probing (NEON, SVE, SVE2 presence and vector-length queries) added alongside the existing x86 CPUID path.
  • Meson build — three AArch64 ISA variant targets added; SVE/SVE2 targets skip gracefully on Clang < 22 or non-Linux hosts where SVE is unavailable.
  • Cross-compilation — Meson cross-files and updated READMEs provided for building the AArch64 native library from an x86-64 host.
  • CI — a dedicated AArch64 GitHub Actions runner added to the matrix so native builds and kernel correctness are verified on real ARM hardware on every PR.

Purpose / Impact

Benchmarked on 1M-scale datasets on both AWS Graviton 3 and Graviton 4, Native SIMD (Highway) consistently outperforms Panama SIMD on AArch64:

  • Up to 40% lower search latency at the same recall level

  • Up to 29% faster index construction

  • All kernels already ported to Highway for x86-64 (FP32 similarity, PQ, NVQ, element-wise arithmetic) benefit immediately on AArch64 — no separate ARM implementation was required.

  • On AArch64 Linux with native vectorization enabled, the Highway backend is used exclusively for all similarity and quantization operations; the Panama Vector API path is bypassed.
  • On platforms where the native library cannot be loaded, JVector falls back to the Panama or pure-Java provider transparently, as before.

How to Enable

Both libjvector.so variants — x86-64 and AArch64 — are built and bundled into the release JAR. At JVM startup, NativeVectorizationProvider detects the current architecture and loads the matching native library automatically. The same flags work on both architectures:

java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -Djvector.experimental.enable_native_vectorization=true \
     -jar your-app.jar

To cap the ISA tier for debugging or benchmarking:

JVECTOR_MAX_ISA=neon java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -Djvector.experimental.enable_native_vectorization=true \
     -jar your-app.jar

Building releases:

To produce a release JAR with native libraries for all supported architectures (x86-64 and AArch64), the build must be run with the -Dnative.crossarch Maven property. Without this flag, only the native library for the current host architecture is built and bundled.

The release Maven profile (in jvector-native) automatically sets -Dnative.crossarch, so no extra flag is needed on the command line:

# verify (run before the verification script)
mvn verify -Prelease

# publish
mvn -Prelease clean deploy

Notes

  • SVE/SVE2 compilation requires Clang ≥ 22; older compilers silently skip those targets and fall back to NEON.
  • There is no change to the on-disk index format; AArch64 and x86-64 indexes are fully interchangeable.

docs.title: Compaction: level-0 candidates found by scanning cells instead of searching
docs.text:
PR: #740

Description

Compaction merges several pre-built partition indexes into one. At level 0 it must give every node its nearest neighbours in each of the other partitions, and until now it found them with one graph search per node per other partition — a walk whose every hop reads a different record from a different place on disk. Cost scales with nodes times hops, and the reads are scattered, so once the inputs stop fitting in page cache the merge becomes bound by major faults rather than by computation.

This change computes the same thing by scanning. Three pieces make it work:

  1. Cells. The compactor's own upper-layer merge now runs first, and its merged level-1 nodes become cells. Every live node is assigned to the cell its vector descends to.
  2. Ordinals in cell order. Output ordinals are assigned cell by cell, so one partition's members of one cell occupy consecutive rows of the output, and reading a cell is one sequential read.
  3. A shared scan. Each node names the cells it wants, ranked by a width-64 beam over the merged top layer and cut off after a fixed budget of 4,096 vectors per larger partition. Those requests are then inverted, so a cell is read once per group and scored against every node that asked for it, rather than once per node.

Partitions are processed smallest first: a node scans only the partitions larger than its own, and the reverse direction arrives as a bounded set of offers, so the largest partition scans nothing.

The merge remains exact. Every score that orders a candidate is computed on the vectors themselves. Approximation appears in exactly two places: which cells a node asks for, and the pairwise comparisons inside diversity selection, which run on vectors decoded from a wide PQ code. The wide code measures slightly better there than exact comparisons, because coarse codes collide near-duplicates and near-duplicate detection is what the diversity test exists to do.

Breaking API change

OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor now assigns its own output ordinals, because locality in the output ordinal space is what makes a cell's members contiguous and therefore readable in one pass. A caller-supplied mapping cannot provide that. Both constructors lose their remappers parameter and the mapping is published afterwards:

// before
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, remappers, similarityFunction, executor);
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, sourceCompressed, liveNodes, remappers, similarityFunction, executor);

// after
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, similarityFunction, executor);
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, sourceCompressed, liveNodes, similarityFunction, executor);

// then, once compact() has run:
List<OrdinalMapper> mappers = compactor.ordinalMappers();

Callers that previously passed OrdinalMapper.OffsetMapper simply drop the argument and read ordinalMappers() afterwards to learn where each source node landed. oldToNew of a deleted node is OrdinalMapper.OMITTED; live ordinals are dense.

Also removed: setRefineAfterCompaction and the optional refinement pass it gated.

Both compact(Path) and compact(Path, Path) are unchanged, as is the requirement that every source carries the INLINE_VECTORS feature. Full-precision, fused-PQ and PQ-sidecar sources are all still supported, through the same entry points as before.

How to Enable

No configuration required, and no system properties are introduced. The behaviour is fixed at the measured operating point: merged cells, probe beam width 64, scan budget 4,096 vectors per larger partition.

The cell join engages when the merged upper layers yield level-1 nodes and the similarity function is dot product, Euclidean or cosine. If either does not hold — for example merging flat indexes with no hierarchy — level 0 falls back to the existing per-node graph search and output ordinals fall back to a PQ-code prefix. The merge is correct either way; only the level-0 strategy changes, and the compactor logs which path it took.

Results

Three datasets of 6M to 10M vectors, four partitions each, graph degree 32, 64 threads, cold page cache before every run, no swap, one run at a time on a 32-physical-core host with 495 GB RAM and NVMe RAID 0. Memory is a cgroup v2 MemoryMax set as a fraction of the on-disk input index size S. Ratio is S divided by that limit, so ratio above 1 means the index does not fit in the memory the process may use.

Speedup is the previous implementation's compaction time divided by the new one's.

Dataset dim unconstrained ratio 1.00 ratio 1.33 ratio 1.97 CAP-6M 1536 2.10× 2.54× est. 16× est. 47× DPR-10M 768 2.58× 3.05× est. 28× est. 76× Cohere-10M 1024 2.63× 2.50× 9.72× est. 40×

Values marked est. are runs where the old implementation was stopped once it had taken ten times the new one's wall clock; their throughput is measured over the nodes actually completed, so those figures are lower bounds on the gap. 9.72× is the one above-RAM figure where both implementations ran to completion.

The mechanism is visible in the fault counts. The old implementation services major faults at a near-constant rate, so its wall clock is essentially its fault count divided by a constant, and memory pressure multiplies that count:

Dataset major faults/node, ratio 1.00 ratio 1.33 CAP-6M 43.1 472 DPR-10M 40.9 582

The cell join moves from 4.07 to 4.26 and from 2.64 to 2.86 over the same step. On CAP-6M at ratio 1.97 both implementations spend almost identical user CPU, 44,764 s against 46,816 s, so they compute comparable distances; the old one then adds 349,979 s of kernel time servicing page faults and spends 80% of its wall clock stalled on I/O at 17% CPU utilisation, against 76% for the cell join.

Throughput, nodes per second, shows the same thing from the other side: the cell join varies by only 1.24× to 1.39× across the entire memory range and tracks vector width rather than available memory, while the old implementation falls by 20× to 41×.

Quantized inputs

At ratio 1.33, by input layout:

Layout Speedup Recall change fused PQ 2.34× – 4.58× −0.23 to +1.54 pt full precision est. 16× – 28× see below PQ sidecar est. 20× – 47× not measured

The ordering is explained entirely by whether the old implementation can navigate on codes. Fused codes are inline and it uses them, so its faults fall to 43–75 per node and the gap narrows. Full-precision sources have no codes. A PQ sidecar is the worst case for it: codes exist but are only consulted when written inline, so a sidecar's codes are retrained and rewritten yet never navigated on, and its faults rise to 474–962 per node.

Notes and trade-offs

Recall. On full-precision inputs the cell join gives up 0.3 to 1.0 points of recall@10. The old implementation's recall is identical to five decimal places at every memory setting, so it is deterministic; the cell join varies about 0.4 points run to run, from thread scheduling and a per-run wide-code retrain, which puts the smallest deficits inside its own noise. On fused inputs the deficit disappears.

Attribution. The figures above compare against main, which is what users have today, so they credit this change with everything in the PR rather than the cell join alone. Measured against the same branch with the cell join switched off and its other changes kept, the cell join is 1.4× to 1.6× slower in RAM: most of the in-RAM gain comes from processing partitions smallest-first with bounded reverse offers, which halves the number of searches. The cell join's own contribution is the above-RAM columns, where it converts scattered reads into sequential ones.

Scope. Every behavioural change is confined to the compaction path. Outside it, four files are touched and all four are additions only: a dotProductMulti kernel added to VectorUtilSupport as a default method, so existing implementors are unaffected, its Panama override, a static entry point on VectorUtil, and three read-only getters on ProductQuantization. Eighty-four lines added, none removed, and no existing non-compaction code path is modified or re-routed.

Measurement scope. All figures are a single run per configuration; repeats were not taken. Where the old implementation was stopped the effect sizes are above 10×, far outside the run-to-run variation observed elsewhere, but the completed in-RAM and ratio-1.00 comparisons should not be read to two decimal places.

docs.title: Deferred batch graph serialization
docs.text:
PR: #747

Parallel graph serialization can now write complete layer-zero records in bounded batches of 64, with an optional positive batch-size override. When the parallel writer is selected, Grid supplies inline NVQ or full-precision features during final serialization, after graph cleanup, and uses buffered vector ranges when the input source supports them. With the sequential writer selected, Grid keeps encoding those features during insertion.

The core writer accepts application-supplied feature states independently of the benchmark harness or dataset prefetching. Complete-record batching applies equally to fully preloaded inputs; the source does not have to preload the whole dataset.

Integrators should use the parallel writer when deferring NVQ/FP encoding to final serialization. A sequential final writer performs that encoding on one thread and can regress construction time. Sequential callers should retain encoding during insertion and writeFeaturesInline.

The existing V6 layout, readers, ordinary vector sources, and incremental writeFeaturesInline API remain supported. Prewritten features are preserved. Concurrent feature suppliers must keep their input source available until writing finishes. BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML default to parallel writing, with -Djvector.parallel_writer=false selecting the sequential path. The library writer default remains unchanged.

Recorded construction studies with dataset prefetching reduced ample-memory final write time from 136.10 to 50.69 seconds on MPNet 10M, 148.50 to 64.02 seconds on Cohere 10M, and 162.64 to 51.76 seconds on CAP 6M.[^machine] These are separate fresh runs, not a universal throughput or memory guarantee. See Deferred batch serialization for usage.

Construction tutorials and examples now demonstrate final feature suppliers for deferred FP/NVQ writing, with per-worker source views and an explicit source-lifetime requirement. The query algorithms and quantization settings are unchanged.

[^machine]: GCE VM, 48-core Intel Xeon 6985P-C (96 threads), local SSD RAID10, JDK 23, 128 GiB heap; native Highway, 48 workers.

docs.title: Extend Native SIMD Coverage for Vector Operations
docs.text:
PR: #753

Description

Move minimum and sum reductions, in-place scaling, and vector and scalar subtraction from Panama Vector API fallbacks to native Google Highway kernels, using the existing x86-64 and AArch64 ISA dispatch.

Subtraction ranges and input lengths are validated before processing. Minimum reduction preserves Java’s NaN propagation and signed-zero behavior.

How to Enable

These operations use the existing experimental native-vectorization setting. No new configuration is required.

Notes

Hamming distance continues to use the Panama Vector API implementation. No public API or index-format changes.

docs.title: Batch Native Highway Operations
docs.text:
PR: #761

Description

Reduce Java/native calls and temporary allocation during PQ training, PQ encoding, and NVQ processing. Batch closest-centroid scans and KMeans updates, use lazy array-backed native views, batch NVQ growth-rate search, and keep cosine results packed.

How to Enable

No new configuration is required. These optimizations apply when the native provider is selected, which is the default on supported Java 22+ runtimes.

Notes

Existing native function signatures and ABI 1 are unchanged. Four additional native kernels are included in the bundled library; deployments supplying their own native library must include these kernels. No index-format changes.

docs.title: Enforce Neighbor-ID Uniqueness
docs.text:
PR: #738

Description

Asymmetric scoring, such as A · quant(B) ≠ B · quant(A), can assign different scores to the same neighbor, defeating score-local duplicate checks and reducing effective graph degree.

NodeArray now checks IDs independently of scores and deduplicates complete candidate merges, retaining existing scores and score ordering. ConcurrentNeighborMap also deduplicates initial candidate batches and rejects duplicate offers before copying or changing pruning state.

For an existing neighbor, subsequent backlink offers are rejected regardless of their score; the stored edge score is retained. During concurrent construction, which score is installed first can depend on thread timing.

More distinct edges can improve recall but increase traversal work and reduce QPS at fixed search settings. Results vary by dataset and construction seed.

How to Enable

Automatic; no configuration required.

Notes

Library API and index format are unchanged. A full rebuild is required to remove previously stored duplicate neighbor IDs: loading an existing index or incrementally adding nodes does not guarantee that all old neighborhoods are repaired. Supersedes #522.

docs.title: Publish S3 Dataset Downloads Only After Completion
docs.text:
PR: #745

Description

Download S3 dataset files into private temporary files and atomically publish the cache path after successful completion and content-length validation. This prevents other benchmark processes from reading an in-progress download or losing a completed cache file when another download attempt fails.

How to Enable

No configuration is required. This applies to S3 downloads made by the example benchmark dataset loader; HTTP downloads already use atomic publication.

Notes

Normal failures remove their temporary files. A hard process termination may leave an unreferenced temporary file, which is not accepted as cached data. Existing cache files are not retroactively validated; remove any files known to come from an interrupted download before reusing that cache.

docs.title: Fix Hierarchical Search Failure with Non-Normalized Dot Product Vectors
docs.text:
Description

Resolves #713. When searching a hierarchical graph with VectorSimilarityFunction.DOT_PRODUCT and vectors that are not unit-normalized, search could return no matches for an upper layer and fail with AssertionError in GraphSearcher.internalSearch.

The descent through layers above level 0 searched each layer with a threshold of 0.0f, treating it as "accept everything". That only holds for similarity functions bounded to (0, 1] (COSINE and EUCLIDEAN). DOT_PRODUCT is only bounded when vectors are unit length; with larger-magnitude vectors, scores can be negative. If every candidate reachable in an upper layer scored below 0, all were discarded, no entry point was found for the next layer, and the assertion fired. This surfaced in Cassandra's VectorDotProductWithLengthTest.testTrueDotproduct, which uses non-unit 2D vectors with components in [-100, 100].

Upper-layer descent now uses a threshold of Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY. The search(scoreProvider, topK, acceptOrds) overload, which has no threshold parameter, now also defaults to Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY instead of 0.0f.

How to Enable

Automatic; no configuration required.

Notes

Results from COSINE, EUCLIDEAN, and unit-normalized DOT_PRODUCT searches are unchanged. For non-normalized DOT_PRODUCT, the search(scoreProvider, topK, acceptOrds) overload can now return results with negative scores that were previously filtered out. Callers who pass an explicit threshold and need to accept every result for non-normalized DOT_PRODUCT should pass Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY rather than 0. Index format and library API are unchanged. Regression coverage is in TestHierarchyDotProductSearch.

docs.title: Optional Compaction Benchmark and Dedicated Runner for Regression Benchmarks
docs.text:
PR: #736

Description Two changes to the automated regression benchmark (AutoBenchYAML / run-bench.yml):

  • CompactionBench is now opt-in. AutoBenchYAML previously ran CompactionBench for every dataset after the main benchmark. Compaction benchmarking now runs only when a dataset's YAML configuration enables it with the new top-level withCompaction parameter. When it is not enabled, the step is skipped and logged, and the -compaction.csv / -compaction.json output files are not produced.
  • Benchmarks run on the large runner. The test-avx512 job in run-bench.yml previously matched any self-hosted runner with the isa-avx512f label, so results could come from different machines between runs. The job now also requires the jvector-runner-large label, so every benchmark runs on the same hardware and results are comparable across runs.

How to Enable Compaction benchmarking is disabled by default; no existing YAML files were changed. To enable it for a dataset, add withCompaction at the same level as yamlSchemaVersion and dataset:

yamlSchemaVersion: 1
onDiskIndexVersion: 6

dataset: cap-10M
withCompaction: [Yes]

construction:
  ...

If the parameter is absent or set to [No], CompactionBench is not run. When --config is passed to AutoBenchYAML, that single file controls compaction for all datasets.

The runner change requires no configuration in the repository, but the self-hosted runner must carry the custom label jvector-runner-large, as runs-on matches labels rather than runner names.

Notes - Used internally by JVector benchmarking, no client impact. - With both branch runs of a PR pinned to the same runner, they now execute sequentially rather than potentially in parallel on separate runners.

docs.title: Native SIMD Acceleration on AArch64 (NEON, SVE, SVE2)
docs.text:
Description

This PR extends JVector's native Highway SIMD backend to AArch64 (64-bit ARM), bringing the same native acceleration that x86-64 users already have to ARM-based servers and development machines (e.g. AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon under Linux, Ampere Altra).

AArch64 support was previously absent from the native layer — ARM hosts silently fell back to the Panama Vector API path. The native binary now ships three AArch64 ISA tiers, all compiled as vector-length-agnostic (scalable) code:

Tier Highway target Notes NEON HWY_NEON Baseline; all AArch64 CPUs SVE HWY_SVE Scalable Vector Extension SVE2 HWY_SVE2 SVE2 + i8mm + bf16

SVE and SVE2 are compiled as VL-agnostic (scalable) code, so the same binary runs correctly on any SVE/SVE2-capable CPU regardless of its physical vector length. NEON operates on fixed 128-bit vectors. At JVM startup, the best available tier is selected automatically via CPU feature detection — identical to the existing CPUID-based dispatch on x86-64.

The following changes were made:

  • NativeVectorizationProvider — the hard-coded x86_64 architecture check is extended to include aarch64, so the provider is offered on ARM Linux hosts.
  • jvector_arch.h — new header introducing JV_ARCH_X86_64 / JV_ARCH_AARCH64 preprocessor macros; all arch-specific code is guarded with #if/#elif/#endif.
  • jvector_cpu_features.h — AArch64 feature probing (NEON, SVE, SVE2 presence and vector-length queries) added alongside the existing x86 CPUID path.
  • Meson build — three AArch64 ISA variant targets added; SVE/SVE2 targets skip gracefully on Clang < 22 or non-Linux hosts where SVE is unavailable.
  • Cross-compilation — Meson cross-files and updated READMEs provided for building the AArch64 native library from an x86-64 host.
  • CI — a dedicated AArch64 GitHub Actions runner added to the matrix so native builds and kernel correctness are verified on real ARM hardware on every PR.

Purpose / Impact

Benchmarked on 1M-scale datasets on both AWS Graviton 3 and Graviton 4, Native SIMD (Highway) consistently outperforms Panama SIMD on AArch64:

  • Up to 40% lower search latency at the same recall level

  • Up to 29% faster index construction

  • All kernels already ported to Highway for x86-64 (FP32 similarity, PQ, NVQ, element-wise arithmetic) benefit immediately on AArch64 — no separate ARM implementation was required.

  • On AArch64 Linux with native vectorization enabled, the Highway backend is used exclusively for all similarity and quantization operations; the Panama Vector API path is bypassed.
  • On platforms where the native library cannot be loaded, JVector falls back to the Panama or pure-Java provider transparently, as before.

How to Enable

Both libjvector.so variants — x86-64 and AArch64 — are built and bundled into the release JAR. At JVM startup, NativeVectorizationProvider detects the current architecture and loads the matching native library automatically. The same flags work on both architectures:

java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -Djvector.experimental.enable_native_vectorization=true \
     -jar your-app.jar

To cap the ISA tier for debugging or benchmarking:

JVECTOR_MAX_ISA=neon java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -Djvector.experimental.enable_native_vectorization=true \
     -jar your-app.jar

Building releases:

To produce a release JAR with native libraries for all supported architectures (x86-64 and AArch64), the build must be run with the -Dnative.crossarch Maven property. Without this flag, only the native library for the current host architecture is built and bundled.

The release Maven profile (in jvector-native) automatically sets -Dnative.crossarch, so no extra flag is needed on the command line:

# verify (run before the verification script)
mvn verify -Prelease

# publish
mvn -Prelease clean deploy

Notes

  • SVE/SVE2 compilation requires Clang ≥ 22; older compilers silently skip those targets and fall back to NEON.
  • There is no change to the on-disk index format; AArch64 and x86-64 indexes are fully interchangeable.

docs.title: Compaction: level-0 candidates found by scanning cells instead of searching
docs.text:
Description

Compaction merges several pre-built partition indexes into one. At level 0 it must give every node its nearest neighbours in each of the other partitions, and until now it found them with one graph search per node per other partition — a walk whose every hop reads a different record from a different place on disk. Cost scales with nodes times hops, and the reads are scattered, so once the inputs stop fitting in page cache the merge becomes bound by major faults rather than by computation.

This change computes the same thing by scanning. Three pieces make it work:

  1. Cells. The compactor's own upper-layer merge now runs first, and its merged level-1 nodes become cells. Every live node is assigned to the cell its vector descends to.
  2. Ordinals in cell order. Output ordinals are assigned cell by cell, so one partition's members of one cell occupy consecutive rows of the output, and reading a cell is one sequential read.
  3. A shared scan. Each node names the cells it wants, ranked by a width-64 beam over the merged top layer and cut off after a fixed budget of 4,096 vectors per larger partition. Those requests are then inverted, so a cell is read once per group and scored against every node that asked for it, rather than once per node.

Partitions are processed smallest first: a node scans only the partitions larger than its own, and the reverse direction arrives as a bounded set of offers, so the largest partition scans nothing.

The merge remains exact. Every score that orders a candidate is computed on the vectors themselves. Approximation appears in exactly two places: which cells a node asks for, and the pairwise comparisons inside diversity selection, which run on vectors decoded from a wide PQ code. The wide code measures slightly better there than exact comparisons, because coarse codes collide near-duplicates and near-duplicate detection is what the diversity test exists to do.

Breaking API change

OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor now assigns its own output ordinals, because locality in the output ordinal space is what makes a cell's members contiguous and therefore readable in one pass. A caller-supplied mapping cannot provide that. Both constructors lose their remappers parameter and the mapping is published afterwards:

// before
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, remappers, similarityFunction, executor);
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, sourceCompressed, liveNodes, remappers, similarityFunction, executor);

// after
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, similarityFunction, executor);
new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, sourceCompressed, liveNodes, similarityFunction, executor);

// then, once compact() has run:
List<OrdinalMapper> mappers = compactor.ordinalMappers();

Callers that previously passed OrdinalMapper.OffsetMapper simply drop the argument and read ordinalMappers() afterwards to learn where each source node landed. oldToNew of a deleted node is OrdinalMapper.OMITTED; live ordinals are dense.

Also removed: setRefineAfterCompaction and the optional refinement pass it gated.

Both compact(Path) and compact(Path, Path) are unchanged, as is the requirement that every source carries the INLINE_VECTORS feature. Full-precision, fused-PQ and PQ-sidecar sources are all still supported, through the same entry points as before.

How to Enable

No configuration required, and no system properties are introduced. The behaviour is fixed at the measured operating point: merged cells, probe beam width 64, scan budget 4,096 vectors per larger partition.

The cell join engages when the merged upper layers yield level-1 nodes and the similarity function is dot product, Euclidean or cosine. If either does not hold — for example merging flat indexes with no hierarchy — level 0 falls back to the existing per-node graph search and output ordinals fall back to a PQ-code prefix. The merge is correct either way; only the level-0 strategy changes, and the compactor logs which path it took.

Results

Three datasets of 6M to 10M vectors, four partitions each, graph degree 32, 64 threads, cold page cache before every run, no swap, one run at a time on a 32-physical-core host with 495 GB RAM and NVMe RAID 0. Memory is a cgroup v2 MemoryMax set as a fraction of the on-disk input index size S. Ratio is S divided by that limit, so ratio above 1 means the index does not fit in the memory the process may use.

Speedup is the previous implementation's compaction time divided by the new one's.

Dataset dim unconstrained ratio 1.00 ratio 1.33 ratio 1.97 CAP-6M 1536 2.10× 2.54× est. 16× est. 47× DPR-10M 768 2.58× 3.05× est. 28× est. 76× Cohere-10M 1024 2.63× 2.50× 9.72× est. 40×

Values marked est. are runs where the old implementation was stopped once it had taken ten times the new one's wall clock; their throughput is measured over the nodes actually completed, so those figures are lower bounds on the gap. 9.72× is the one above-RAM figure where both implementations ran to completion.

The mechanism is visible in the fault counts. The old implementation services major faults at a near-constant rate, so its wall clock is essentially its fault count divided by a constant, and memory pressure multiplies that count:

Dataset major faults/node, ratio 1.00 ratio 1.33 CAP-6M 43.1 472 DPR-10M 40.9 582

The cell join moves from 4.07 to 4.26 and from 2.64 to 2.86 over the same step. On CAP-6M at ratio 1.97 both implementations spend almost identical user CPU, 44,764 s against 46,816 s, so they compute comparable distances; the old one then adds 349,979 s of kernel time servicing page faults and spends 80% of its wall clock stalled on I/O at 17% CPU utilisation, against 76% for the cell join.

Throughput, nodes per second, shows the same thing from the other side: the cell join varies by only 1.24× to 1.39× across the entire memory range and tracks vector width rather than available memory, while the old implementation falls by 20× to 41×.

Quantized inputs

At ratio 1.33, by input layout:

Layout Speedup Recall change fused PQ 2.34× – 4.58× −0.23 to +1.54 pt full precision est. 16× – 28× see below PQ sidecar est. 20× – 47× not measured

The ordering is explained entirely by whether the old implementation can navigate on codes. Fused codes are inline and it uses them, so its faults fall to 43–75 per node and the gap narrows. Full-precision sources have no codes. A PQ sidecar is the worst case for it: codes exist but are only consulted when written inline, so a sidecar's codes are retrained and rewritten yet never navigated on, and its faults rise to 474–962 per node.

Notes and trade-offs

Recall. On full-precision inputs the cell join gives up 0.3 to 1.0 points of recall@10. The old implementation's recall is identical to five decimal places at every memory setting, so it is deterministic; the cell join varies about 0.4 points run to run, from thread scheduling and a per-run wide-code retrain, which puts the smallest deficits inside its own noise. On fused inputs the deficit disappears.

Attribution. The figures above compare against main, which is what users have today, so they credit this change with everything in the PR rather than the cell join alone. Measured against the same branch with the cell join switched off and its other changes kept, the cell join is 1.4× to 1.6× slower in RAM: most of the in-RAM gain comes from processing partitions smallest-first with bounded reverse offers, which halves the number of searches. The cell join's own contribution is the above-RAM columns, where it converts scattered reads into sequential ones.

Scope. Every behavioural change is confined to the compaction path. Outside it, four files are touched and all four are additions only: a dotProductMulti kernel added to VectorUtilSupport as a default method, so existing implementors are unaffected, its Panama override, a static entry point on VectorUtil, and three read-only getters on ProductQuantization. Eighty-four lines added, none removed, and no existing non-compaction code path is modified or re-routed.

Measurement scope. All figures are a single run per configuration; repeats were not taken. Where the old implementation was stopped the effect sizes are above 10×, far outside the run-to-run variation observed elsewhere, but the completed in-RAM and ratio-1.00 comparisons should not be read to two decimal places.

See docs/compaction.md for the pipeline description.

Missing native access can produce JVM warnings; denied native access, an unsupported ABI, a missing ABI query, or missing required library symbols cause automatic selection to fall back to the Java provider. Explicitly forcing native fails during initialization.

Java requires ABI 1 and checks the native library's explicit supported set before calling kernels. Compatible native releases keep the same ABI ID. Libraries that predate the ABI query are rejected; the bundled library supports ABI 1.

docs.title: Native Int8 (Byte) Vector Support
docs.text:
PR: #709

Description JVector can now build, store and search signed int8 vectors natively, without converting them to float32. This is useful when an embedding model already emits int8 vectors, or when vectors have been scaled to int8 up front: they take 4x less space on disk and in memory than float32, and all scoring is done byte-by-byte. On 176,582 mixedbread-large int8 embeddings (1,024 dimensions), an int8 index matched the recall of a float32 index of the same vectors, with about 3.6x the queries per second, half the build time and a 3.6x smaller file.

  • RandomAccessByteVectorValues (and ListRandomAccessByteVectorValues) provide random access to ByteSequence vectors. It and RandomAccessVectorValues now share a common VectorValues<V> interface, which also provides getVectorInto(node, destination, offset) for reading a vector into a caller-owned buffer.
  • ByteVectorSimilarityFunction scores two int8 vectors: EUCLIDEAN is 1 / (1 + squaredL2), DOT_PRODUCT is dot < 0 ? 1 / (1 - dot) : dot + 1, and COSINE is (1 + cosine) / 2. The scores are not normalised by dimension, so distinct integer distances stay distinct at high dimensions. DOT_PRODUCT scores are positive but not bounded above by 1.
  • GraphIndexBuilder.builder(RandomAccessByteVectorValues, ByteVectorSimilarityFunction, M) builds a graph from int8 vectors, and GraphIndexBuilder.build(VectorValues<?>) accepts either vector type.
  • The InlineByteVectors on-disk feature (FeatureId.INLINE_BYTE_VECTORS) stores each vector as dimension raw bytes. OnDiskGraphIndex.View.byteVectorRerankerFor(...) scores candidates directly from disk, and getByteVectorInto(...) reads a vector into a reusable buffer.
  • Int8 distance kernels (squared L2, dot product, cosine) are available in the default, Panama and native SIMD implementations, and accumulate in integers so all execution paths return identical results.
  • BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML support int8 datasets: mark a dataset with is_int8: true in dataset-metadata.yml, and configure it with construction.type: onDisk, compression None, reranking.type: None and fusedGraph: [No], as the int8 configs in index-parameters do. A runnable example is in Int8Example (-Dtutorial=int8).

How to Enable No configuration is required; the float32 APIs are unchanged. To use int8 vectors, build with the byte-vector builder and write the index with the InlineByteVectors feature:

RandomAccessByteVectorValues vectors = new ListRandomAccessByteVectorValues(byteVectors, dimension);
try (var builder = GraphIndexBuilder.builder(vectors, ByteVectorSimilarityFunction.EUCLIDEAN, 32).build()) {
    var graph = builder.build(vectors);
    try (var writer = GraphIndexWriter.getBuilderFor(GraphIndexWriterTypes.RANDOM_ACCESS_PARALLEL, graph, path)
            .with(new InlineByteVectors(dimension)).build()) {
        writer.write(Map.of(FeatureId.INLINE_BYTE_VECTORS, n -> new InlineByteVectors.State(vectors.getVector(n))));
    }
}

Notes * The new interfaces and classes are marked @Experimental and the API may change in later releases. * Only signed int8 (-128..127) is supported. Unsigned uint8 data, such as conventional SIFT1B/BIGANN .bvecs files, must be converted first; it is not detected, and reading it as signed silently changes distances. * Quantization and compression (ASH, PQ, BQ, NVQ, fused graphs) are not supported for int8 vectors. Traversal already scores exactly, so a separate reranking step is not needed. rerankK still controls how much of the graph is searched. * Zero vectors are not supported with COSINE, as with ASH: adding one to a graph or searching with one throws IllegalArgumentException. * OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor does not compact int8 indexes; AutoBenchYAML skips its compaction benchmark for them. * Existing float32 callers keep working: RandomAccessVectorValues.getVector keeps its VectorFloat<?> signature and GraphIndexBuilder.build(RandomAccessVectorValues) is retained as a forwarding overload. * Int8 indexes require on-disk format version 7 or later. JVector 4.0.x reads formats up to 6 and rejects version 7 files; a version 6 writer rejects INLINE_BYTE_VECTORS.

docs.title: Asymmetric Scalar Hashing (ASH) quantization
docs.text:
PR: #796

Description

JVector adds ASH, from ASH: Asymmetric Scalar Hashing With Learned Dimensionality Reduction for High-Fidelity Vector Quantization (Tepper and Willke, CIKM 2026). ASH projects database vectors with a learned orthonormal matrix and stores each projected dimension in 1 to 9 bits, while queries stay full precision. On large datasets at matched code sizes, fused ASH builds faster than fused PQ, is more accurate, and searches faster in nearly every case; see ASH performance. ASH is @Experimental; PQ remains the stable default.

  • Training and encoding: AsymmetricHashing.initialize and encodeAll, producing ASHVectors.
  • In-memory graphs: ASHVectors score construction and search; BuildScoreProvider.ashBuildScoreProvider builds with code-to-code scoring.
  • Fused ASH on disk: the FusedASH feature stores neighbors' codes with each adjacency list, reranking with NVQ or full-precision vectors.
  • Streaming construction: StreamingASHIndex builds and searches while vectors arrive, training its model cold if needed.
  • Native query projection: INT8, FP16 or FP32, chosen automatically by CPU; FP16 and some INT8 paths use the optional oneDNN add-on.
  • Prepared and queued queries: QueryPreparer, PreparedQuery and BatchingExecutor share batched query projection.
  • Page-aligned records: withPageAlignment(pageBytes) keeps base-layer records from crossing page boundaries, for indexes larger than memory.

How to Enable

ASH is opt-in. See HelloASHWorldFp16 for a complete fused ASH build and search, and ASH configuration and defaults for settings.

Notes

  • Format version 7. New files default to version 7, which JVector 4.0.x cannot read; pass withVersion(6) to keep rollback possible. See UPGRADING.md.
  • Similarity. A model is trained for DOT_PRODUCT, EUCLIDEAN or COSINE and rejects other functions; vectors need not be normalized.
  • Adaptive termination. GraphSearcher.useAdaptiveTermination(true) is experimental and off by default for search.
  • BLAS threads. ASH training sets the native BLAS thread count; MKL_NUM_THREADS is no longer needed.
  • Compaction. OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor does not yet compact fused ASH or page-aligned indexes.
  • Native build. Highway is a Meson wrap instead of a git submodule; the oneDNN add-on is a separate Meson project.

Documentation

ASH configuration, database integration, projection precision, larger-than-memory indexes, reproducing ASH versus PQ, native build and Hello ASH examples.

docs.title: Compaction: sharded compaction sessions and a choice of output format version
docs.text:
PR: #798

Description

JVector 4.0.2 made OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor find level-0 neighbours by scanning cells instead of searching (#740). This change builds on it in three ways.

  • Sharded compaction sessions. A host that splits a merge into several outputs (Cassandra writes one sstable per token range) previously ran one compaction per output. Each run trained the codebooks again, and each lost recall: a shard keeps only a small part of every source, so a node kept few of its same-source edges and nothing replaced them. A session trains the codebooks once, on the live nodes of every shard, and shares them. In each shard it also searches a source with fewer than half its nodes live for the node's own neighbours. Ordinary compact calls are unchanged.
  • withVersion(int) writes the output at any on-disk format version the writer supports instead of only OnDiskGraphIndex.CURRENT_VERSION. Sources may be at different versions. A version that cannot hold the output is rejected: fused PQ needs 6, and upper layers need 4 or above.
  • Faster merges larger than memory. The cell walk sizes its ranges from the heap and from what it measures, announces source records to the page cache ahead of reading them, frees its tables before writing the upper layers, and reads the merge store with direct I/O when the store does not fit in memory beside the heap.

tessera-2M, two 1M-vector sources (1024 dimensions, cosine, degree 32) merged into hash shards, 8 cores. Each cell shows total time and recall@10:

Shards One compaction per shard One session Rebuild of every shard 4 454 s, 0.781 566 s, 0.825 876 s, 0.836 16 981 s, 0.823 567 s, 0.894 946 s, 0.903 64 1203 s, 0.875 627 s, 0.945 886 s, 0.947

How to Enable

Open a session on a compactor built with the live nodes of every shard, then merge each shard:

var compactor = new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, VectorSimilarityFunction.COSINE, null);
var session = compactor.sharded();
List<OrdinalMapper> shard0 = session.compactShard(shard0LiveNodes, output0);
List<OrdinalMapper> shard1 = session.compactShard(shard1LiveNodes, output1);

Sources with a compressed sidecar use compactShard(shardLiveNodes, graphPath, compressedPath). To choose the output's format version, call compactor.withVersion(6) before compacting; a session writes every shard at its compactor's version. The large-merge changes need no configuration.

Notes

  • sharded(), compactShard and withVersion are @Experimental. A session is not thread-safe: shards are compacted one at a time, and may become known one at a time.
  • At 4 shards the same-source search costs more time than shared training saves; from 16 shards the session is faster and its recall is within a point of a rebuild.
  • A merge whose top levels have no live node, which a shard can produce, now ends its hierarchy at the highest level that still has one instead of failing.
  • Record announce-ahead is asynchronous (POSIX_MADV_WILLNEED) only with the jvector-native reader. Other readers fall back to their synchronous prefetch.
  • See compaction for details.

docs.title: BenchYAML: ASH defaults, explicit pipelines and one-JVM experiments
docs.text:
PR: #796

Description

BenchYAML's index YAML schema 3 states each pipeline explicitly: index type, construction and search compression, construction scoring, reranking, query execution (direct or queued), and construction and search worker counts. It can also sweep the upper layers' degree separately from the base layer's. Schema 1 files are still accepted.

  • Defaults. Without arguments, BenchYAML runs a few small public datasets and prints the key results. Compressed dataset defaults now use fused ASH.
  • Results. Runs report stored-code load and write times and the codes file size. Every console and CSV result field is defined in the BenchYAML Guide.
  • Measurement settings. Run configurations can measure cold queries, and a larger-than-memory run configuration is included.
  • One-JVM experiments. benchyaml-play.sh builds the checkout and runs one experiment in one JVM from the command line or IntelliJ.

How to Enable

Set yamlSchemaVersion: 3 to use the new fields. See the BenchYAML Guide, the example pipelines and the benchmark launcher.

docs.title: MutablePQVectors Updates Its Vector Count Without a Capturing Lambda
docs.text:
PR: #639

Description

MutablePQVectors.encodeAndSet and setZero raised the vector count with updateAndGet(current -> max(current, ordinal + 1)), a lambda that captures ordinal and so may allocate on every call. They now use accumulateAndGet(ordinal + 1, Math::max), which passes the value as an argument and needs no allocation. The result and its atomicity are unchanged. In JMH runs on JDK 22 and 25, the JIT already removed the old allocation once the code was warm, so encodeAndSet time and allocation are unchanged in steady state.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

docs.title: GraphIndexBuilder Closes the Per-Thread Vector Copies It Creates
docs.text:
PR: #715

Description

For a shared RandomAccessVectorValues (one that reuses a buffer, such as a file-backed source), threadLocalSupplier() hands each thread its own copy(), but nothing could close those copies, so AutoCloseable copies (for example, ones holding a mapped file) stayed open. The supplier for shared sources is now AutoCloseable: closing it closes every AutoCloseable copy it created and clears the per-thread cache. GraphIndexBuilder.build and buildAndMergeNewNodes close their supplier when construction ends, and only after every parallel worker has stopped, even if one fails. Copies made by RemappedRandomAccessVectorValues now close their copy of the wrapped source, which is never closed itself. See #635.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

Code that calls threadLocalSupplier() itself can close the returned supplier when it is an AutoCloseable to release its copies; the supplier stays usable afterwards and makes new copies on demand. Un-shared sources still get a supplier that returns the source itself. Copies held by the exact-scoring build score providers are not yet closed; that is tracked in #764.

docs.title: Correct Fused PQ Retained Memory Accounting
docs.text:
PR: #781

Description

Correct ramBytesUsed() for fused PQ sources, byte sequences, and shared on-disk graph caches. Remove the erroneous four-times multiplier on source byte counts, include retained buffer wrappers, native heap segment scopes, graph metadata, cache capacity, adjacency-array overhead, and models read from the index header (fused PQ codebooks, NVQ parameters), which only the index holds. PQ and NVQ models, float vectors and PQ scoring tables report their full retained storage, including caches created after loading. Sizing follows the running JVM's reference sizes, headers, array element offsets, and alignment, including JDK 25 compact object headers, without sun.misc.Unsafe.

Graph and built-in PQ vector memory checks use cached totals. Loading and storage growth update these totals, including spare chunk-reference capacity; repeated checks allocate nothing, and their cost does not grow with the number of vectors.

How to Enable

Automatic; no configuration is required.

Notes

Reported sizes can increase or decrease, affecting applications that use these estimates for memory limits or cache sizing. Existing indexes do not require rebuilding; the on-disk format and search results are unchanged.

Loaded graph feature metadata is read-only. Resident buffers are counted at their allocation sites; fixed per-index metadata is a small estimate. Feature implementations can override Feature.ramBytesUsed(); worker scratch remains excluded. See retained memory accounting for the ownership boundary, reporting cost, and validation details.

docs.title: GraphSearcher Returns an Empty Result for topK == 0
docs.text:
PR: #812

Description

GraphSearcher.search with topK == 0 read the empty results queues: with a reranker it threw a NullPointerException from NodeQueue.rerank, and with rerankK == 0 it compared against and evicted stale heap slots, which could throw on a later resume or make the search depend on the previous query. search and resume now return an empty result without searching when topK (or additionalK) is 0, and NodeQueue.rerank sends every candidate to the unused pile when topK is 0. See #811.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

Callers that short-circuit k == 0 before calling search as a workaround can keep doing so; it is no longer necessary.

docs.title: GraphIndexBuilder Searches With No Score Floor, So DOT_PRODUCT Vectors Dissimilar to Everything Get Neighbors
docs.text:
PR: #814

Description

GraphIndexBuilder.addGraphNode and improveConnections searched with a score threshold of 0.0f. That accepts everything for COSINE and EUCLIDEAN, but DOT_PRODUCT scores are (1 + dot) / 2, which is negative for non-normalized vectors. Every candidate of a vector that is dissimilar to all the others was discarded, so it was inserted with no neighbors; if it was the entry node, the index was built without any edges and searches returned a single result. The builder now uses Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, as GraphSearcher.internalSearch already does. See #813.

How to Enable

No configuration is required. COSINE and EUCLIDEAN builds are unchanged.

Notes

On ordinary non-unit DOT_PRODUCT data recall did not change (20,000 x 128-dimension vectors, recall@10 1.0000 to 0.9993 across four scalings, the same with and without the change). Non-normalized DOT_PRODUCT graphs can still be poorly connected for other reasons.

docs.title: GraphIndexBuilder Uses No Rerank Floor in the Layer-0 Resume, and improveConnections Is Tested
docs.text:
PR: #820

Description

Follow-up to #814. The layer-0 resume in GraphIndexBuilder.addGraphNode still passed a rerank floor of 0.0f. A score provider with a reranker only reranks candidates at or above the floor, so with a custom provider and non-normalized DOT_PRODUCT vectors, a node dissimilar to everything got only its single best candidate as a neighbor. The floor is now Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY. The built-in build score providers have no reranker and were not affected. A test now also covers improveConnections on an upper-layer node whose similarities are all negative. See #817.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

Only builds with a custom BuildScoreProvider that supplies a reranker, and DOT_PRODUCT on non-normalized vectors, change.

docs.title: neighborOverflow Values Such as 1.3 and 1.4 No Longer Trip an Assertion
docs.text:
PR: #823

Description

Inserting a backlink capped the neighbor list at M * neighborOverflow computed in float, while the neighbor arrays were sized from the same product computed in double. For overflow factors such as 1.3, 1.4, 1.8 and 1.9 the float product rounds up to the next integer for some M (for example 1.4 with M = 5, 10, 15, ...), so with assertions enabled the build failed with "could exceed max overflow degree", and without them a neighbor list could briefly hold one neighbor more than intended. Both now use the double product. See #822.

A builder over an existing graph could also be given a larger neighborOverflow than the graph's arrays were sized for; the build then failed with "Cannot copy ... nodes to a smaller size". The cap now never exceeds the arrays' size.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

The default overflow of 1.2 is not affected.

docs.title: Documentation Site
docs.text:
PR: #825

Description

JVector's documentation in docs/ is published at datastax.github.io/jvector, which the README and the repository's About section now link to.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

docs.title: Modular Benchmark Harness: Grid Refactor for BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML
docs.text:
PR: #776

Description Grid, the engine behind BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML, was refactored so that each benchmarking initiative can put its changes in its own files. Almost every core change also changed Grid.java, and with several initiatives in flight at once it had merge conflicts at nearly every release. The class is now a small orchestrator (692 lines, down from 1,395). Its extension points live in separate files in io.github.jbellis.jvector.example:

Concern Before Now Two pipelines runAll and runAllAndCollectResults were near-copies One pipeline; AutoBenchYAML adds a result collector Build parameters 5–7 positional arguments threaded through every method BuildConfig (one build point) and SearchConfig (the search sweep) Construction sweep Six hand-nested for loops GridSpec with ordered SweepDimensions; GridSpec.fromGrids(...) sets the order, and GridSpec.fromConfig(MultiConfig) maps the YAML onto it Graph construction Inline buildInMemory / buildOnDisk IndexBuildStrategy: InMemoryBuild, CompressedOnDiskBuild (includes the index cache) Core builder/writer calls Spread through Grid GraphBuilderFactory only On-disk features A switch on FeatureId plus FUSED_PQ checks in five other places FeatureProvider per feature (InlineVectorsProvider, NVQProvider, FusedPQProvider), registered in FeatureProviders Console, experiments.csv, AutoBench results Inline in testConfiguration GridListeners: ConsoleReportListener, ExperimentsLogListener, BenchResultCollector Reported build parameters Listed separately by each output BuildConfig.reportedParameters()

Each step was checked against the previous code on lastfm-64-dot by comparing experiments.csv rows, AutoBench BenchResult output, console tables, and the builds, cache hits and skip messages logged. Output matched except for the changes listed below.

How to Enable No configuration is required. Command lines, dataset YAML files (yaml-configs/index-parameters/), run-config.yml, and the experiments.csv schema (v1) are unchanged.

Running BenchYAML: what changes

  • Unchanged: command line, YAML configs, run-config.yml selections, experiments.csv columns and values, console table columns.
  • Feature-set order is stable. Indexes are searched in the configured order. That is the reranking list order, with each fusedGraph value producing a full pass over it, e.g. reranking: [NVQ, FP] gives NVQ then FP. Previously the order of console blocks and experiments.csv rows changed between runs, because EnumSet hash codes come from identity hashes.
  • No stale search timings on fused rows. Fused-PQ indexes skip search compression, but they could report the previous index's Search PQ encoding (s). They no longer do.
  • PQ codebooks are reused within a run. The in-memory compressor cache never hit, so every lookup reloaded the codebooks from pq_cache (one codebooks loaded from line each). Results are unchanged; repeat loads are gone.
  • NVQ compressors can be cached. NVQParameters.idStringFor no longer throws (same fix as #780), and cached compressors are now read back by the CompressorParameters that saved them (loadCompressor) instead of always as PQ, which would have returned a corrupt PQ or failed on the second run. Files still go in pq_cache; the load message is now <compressor> loaded from <file>.
  • Clearer errors for incomplete configs. A missing construction sweep field fails with its name, e.g. No values to sweep for outDegree or construction.useSavedIndexIfExists must be set, instead of a bare NullPointerException. The whole sweep is validated before the first build.
  • Features without a provider are rejected. A feature set containing a feature Grid cannot write (e.g. SEPARATED_VECTORS) fails when the GridSpec is built, with Grid has no FeatureProvider for <id>. Previously the index was built without that feature and the results were still labeled with it. YAML configs cannot produce such a feature set (reranking accepts only FP and NVQ), so this affects only harnesses that build feature sets in code.
  • Feature checks run before any file is written. "Bench looks for either NVQ_VECTORS or INLINE_VECTORS feature set for scoring compressed builds" and "FusedPQ requires PQ build compression with 256 clusters" now fail before any index writer is opened, so a failed run no longer leaves partial index files.
  • Console messages. In-memory builds now print Skipping [INLINE_VECTORS, FUSED_PQ] when building in memory: it needs a compressed build.

Running AutoBenchYAML: what changes
