AutoBenchYAML now runs through the same pipeline as BenchYAML. Its command line (--output, --config, --diag, dataset patterns), output files (<output>.csv, <output>.json, checkpoint), and fixed regression benchmark set are unchanged.

  • One graph per build configuration. Each feature set is still written to, and searched in, its own index file. The difference is that the old path rebuilt the graph and rewrote every feature set's file for each feature set and each search compressor, then searched only one of them. With F feature sets and S search compressors (index cache off), it did F × S graph builds and F × F × S file writes; it now does 1 and F. The graph does not depend on the feature set (compressed builds score with the PQ/BQ build vectors), and search compression is not stored in the index, so the repeats only produced more random graphs with the same parameters.
  • Results to expect when comparing against an earlier run:
  • CSV columns unchanged; Build Heap / Build Off-Heap values shift. The build memory snapshot is now taken right after the build, before search vectors are encoded. Expect one comparison cycle where these move.
  • Index Build Time. On earlier code this was the last of the redundant builds, each doing the same work as the single build now, so values are comparable with less run-to-run noise. When every index for a build config is loaded from the index cache, no build time is reported for it; earlier code reported the previous build config's time.
  • Within a build config, INLINE and NVQ rows search the same graph. Comparisons between feature sets then differ only in stored features and reranking, and Avg Visited matches between them.
  • Total run time drops, and off-heap memory stays flat because indexes are now closed after use, including when a search fails.
  • JSON (<output>.json):
  • Parameter keys are unchanged. buildCompressor / searchCompressor remain lambda toString() values, which differ between runs; exclude them when diffing.
  • Existing metric keys are unchanged. Construction metrics are added when measured: Index build time (s), Index file size (MB), Idx PQ compute (s), Idx PQ encoding (s), Idx NVQ compute (s), Search PQ compute (s), Search PQ encoding (s). BenchmarkSummarizer does not read these, so the CSV is unaffected.
  • Rows follow the configured feature-set order.
  • Rows follow BenchYAML's sweep order. Construction parameters now vary as addHierarchy → refineFinalGraph → outDegree → neighborOverflow → efConstruction → build compression (first slowest), where AutoBench previously used M → efConstruction → neighborOverflow → addHierarchy → refineFinalGraph. Within each index, usePruning now varies slower than topK (previously the reverse). Parameter values per row are unchanged, so match rows by their params rather than position. The CSV is unaffected: BenchmarkSummarizer averages over rows, and the last row, whose Index Build Time it reports, is the same build config in both orders.
  • Console. AutoBenchYAML now prints the same per-configuration tables as BenchYAML.
  • Checkpoints. The BenchResult format is unchanged, so a checkpoint from an earlier build can be resumed. Datasets completed before the upgrade keep their earlier metrics (no construction metrics, earlier memory snapshot timing).

Updating the harnesses

Entry points (all callers in the repository have been migrated):

// BenchYAML, HelloVectorWorld
Grid.run(ds, GridSpec.fromConfig(config), artifacts);

// AutoBenchYAML
List<BenchResult> results = Grid.runAndCollectResults(ds, GridSpec.fromConfig(config));
To add Change A construction parameter A field and builder setter with a default in BuildConfig; its use, usually in GraphBuilderFactory; its field in ConstructionParameters. If swept, a parameter and one sweep(...) line in GridSpec.fromGrids, and the argument at its callers (fromConfig, Bench, and a single default value in the deprecated runAllAndCollectResults). To report it, one line in BuildConfig.reportedParameters() (it then appears in the console config block and AutoBench JSON params). An experiments.csv column for it Its name in ExperimentsSchemaV1.BUILD_PARAMETER_COLUMNS. This changes the versioned CSV schema, so it is deliberate, not automatic. A search parameter A field and builder setter in SearchConfig, and its loop in Grid.testConfiguration. An on-disk feature A new FeatureProvider file and one register(...) line in FeatureProviders. A report or output format A new GridListener file and one line where the entry point builds its listener list (Grid.reportingListeners or Grid.runAndCollectResults). Data for listeners A field on SearchContext, set where Grid.runOneGraph creates it.

Example: a new swept construction parameter myKnob:

// BuildConfig: field, constructor assignment, and a builder setter with a default
public final int myKnob;
private int myKnob = 4;
public Builder myKnob(int myKnob) { this.myKnob = myKnob; return this; }

// ConstructionParameters: the YAML field
public List<Integer> myKnob;

// GridSpec.fromGrids: a List<Integer> myKnobGrid parameter and its sweep. The position in the chain
// sets its place in the output order; SweepDimension rejects a null list, so default it if the YAML
// field is optional. Then pass construction.myKnob from fromConfig, and a grid from Bench.
.sweep("myKnob", myKnobGrid, BuildConfig.Builder::myKnob)

// BuildConfig.reportedParameters(): show it in console and JSON results
params.put("myKnob", myKnob);

// GraphBuilderFactory: pass build.myKnob to the core builder

Example: a new on-disk feature:

final class MyFeatureProvider implements FeatureProvider {
    public FeatureId id() { return FeatureId.MY_FEATURE; }
    public void configure(FeatureWriteContext ctx) {
        ctx.add(new MyFeature(ctx.vectors().dimension()));
        ctx.supplyFromVector(FeatureId.MY_FEATURE, vector -> new MyFeature.State(vector));
    }
    // Override supportsInMemoryBuild, providesRerankVectors, providesApproximateScoring or
    // checkCompressedBuild if the defaults do not fit.
}
// FeatureProviders: register(new MyFeatureProvider());

Porting in-flight branches that changed Grid

Old location in Grid.java New location runAll(...) overloads Removed (package-private); use Grid.run(ds, spec, artifacts) Sweep loops in runAll / runAllAndCollectResults GridSpec.fromGrids and GridSpec.buildPoints() runAllAndCollectResults body Grid.runAndCollectResults; the old method is a @Deprecated adapter buildInMemory InMemoryBuild buildOnDisk, writeInlineStates, index-cache lookup in runOneGraph CompressedOnDiskBuild new GraphIndexBuilder(...), BuildScoreProvider.*, writer builder setup GraphBuilderFactory builderWithSuppliers switch cases InlineVectorsProvider, NVQProvider, FusedPQProvider FUSED_PQ / INLINE_VECTORS / NVQ_VECTORS checks FeatureProvider hooks Console table code in testConfiguration ConsoleReportListener artifacts.logRow(...) in testConfiguration ExperimentsLogListener BenchResult construction for AutoBench BenchResultCollector ConstructionMetrics, FinalWriteVectors (nested classes) Their own files, unchanged AutoBench benchmark list Grid.regressionBenchmarks()

Deprecated, still working: Grid.runAllAndCollectResults(...), the positional RunArtifacts.logRow(...), and the positional ExperimentsSchemaV1.fixedValues(...). Use Grid.runAndCollectResults, and the overloads that take the build parameters as a map. Grid.runOneGraph(...) keeps its signature for the tests that call it.

Notes - Used internally by JVector benchmarking, no client impact. No core library code changed. - TestBufferedGraphCompatibility now compares search scores within 1e-6. Panama's float reductions round differently before and after C2 compiles them, which made the test fail intermittently on machines without the native vector library (all macOS machines). CI builds the native library, so it was not affected. - New tests: TestGridSpec (sweep order against the old loop nest, empty and missing dimensions, YAML mapping) and TestReportedParameters (reported parameter names and order, experiments.csv columns).

docs.title: MutablePQVectors Updates Its Vector Count Without a Capturing Lambda
docs.text:
Description

MutablePQVectors.encodeAndSet and setZero raised the vector count with updateAndGet(current -> max(current, ordinal + 1)), a lambda that captures ordinal and so may allocate on every call. They now use accumulateAndGet(ordinal + 1, Math::max), which passes the value as an argument and needs no allocation. The result and its atomicity are unchanged. In JMH runs on JDK 22 and 25, the JIT already removed the old allocation once the code was warm, so encodeAndSet time and allocation are unchanged in steady state.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

docs.title: Native Int8 (Byte) Vector Support
docs.text:
Description JVector can now build, store and search signed int8 vectors natively, without converting them to float32. This is useful when an embedding model already emits int8 vectors, or when vectors have been scaled to int8 up front: they take 4x less space on disk and in memory than float32, and all scoring is done byte-by-byte. On 176,582 mixedbread-large int8 embeddings (1,024 dimensions), an int8 index matched the recall of a float32 index of the same vectors, with about 3.6x the queries per second, half the build time and a 3.6x smaller file.

  • RandomAccessByteVectorValues (and ListRandomAccessByteVectorValues) provide random access to ByteSequence vectors. It and RandomAccessVectorValues now share a common VectorValues<V> interface, which also provides getVectorInto(node, destination, offset) for reading a vector into a caller-owned buffer.
  • ByteVectorSimilarityFunction scores two int8 vectors: EUCLIDEAN is 1 / (1 + squaredL2), DOT_PRODUCT is dot < 0 ? 1 / (1 - dot) : dot + 1, and COSINE is (1 + cosine) / 2. The scores are not normalised by dimension, so distinct integer distances stay distinct at high dimensions. DOT_PRODUCT scores are positive but not bounded above by 1.
  • GraphIndexBuilder.builder(RandomAccessByteVectorValues, ByteVectorSimilarityFunction, M) builds a graph from int8 vectors, and GraphIndexBuilder.build(VectorValues<?>) accepts either vector type.
  • The InlineByteVectors on-disk feature (FeatureId.INLINE_BYTE_VECTORS) stores each vector as dimension raw bytes. OnDiskGraphIndex.View.byteVectorRerankerFor(...) scores candidates directly from disk, and getByteVectorInto(...) reads a vector into a reusable buffer.
  • Int8 distance kernels (squared L2, dot product, cosine) are available in the default, Panama and native SIMD implementations, and accumulate in integers so all execution paths return identical results.
  • BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML support int8 datasets: mark a dataset with is_int8: true in dataset-metadata.yml, and configure it with construction.type: onDisk, compression None, reranking.type: None and fusedGraph: [No], as the int8 configs in index-parameters do. A runnable example is in Int8Example (-Dtutorial=int8).

How to Enable No configuration is required; the float32 APIs are unchanged. To use int8 vectors, build with the byte-vector builder and write the index with the InlineByteVectors feature:

RandomAccessByteVectorValues vectors = new ListRandomAccessByteVectorValues(byteVectors, dimension);
try (var builder = GraphIndexBuilder.builder(vectors, ByteVectorSimilarityFunction.EUCLIDEAN, 32).build()) {
    var graph = builder.build(vectors);
    try (var writer = GraphIndexWriter.getBuilderFor(GraphIndexWriterTypes.RANDOM_ACCESS_PARALLEL, graph, path)
            .with(new InlineByteVectors(dimension)).build()) {
        writer.write(Map.of(FeatureId.INLINE_BYTE_VECTORS, n -> new InlineByteVectors.State(vectors.getVector(n))));
    }
}

Notes * The new interfaces and classes are marked @Experimental and the API may change in later releases. * Only signed int8 (-128..127) is supported. Unsigned uint8 data, such as conventional SIFT1B/BIGANN .bvecs files, must be converted first; it is not detected, and reading it as signed silently changes distances. * Quantization and compression (ASH, PQ, BQ, NVQ, fused graphs) are not supported for int8 vectors. Traversal already scores exactly, so a separate reranking step is not needed. rerankK still controls how much of the graph is searched. * Zero vectors are not supported with COSINE, as with ASH: adding one to a graph or searching with one throws IllegalArgumentException. * OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor does not compact int8 indexes; AutoBenchYAML skips its compaction benchmark for them. * Existing float32 callers keep working: RandomAccessVectorValues.getVector keeps its VectorFloat<?> signature and GraphIndexBuilder.build(RandomAccessVectorValues) is retained as a forwarding overload. * Int8 indexes require on-disk format version 7 or later. JVector 4.0.x reads formats up to 6 and rejects version 7 files; a version 6 writer rejects INLINE_BYTE_VECTORS.

docs.title: GraphIndexBuilder Closes the Per-Thread Vector Copies It Creates
docs.text:
Description

For a shared RandomAccessVectorValues (one that reuses a buffer, such as a file-backed source), threadLocalSupplier() hands each thread its own copy(), but nothing could close those copies, so AutoCloseable copies (for example, ones holding a mapped file) stayed open. The supplier for shared sources is now AutoCloseable: closing it closes every AutoCloseable copy it created and clears the per-thread cache. GraphIndexBuilder.build and buildAndMergeNewNodes close their supplier when construction ends, and only after every parallel worker has stopped, even if one fails. Copies made by RemappedRandomAccessVectorValues now close their copy of the wrapped source, which is never closed itself. See #635.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

Code that calls threadLocalSupplier() itself can close the returned supplier when it is an AutoCloseable to release its copies; the supplier stays usable afterwards and makes new copies on demand. Un-shared sources still get a supplier that returns the source itself. Copies held by the exact-scoring build score providers are not yet closed; that is tracked in #764.

docs.title: Modular Benchmark Harness: Grid Refactor for BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML
docs.text:
Description Grid, the engine behind BenchYAML and AutoBenchYAML, was refactored so that each benchmarking initiative can put its changes in its own files. Almost every core change also changed Grid.java, and with several initiatives in flight at once it had merge conflicts at nearly every release. The class is now a small orchestrator (692 lines, down from 1,395). Its extension points live in separate files in io.github.jbellis.jvector.example:

Concern Before Now Two pipelines runAll and runAllAndCollectResults were near-copies One pipeline; AutoBenchYAML adds a result collector Build parameters 5–7 positional arguments threaded through every method BuildConfig (one build point) and SearchConfig (the search sweep) Construction sweep Six hand-nested for loops GridSpec with ordered SweepDimensions; GridSpec.fromGrids(...) sets the order, and GridSpec.fromConfig(MultiConfig) maps the YAML onto it Graph construction Inline buildInMemory / buildOnDisk IndexBuildStrategy: InMemoryBuild, CompressedOnDiskBuild (includes the index cache) Core builder/writer calls Spread through Grid GraphBuilderFactory only On-disk features A switch on FeatureId plus FUSED_PQ checks in five other places FeatureProvider per feature (InlineVectorsProvider, NVQProvider, FusedPQProvider), registered in FeatureProviders Console, experiments.csv, AutoBench results Inline in testConfiguration GridListeners: ConsoleReportListener, ExperimentsLogListener, BenchResultCollector Reported build parameters Listed separately by each output BuildConfig.reportedParameters()

Each step was checked against the previous code on lastfm-64-dot by comparing experiments.csv rows, AutoBench BenchResult output, console tables, and the builds, cache hits and skip messages logged. Output matched except for the changes listed below.

How to Enable No configuration is required. Command lines, dataset YAML files (yaml-configs/index-parameters/), run-config.yml, and the experiments.csv schema (v1) are unchanged.

Running BenchYAML: what changes

  • Unchanged: command line, YAML configs, run-config.yml selections, experiments.csv columns and values, console table columns.
  • Feature-set order is stable. Indexes are searched in the configured order. That is the reranking list order, with each fusedGraph value producing a full pass over it, e.g. reranking: [NVQ, FP] gives NVQ then FP. Previously the order of console blocks and experiments.csv rows changed between runs, because EnumSet hash codes come from identity hashes.
  • No stale search timings on fused rows. Fused-PQ indexes skip search compression, but they could report the previous index's Search PQ encoding (s). They no longer do.
  • PQ codebooks are reused within a run. The in-memory compressor cache never hit, so every lookup reloaded the codebooks from pq_cache (one codebooks loaded from line each). Results are unchanged; repeat loads are gone.
  • NVQ compressors can be cached. NVQParameters.idStringFor no longer throws (same fix as #780), and cached compressors are now read back by the CompressorParameters that saved them (loadCompressor) instead of always as PQ, which would have returned a corrupt PQ or failed on the second run. Files still go in pq_cache; the load message is now <compressor> loaded from <file>.
  • Clearer errors for incomplete configs. A missing construction sweep field fails with its name, e.g. No values to sweep for outDegree or construction.useSavedIndexIfExists must be set, instead of a bare NullPointerException. The whole sweep is validated before the first build.
  • Features without a provider are rejected. A feature set containing a feature Grid cannot write (e.g. SEPARATED_VECTORS) fails when the GridSpec is built, with Grid has no FeatureProvider for <id>. Previously the index was built without that feature and the results were still labeled with it. YAML configs cannot produce such a feature set (reranking accepts only FP and NVQ), so this affects only harnesses that build feature sets in code.
  • Feature checks run before any file is written. "Bench looks for either NVQ_VECTORS or INLINE_VECTORS feature set for scoring compressed builds" and "FusedPQ requires PQ build compression with 256 clusters" now fail before any index writer is opened, so a failed run no longer leaves partial index files.
  • Console messages. In-memory builds now print Skipping [INLINE_VECTORS, FUSED_PQ] when building in memory: it needs a compressed build.

Running AutoBenchYAML: what changes

AutoBenchYAML now runs through the same pipeline as BenchYAML. Its command line (--output, --config, --diag, dataset patterns), output files (<output>.csv, <output>.json, checkpoint), and fixed regression benchmark set are unchanged.

  • One graph per build configuration. Each feature set is still written to, and searched in, its own index file. The difference is that the old path rebuilt the graph and rewrote every feature set's file for each feature set and each search compressor, then searched only one of them. With F feature sets and S search compressors (index cache off), it did F × S graph builds and F × F × S file writes; it now does 1 and F. The graph does not depend on the feature set (compressed builds score with the PQ/BQ build vectors), and search compression is not stored in the index, so the repeats only produced more random graphs with the same parameters.
  • Results to expect when comparing against an earlier run:
  • CSV columns unchanged; Build Heap / Build Off-Heap values shift. The build memory snapshot is now taken right after the build, before search vectors are encoded. Expect one comparison cycle where these move.
  • Index Build Time. On earlier code this was the last of the redundant builds, each doing the same work as the single build now, so values are comparable with less run-to-run noise. When every index for a build config is loaded from the index cache, no build time is reported for it; earlier code reported the previous build config's time.
  • Within a build config, INLINE and NVQ rows search the same graph. Comparisons between feature sets then differ only in stored features and reranking, and Avg Visited matches between them.
  • Total run time drops, and off-heap memory stays flat because indexes are now closed after use, including when a search fails.
  • JSON (<output>.json):
  • Parameter keys are unchanged. buildCompressor / searchCompressor remain lambda toString() values, which differ between runs; exclude them when diffing.
  • Existing metric keys are unchanged. Construction metrics are added when measured: Index build time (s), Index file size (MB), Idx PQ compute (s), Idx PQ encoding (s), Idx NVQ compute (s), Search PQ compute (s), Search PQ encoding (s). BenchmarkSummarizer does not read these, so the CSV is unaffected.
  • Rows follow the configured feature-set order.
  • Rows follow BenchYAML's sweep order. Construction parameters now vary as addHierarchy → refineFinalGraph → outDegree → neighborOverflow → efConstruction → build compression (first slowest), where AutoBench previously used M → efConstruction → neighborOverflow → addHierarchy → refineFinalGraph. Within each index, usePruning now varies slower than topK (previously the reverse). Parameter values per row are unchanged, so match rows by their params rather than position. The CSV is unaffected: BenchmarkSummarizer averages over rows, and the last row, whose Index Build Time it reports, is the same build config in both orders.
  • Console. AutoBenchYAML now prints the same per-configuration tables as BenchYAML.
  • Checkpoints. The BenchResult format is unchanged, so a checkpoint from an earlier build can be resumed. Datasets completed before the upgrade keep their earlier metrics (no construction metrics, earlier memory snapshot timing).

Updating the harnesses

Entry points (all callers in the repository have been migrated):

// BenchYAML, HelloVectorWorld
Grid.run(ds, GridSpec.fromConfig(config), artifacts);

// AutoBenchYAML
List<BenchResult> results = Grid.runAndCollectResults(ds, GridSpec.fromConfig(config));
To add Change A construction parameter A field and builder setter with a default in BuildConfig; its use, usually in GraphBuilderFactory; its field in ConstructionParameters. If swept, a parameter and one sweep(...) line in GridSpec.fromGrids, and the argument at its callers (fromConfig, Bench, and a single default value in the deprecated runAllAndCollectResults). To report it, one line in BuildConfig.reportedParameters() (it then appears in the console config block and AutoBench JSON params). An experiments.csv column for it Its name in ExperimentsSchemaV1.BUILD_PARAMETER_COLUMNS. This changes the versioned CSV schema, so it is deliberate, not automatic. A search parameter A field and builder setter in SearchConfig, and its loop in Grid.testConfiguration. An on-disk feature A new FeatureProvider file and one register(...) line in FeatureProviders. A report or output format A new GridListener file and one line where the entry point builds its listener list (Grid.reportingListeners or Grid.runAndCollectResults). Data for listeners A field on SearchContext, set where Grid.runOneGraph creates it.

Example: a new swept construction parameter myKnob:

// BuildConfig: field, constructor assignment, and a builder setter with a default
public final int myKnob;
private int myKnob = 4;
public Builder myKnob(int myKnob) { this.myKnob = myKnob; return this; }

// ConstructionParameters: the YAML field
public List<Integer> myKnob;

// GridSpec.fromGrids: a List<Integer> myKnobGrid parameter and its sweep. The position in the chain
// sets its place in the output order; SweepDimension rejects a null list, so default it if the YAML
// field is optional. Then pass construction.myKnob from fromConfig, and a grid from Bench.
.sweep("myKnob", myKnobGrid, BuildConfig.Builder::myKnob)

// BuildConfig.reportedParameters(): show it in console and JSON results
params.put("myKnob", myKnob);

// GraphBuilderFactory: pass build.myKnob to the core builder

Example: a new on-disk feature:

final class MyFeatureProvider implements FeatureProvider {
    public FeatureId id() { return FeatureId.MY_FEATURE; }
    public void configure(FeatureWriteContext ctx) {
        ctx.add(new MyFeature(ctx.vectors().dimension()));
        ctx.supplyFromVector(FeatureId.MY_FEATURE, vector -> new MyFeature.State(vector));
    }
    // Override supportsInMemoryBuild, providesRerankVectors, providesApproximateScoring or
    // checkCompressedBuild if the defaults do not fit.
}
// FeatureProviders: register(new MyFeatureProvider());

Porting in-flight branches that changed Grid

Old location in Grid.java New location runAll(...) overloads Removed (package-private); use Grid.run(ds, spec, artifacts) Sweep loops in runAll / runAllAndCollectResults GridSpec.fromGrids and GridSpec.buildPoints() runAllAndCollectResults body Grid.runAndCollectResults; the old method is a @Deprecated adapter buildInMemory InMemoryBuild buildOnDisk, writeInlineStates, index-cache lookup in runOneGraph CompressedOnDiskBuild new GraphIndexBuilder(...), BuildScoreProvider.*, writer builder setup GraphBuilderFactory builderWithSuppliers switch cases InlineVectorsProvider, NVQProvider, FusedPQProvider FUSED_PQ / INLINE_VECTORS / NVQ_VECTORS checks FeatureProvider hooks Console table code in testConfiguration ConsoleReportListener artifacts.logRow(...) in testConfiguration ExperimentsLogListener BenchResult construction for AutoBench BenchResultCollector ConstructionMetrics, FinalWriteVectors (nested classes) Their own files, unchanged AutoBench benchmark list Grid.regressionBenchmarks()

Deprecated, still working: Grid.runAllAndCollectResults(...), the positional RunArtifacts.logRow(...), and the positional ExperimentsSchemaV1.fixedValues(...). Use Grid.runAndCollectResults, and the overloads that take the build parameters as a map. Grid.runOneGraph(...) keeps its signature for the tests that call it.

Notes - Used internally by JVector benchmarking, no client impact. No core library code changed. - TestBufferedGraphCompatibility now compares search scores within 1e-6. Panama's float reductions round differently before and after C2 compiles them, which made the test fail intermittently on machines without the native vector library (all macOS machines). CI builds the native library, so it was not affected. - New tests: TestGridSpec (sweep order against the old loop nest, empty and missing dimensions, YAML mapping) and TestReportedParameters (reported parameter names and order, experiments.csv columns).

docs.title: Correct Fused PQ Retained Memory Accounting
docs.text:
Description

Correct ramBytesUsed() for fused PQ sources, byte sequences, and shared on-disk graph caches. Remove the erroneous four-times multiplier on source byte counts, include retained buffer wrappers, native heap segment scopes, graph metadata, cache capacity, adjacency-array overhead, and models read from the index header (fused PQ codebooks, NVQ parameters), which only the index holds. PQ and NVQ models, float vectors and PQ scoring tables report their full retained storage, including caches created after loading. Sizing follows the running JVM's reference sizes, headers, array element offsets, and alignment, including JDK 25 compact object headers, without sun.misc.Unsafe.

Graph and built-in PQ vector memory checks use cached totals. Loading and storage growth update these totals, including spare chunk-reference capacity; repeated checks allocate nothing, and their cost does not grow with the number of vectors.

How to Enable

Automatic; no configuration is required.

Notes

Reported sizes can increase or decrease, affecting applications that use these estimates for memory limits or cache sizing. Existing indexes do not require rebuilding; the on-disk format and search results are unchanged.

Loaded graph feature metadata is read-only. Resident buffers are counted at their allocation sites; fixed per-index metadata is a small estimate. Feature implementations can override Feature.ramBytesUsed(); worker scratch remains excluded. See retained memory accounting for the ownership boundary, reporting cost, and validation details.

docs.title: BenchYAML: ASH defaults, explicit pipelines and one-JVM experiments
docs.text:
Description

BenchYAML's index YAML schema 3 states each pipeline explicitly: index type, construction and search compression, construction scoring, reranking, query execution (direct or queued), and construction and search worker counts. It can also sweep the upper layers' degree separately from the base layer's. Schema 1 files are still accepted.

  • Defaults. Without arguments, BenchYAML runs a few small public datasets and prints the key results. Compressed dataset defaults now use fused ASH.
  • Results. Runs report stored-code load and write times and the codes file size. Every console and CSV result field is defined in the BenchYAML Guide.
  • Measurement settings. Run configurations can measure cold queries, and a larger-than-memory run configuration is included.
  • One-JVM experiments. benchyaml-play.sh builds the checkout and runs one experiment in one JVM from the command line or IntelliJ.

How to Enable

Set yamlSchemaVersion: 3 to use the new fields. See the BenchYAML Guide, the example pipelines and the benchmark launcher.

docs.title: Asymmetric Scalar Hashing (ASH) quantization
docs.text:
Description

JVector adds ASH, from ASH: Asymmetric Scalar Hashing With Learned Dimensionality Reduction for High-Fidelity Vector Quantization (Tepper and Willke, CIKM 2026). ASH projects database vectors with a learned orthonormal matrix and stores each projected dimension in 1 to 9 bits, while queries stay full precision. On large datasets at matched code sizes, fused ASH builds faster than fused PQ, is more accurate, and searches faster in nearly every case; see ASH performance. ASH is @Experimental; PQ remains the stable default.

  • Training and encoding: AsymmetricHashing.initialize and encodeAll, producing ASHVectors.
  • In-memory graphs: ASHVectors score construction and search; BuildScoreProvider.ashBuildScoreProvider builds with code-to-code scoring.
  • Fused ASH on disk: the FusedASH feature stores neighbors' codes with each adjacency list, reranking with NVQ or full-precision vectors.
  • Streaming construction: StreamingASHIndex builds and searches while vectors arrive, training its model cold if needed.
  • Native query projection: INT8, FP16 or FP32, chosen automatically by CPU; FP16 and some INT8 paths use the optional oneDNN add-on.
  • Prepared and queued queries: QueryPreparer, PreparedQuery and BatchingExecutor share batched query projection.
  • Page-aligned records: withPageAlignment(pageBytes) keeps base-layer records from crossing page boundaries, for indexes larger than memory.

How to Enable

ASH is opt-in. See HelloASHWorldFp16 for a complete fused ASH build and search, and ASH configuration and defaults for settings.

Notes

  • Format version 7. New files default to version 7, which JVector 4.0.x cannot read; pass withVersion(6) to keep rollback possible. See UPGRADING.md.
  • Similarity. A model is trained for DOT_PRODUCT, EUCLIDEAN or COSINE and rejects other functions; vectors need not be normalized.
  • Adaptive termination. GraphSearcher.useAdaptiveTermination(true) is experimental and off by default for search.
  • BLAS threads. ASH training sets the native BLAS thread count; MKL_NUM_THREADS is no longer needed.
  • Compaction. OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor does not yet compact fused ASH or page-aligned indexes.
  • Native build. Highway is a Meson wrap instead of a git submodule; the oneDNN add-on is a separate Meson project.

Documentation

ASH configuration, database integration, projection precision, larger-than-memory indexes, reproducing ASH versus PQ, native build and Hello ASH examples.

docs.title: Compaction: sharded compaction sessions and a choice of output format version
docs.text:
Description

JVector 4.0.2 made OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor find level-0 neighbours by scanning cells instead of searching (#740). This change builds on it in three ways.

  • Sharded compaction sessions. A host that splits a merge into several outputs (Cassandra writes one sstable per token range) previously ran one compaction per output. Each run trained the codebooks again, and each lost recall: a shard keeps only a small part of every source, so a node kept few of its same-source edges and nothing replaced them. A session trains the codebooks once, on the live nodes of every shard, and shares them. In each shard it also searches a source with fewer than half its nodes live for the node's own neighbours. Ordinary compact calls are unchanged.
  • withVersion(int) writes the output at any on-disk format version the writer supports instead of only OnDiskGraphIndex.CURRENT_VERSION. Sources may be at different versions. A version that cannot hold the output is rejected: fused PQ needs 6, and upper layers need 4 or above.
  • Faster merges larger than memory. The cell walk sizes its ranges from the heap and from what it measures, announces source records to the page cache ahead of reading them, frees its tables before writing the upper layers, and reads the merge store with direct I/O when the store does not fit in memory beside the heap.

tessera-2M, two 1M-vector sources (1024 dimensions, cosine, degree 32) merged into hash shards, 8 cores. Each cell shows total time and recall@10:

Shards One compaction per shard One session Rebuild of every shard 4 454 s, 0.781 566 s, 0.825 876 s, 0.836 16 981 s, 0.823 567 s, 0.894 946 s, 0.903 64 1203 s, 0.875 627 s, 0.945 886 s, 0.947

How to Enable

Open a session on a compactor built with the live nodes of every shard, then merge each shard:

var compactor = new OnDiskGraphIndexCompactor(sources, liveNodes, VectorSimilarityFunction.COSINE, null);
var session = compactor.sharded();
List<OrdinalMapper> shard0 = session.compactShard(shard0LiveNodes, output0);
List<OrdinalMapper> shard1 = session.compactShard(shard1LiveNodes, output1);

Sources with a compressed sidecar use compactShard(shardLiveNodes, graphPath, compressedPath). To choose the output's format version, call compactor.withVersion(6) before compacting; a session writes every shard at its compactor's version. The large-merge changes need no configuration.

Notes

  • sharded(), compactShard and withVersion are @Experimental. A session is not thread-safe: shards are compacted one at a time, and may become known one at a time.
  • At 4 shards the same-source search costs more time than shared training saves; from 16 shards the session is faster and its recall is within a point of a rebuild.
  • A merge whose top levels have no live node, which a shard can produce, now ends its hierarchy at the highest level that still has one instead of failing.
  • Record announce-ahead is asynchronous (POSIX_MADV_WILLNEED) only with the jvector-native reader. Other readers fall back to their synchronous prefetch.
  • See compaction for details.

docs.title: GraphSearcher Returns an Empty Result for topK == 0
docs.text:
Description

GraphSearcher.search with topK == 0 read the empty results queues: with a reranker it threw a NullPointerException from NodeQueue.rerank, and with rerankK == 0 it compared against and evicted stale heap slots, which could throw on a later resume or make the search depend on the previous query. search and resume now return an empty result without searching when topK (or additionalK) is 0, and NodeQueue.rerank sends every candidate to the unused pile when topK is 0. See #811.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

Callers that short-circuit k == 0 before calling search as a workaround can keep doing so; it is no longer necessary.

docs.title: GraphIndexBuilder Searches With No Score Floor, So DOT_PRODUCT Vectors Dissimilar to Everything Get Neighbors
docs.text:
Description

GraphIndexBuilder.addGraphNode and improveConnections searched with a score threshold of 0.0f. That accepts everything for COSINE and EUCLIDEAN, but DOT_PRODUCT scores are (1 + dot) / 2, which is negative for non-normalized vectors. Every candidate of a vector that is dissimilar to all the others was discarded, so it was inserted with no neighbors; if it was the entry node, the index was built without any edges and searches returned a single result. The builder now uses Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, as GraphSearcher.internalSearch already does. See #813.

How to Enable

No configuration is required. COSINE and EUCLIDEAN builds are unchanged.

Notes

On ordinary non-unit DOT_PRODUCT data recall did not change (20,000 x 128-dimension vectors, recall@10 1.0000 to 0.9993 across four scalings, the same with and without the change). Non-normalized DOT_PRODUCT graphs can still be poorly connected for other reasons.

docs.title: GraphIndexBuilder Uses No Rerank Floor in the Layer-0 Resume, and improveConnections Is Tested
docs.text:
Description

Follow-up to #814. The layer-0 resume in GraphIndexBuilder.addGraphNode still passed a rerank floor of 0.0f. A score provider with a reranker only reranks candidates at or above the floor, so with a custom provider and non-normalized DOT_PRODUCT vectors, a node dissimilar to everything got only its single best candidate as a neighbor. The floor is now Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY. The built-in build score providers have no reranker and were not affected. A test now also covers improveConnections on an upper-layer node whose similarities are all negative. See #817.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

Only builds with a custom BuildScoreProvider that supplies a reranker, and DOT_PRODUCT on non-normalized vectors, change.

docs.title: neighborOverflow Values Such as 1.3 and 1.4 No Longer Trip an Assertion
docs.text:
Description

Inserting a backlink capped the neighbor list at M * neighborOverflow computed in float, while the neighbor arrays were sized from the same product computed in double. For overflow factors such as 1.3, 1.4, 1.8 and 1.9 the float product rounds up to the next integer for some M (for example 1.4 with M = 5, 10, 15, ...), so with assertions enabled the build failed with "could exceed max overflow degree", and without them a neighbor list could briefly hold one neighbor more than intended. Both now use the double product. See #822.

A builder over an existing graph could also be given a larger neighborOverflow than the graph's arrays were sized for; the build then failed with "Cannot copy ... nodes to a smaller size". The cap now never exceeds the arrays' size.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

Notes

The default overflow of 1.2 is not affected.

docs.title: Documentation Site
docs.text:
Description

JVector's documentation in docs/ is published at datastax.github.io/jvector, which the README and the repository's About section now link to.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

docs.title: Avoid False Sharing Between Concurrent Graph Searches
docs.text:
Description

With several searchers running concurrently, some JVMs ran graph search about 15% slower for their whole lifetime. For every scored neighbor, GraphSearcher read shared objects (Bits.ALL and the no-op score tracker) and wrote its own visit counter. When one searcher was placed on the same cache line as a shared object, its writes slowed every other searcher. The search now checks for an accept-all filter and a no-op tracker once per layer, and counts visits locally, adding them once per layer. Results and visit counts are unchanged.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

docs.title: Cheaper Closest-Centroid Assertion With -ea
docs.text:
Description

With assertions enabled, VectorUtil.tryClosestCentroid rescanned every centroid after each call, which slowed PQ encoding up to 5x with the native provider. It now checks only the selected distance, and centroids are checked where k-means uses them for the closest-centroid search. Runs without -ea are unchanged.

How to Enable

No configuration is required.

docs.title: JVector Tutorial Part 1: Introduction
docs.text:
JVector provides a graph index for ANN search which is a hybrid of DiskANN and HNSW. You can think of it as a Vamana index with an HNSW-style hierarchy. The rest of this tutorial assumes you have a basic understanding of Vector search, but no prior understanding of HNSW or DiskANN is assumed.

JVector provides a VectorFloat datatype for representing vectors, as an abstraction over the physical vector type. Therefore, the first step to using JVector is to understand how to create a VectorFloat:

// `VectorizationProvider` is automatically picked based on the system, language version and runtime flags
// and determines the actual type of the vector data, and provides implementations for common operations
// like the inner product.
VectorTypeSupport vts = VectorizationProvider.getInstance().getVectorTypeSupport();

int dimension = 3;

// Create a `VectorFloat` from a `float[]`.
// The types that can be converted to a VectorFloat are technically dependent on which VectorizationProvider is picked,
// but `float[]` is generally a safe bet.
float[] vector0Array = new float[]{0.1f, 0.2f, 0.3f};
VectorFloat<?> vector0 = vts.createFloatVector(vector0Array);

[!TIP] For other ways to create vectors, refer to the javadoc for VectorTypeSupport.

Before creating the vector index, we will group all of our base vectors into a container which implements the RandomAccessVectorValues interface. Many APIs in JVector accept an instance of RandomAccessVectorValues as input. In this case, we'll use it to specify the vectors to be used to build the index.

// This toy example uses only three vectors, in practical cases you might have millions or more.
List<VectorFloat<?>> baseVectors = List.of(
    vector0,
    vts.createFloatVector(new float[]{0.01f, 0.15f, -0.3f}),
    vts.createFloatVector(new float[]{-0.2f, 0.1f, 0.35f})
);

// RAVV or `ravv` is convenient shorthand for a RandomAccessVectorValues instance
RandomAccessVectorValues ravv = new ListRandomAccessVectorValues(baseVectors, dimension /* 3 */);

[!TIP] In this example, all vectors are loaded in-memory, but RAVVs are quite versatile. For example, you might have a RAVV backed by disk (check out MMapRandomAccessVectorValues.java) or write your own custom RAVV that transfers data over a network interface.

[!NOTE] A note on terminology: - "Base" vectors are the vectors used to build the index. Each vector becomes a node in the graph. - "Query" vectors are vectors used as queries for ANN search after the index has been built. In some cases you may want to use some base vectors as queries.

We're now ready to create a Graph-based vector index. We'll do this using a GraphIndexBuilder as an intermediate. Let's take a look at the signature of one of it's constructors:

public GraphIndexBuilder(BuildScoreProvider scoreProvider,
                         int dimension,
                         int M,
                         int beamWidth,
                         float neighborOverflow,
                         float alpha,
                         boolean addHierarchy,
                         boolean refineFinalGraph);

This constructor asks for something called a BuildScoreProvider, the vector dimension, and a set of graph parameters.

The BuildScoreProvider is used by the graph builder to compute the similarity scores between any two vectors at build time. We'll use the RAVV we created earlier to generate a BuildScoreProvider:

// The type of similarity score to use. JVector supports EUCLIDEAN (L2 distance), DOT_PRODUCT and COSINE.
VectorSimilarityFunction similarityFunction = VectorSimilarityFunction.EUCLIDEAN;

// A simple score provider which can compute exact similarity scores by holding a reference to all the base vectors.
BuildScoreProvider bsp = BuildScoreProvider.randomAccessScoreProvider(ravv, similarityFunction);

Let's also initialize the graph parameters. For now we will not worry about the exact function of the parameters, except to note that these are reasonable defaults. Refer to the DiskANN and HNSW papers for more details.

// Graph construction parameters
int M = 32;  // maximum degree of each node
int efConstruction = 100;  // search depth during construction
float neighborOverflow = 1.2f;
float alpha = 1.2f;  // note: not the best setting for 3D vectors, but good in the general case
boolean addHierarchy = true;  // use an HNSW-style hierarchy
boolean refineFinalGraph = true;

and now we can create the graph index

// Build the graph index using a Builder
// Remember to close the builder using builder.close() or a try-with-resources block
GraphIndexBuilder builder = new GraphIndexBuilder(bsp,
                                                  dimension,
                                                  M,
                                                  efConstruction,
                                                  neighborOverflow,
                                                  alpha,
                                                  addHierarchy,
                                                  refineFinalGraph);
ImmutableGraphIndex graph = builder.build(ravv);

[!NOTE] You may notice that we supplied the same ravv to builder.build, even though we'd already passed in the RAVV while creating the BuildScoreProvider. This is necessary since generally speaking, the BuildScoreProvider won't keep a reference to the actual base vectors, but it just so happens that we're using an "exact" score provider that does so.

At this point, you have a completed Graph Index that resides in-memory.

To perform a search operation, you need to first create a GraphSearcher.

[!IMPORTANT] The graph index itself can be shared between threads, but GraphSearchers maintain internal state and are therefore NOT thread-safe. To run concurrent searches across multiple threads, each thread should have it's own GraphSearcher. The same searcher can be re-used across different queries in the same thread.

// Remember to close the searcher using searcher.close() or a try-with-resources block
var searcher = new GraphSearcher(graph);

Generally speaking, you can't pass in a VectorFloat<?> directly to the GraphSearcher. You need to wrap the query vector with a SearchScoreProvider, similar in spirit to the BuildScoreProvider we created earlier.

VectorFloat<?> queryVector = vts.createFloatVector(new float[]{0.2f, 0.3f, 0.4f});  // for example
// The in-memory graph index doesn't own the actual vectors used to construct it.
// To compute exact scores at search time, you need to pass in the base RAVV again,
// in addition to the actual query vector
SearchScoreProvider ssp = DefaultSearchScoreProvider.exact(queryVector, similarityFunction, ravv);

Now we can run a search

int topK = 10;  // number of approximate nearest neighbors to fetch
// You can provide a filter to the query as a bit mask.
// In this case we want the actual topK neighbors without filtering,
// so we pass in a virtual bit mask representing all ones.
SearchResult result = searcher.search(ssp, topK, Bits.ALL);

for (NodeScore ns : result.getNodes()) {
    int id = ns.node;  // you can look up this ID in the RAVV
    float score = ns.score;  // the similarity score between this vector and the query vector (higher -> more similar)
    System.out.println("ID: " + id + ", Score: " + score + ", Vector: " + ravv.getVector(id));
}

For the full example, see VectorIntro.java. Run it from the root of this repo using 

mvn compile exec:exec@tutorial -Dtutorial=intro -pl jvector-examples -am

Next tutorial: - The OnDiskGraphIndex

docs.title: JVector Tutorial Part 2: The OnDiskGraphIndex
docs.text:
In-memory indexes are relatively simple to create, but they are not persistent and are fundamentally limited by the amount of memory available on the machine. To solve this, JVector provides an OnDiskGraphIndex backed by a file.

Unlike the previous example, this time we'll use a proper ANN dataset based on OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 embedding model.

// This is a preconfigured dataset that will be downloaded automatically.
DataSet dataset = DataSets.loadDataSet("ada002-100k").orElseThrow(() ->
    new RuntimeException("Dataset doesn't exist or wasn't configured correctly")
).getDataSet();

[!TIP] A DataSet provides the base vectors used to be indexed, the query vectors, and the expected or "ground truth" results used for computing accuracy metrics.

We'll create the graph in-memory in exactly the same way as we did in the introductory tutorial. You can't create larger-than-memory indexes this way, but we'll cover how to do that in a later tutorial.

// The loaded DataSet provides a RAVV over the base vectors
RandomAccessVectorValues ravv = dataset.getBaseRavv();
VectorSimilarityFunction vsf = dataset.getSimilarityFunction();
int dim = dataset.getDimension();

// reasonable defaults
int M = 32;
int ef = 100;
float overflow = 1.2f;
float alpha = 1.2f;
boolean addHierarchy = true;

BuildScoreProvider bsp = BuildScoreProvider.randomAccessScoreProvider(ravv, vsf);

// nothing new here
ImmutableGraphIndex heapGraph;
try (GraphIndexBuilder builder = new GraphIndexBuilder(bsp, dim, M, ef, overflow, alpha, addHierarchy)) {
    heapGraph = builder.build(ravv);
}

We can write this graph to the disk using a GraphIndexWriter.

Path graphPath = Files.createTempFile("jvector-example-graph", null);  // or wherever you want to save the graph

// Create a writer for the on-heap graph we just built.
// Remember to close when done.
GraphIndexWriter writer = new OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter.Builder(heapGraph, graphPath)
    .withParallelWorkerThreads(PhysicalCoreExecutor.getPhysicalCoreCount())
    // Let the writer know that we'll also be passing in the actual vector data
    // to be saved "inline" with the data for each corresponding graph node.
    .with(new InlineVectors(dim))
    .build();

This is a good time to discuss "Features" associated with on-disk JVector indexes. A Feature is any kind of additional information about each node in the graph that gets saved to the same index file. Here, we'll be writing "Inline Vectors" as a feature, which means that the vector value will be stored alongside the neighbor lists for each node in the graph. This will be useful later.

Since we want to include a feature, we need to tell the writer how to obtain the feature's "state" (or value) for each node. For inline vectors, this just means we need to specify the vector associated with each node.

// Supply one map entry for each feature.
// The key is a FeatureId enum corresponding to the feature
// and the value is a function which generates the feature state for each graph node.
var writerVectors = ravv.threadLocalSupplier();
writer.write(Map.of(
    FeatureId.INLINE_VECTORS,
    // we already have a RAVV, so we'll just use that to supply the writer.
    nodeId -> new InlineVectors.State(writerVectors.get().getVector(nodeId))));
// writer.close() if not using try-with-resources

Supplying every inline feature lets the parallel writer serialize complete records in batches of up to 64. The source must remain readable until write finishes. threadLocalSupplier() provides independent views when a source borrows a scratch vector; it also works with ordinary preloaded sources. See Deferred batch serialization for NVQ and migration examples.

At this point the graph index has been written to disk and can be used by creating an instance of OnDiskGraphIndex.

To do so, we'll need to specify a RandomAccessReader implementation which JVector will use to read parts of the file as needed. This interface isn't thread safe, so when creating an OnDiskGraphIndex we pass in a ReaderSupplier object which can be used by the OnDiskGraphIndex to create RandomAccessReaders as needed.

// ReaderSupplierFactory automatically picks an available RandomAccessReader implementation
ReaderSupplier readerSupplier = ReaderSupplierFactory.open(graphPath);
OnDiskGraphIndex graph = OnDiskGraphIndex.load(readerSupplier);

Now we can perform searches exactly as with the in-memory index, with one minor difference: for the in-memory index, we had to keep track of the RAVV we used to build the graph in order to create an exact SearchScoreProvider for each query. In this case, since Inline vectors are available as a feature, we can acquire a RAVV from the index itself.

GraphSearcher searcher = new GraphSearcher(graph);
// Views of an OnDiskGraphIndex with inline or separated vectors can be used as RAVVs!
// In multi-threaded scenarios you should have one searcher per thread
// and extract a view for each thread from the associated searcher.
RandomAccessVectorValues graphRavv = (RandomAccessVectorValues) searcher.getView();

// number of search results we want
int topK = 10;
// `rerankK` controls the number of nodes to fetch from the initial graph search.
// which are then re-ranked to return the actual topK results.
// Increasing rerankK improves accuracy at the cost of latency and throughput.
int rerankK = 20;
VectorFloat<?> query = dataset.getQueryVectors().get(0);
// use the RAVV from the graph instead of the one from the original dataSet
SearchScoreProvider ssp = DefaultSearchScoreProvider.exact(query, vsf, graphRavv);
// A slightly more complex overload of `search` which adds three extra parameters.
// Right now we only care about `rerankK`.
SearchResult sr = searcher.search(ssp, topK, rerankK, 0.0f, 0.0f, Bits.ALL);

The code from this tutorial is available in DiskIntro.java. Run it from the root of this repo using 

mvn compile exec:exec@tutorial -Dtutorial=disk -pl jvector-examples -am
The full example also illustrates the impact that adjusting rerankK has on recall.

Next tutorial: - Larger than memory indexes with Product Quantization

docs.title: JVector Tutorial Part 3: Larger-Than-Memory Indexes with Product Quantization
docs.text:
In the previous tutorials, we built indexes in-memory then wrote them to disk. However, this requires enough memory to hold all the vectors during construction. In this tutorial we'll build larger-than-memory indexes using two key techniques: - Write complete records after graph cleanup, reading FP payloads from a replayable source - Keep compressed versions of the vectors in the memory to allow JVector to compute similarities during construction. We'll use Product Quantization (PQ).

[!TIP] Product Quantization is a lossy compression technique that works by: 1. Dividing each vector into subspaces (e.g., a 128-dimensional vector into 16 subspaces of 8 dimensions each) 2. Learning a codebook of centroids for each subspace 3. Representing each subspace by the index of its nearest centroid

For example, consider 128 dimension vectors. With 16 subspaces of 256 centroids per subspace, each vector is represented by 16 bytes. instead of 512 bytes, achieving a 32x compression ratio.

Read the PQ paper for more details.

For a file-backed vector source with bounded asynchronous reads, see Batched input vector access. Its hello-world examples show how to supply a .fvecs file directly to PQ and NVQ without preloading the complete input dataset.

docs.title: Loading the Dataset
docs.text:
We'll change things up with a different dataset:

// The DataSet provided by loadDataSet is in-memory,
// but you can apply the same technique even when you don't have
// the base vectors in-memory.
DataSet dataset = DataSets.loadDataSet("e5-small-v2-100k").orElseThrow(() ->
    new RuntimeException("Dataset doesn't exist or wasn't configured correctly")
).getDataSet();

// Remember that RAVVs need not be in-memory in the general case.
// We will sample from this RAVV to compute the PQ codebooks.
// In general you don't need to have a RAVV over all the vectors to
// build PQ codebooks, but you do need a "representative set".
RandomAccessVectorValues ravv = dataset.getBaseRavv();
VectorSimilarityFunction vsf = dataset.getSimilarityFunction();
int dim = dataset.getDimension();

docs.title: Computing the Product Quantization Codebook
docs.text:
Before we can compress vectors, we need to compute a PQ codebook using a representative set of vectors. This is just a set of vectors whose distribution matches or approximates the distribution of the entire set of base vectors. In this case we'll select the representative set by randomly sampling from the entire set of vectors.

// PQ parameters
int subspaces = 64;  // number of subspaces to divide each vector into
int centroidsPerSubspace = 256;  // number of centroids per subspace (256 => 1 byte)
boolean centerDataset = false;  // we won't ask to center the dataset before quantization

// This method randomly samples at most MAX_PQ_TRAINING_SET_SIZE vectors
// from the RAVV and considers that a "representative set" used to build the codebooks.
ProductQuantization pq = ProductQuantization.compute(ravv, subspaces, centroidsPerSubspace, centerDataset);

docs.title: Setting Up for Incremental Construction
docs.text:
Now we'll set up the structures needed for incremental index construction:

// MutablePQVectors is a thread-safe, dynamically growing container for compressed vectors.
// As we add vectors to the index, we'll compress them and store them here.
// These compressed vectors are used during graph construction for approximate distance calculations.
var pqVectors = new MutablePQVectors(pq);

// Provides approximate scores during graph construction using the compressed vectors
BuildScoreProvider bsp = BuildScoreProvider.pqBuildScoreProvider(vsf, pqVectors);

The graph builder uses resident compressed vectors for neighbor comparisons. Original input vectors are consumed for insertion and reread for final FP payloads; the source must remain available through serialization. It need not preload the whole dataset. A one-pass source must retain its final feature states or use the compatible incremental-writing API instead.

// Initialize the graph parameters M, ef etc.
Path graphPath = Files.createTempFile("jvector-ltm-graph", null);

// Close the builder after final writing, or use try-with-resources.
GraphIndexBuilder builder = new GraphIndexBuilder(bsp, dim, M, ef, overflow, alpha, addHierarchy);
var vectors = ravv.threadLocalSupplier();

docs.title: Incremental Index Construction
docs.text:
We'll proceed to add vectors to the index one at a time. The general procedure is: - Encode the vector using the PQ codebooks created earlier, and add it to the collection of PQ vectors - Add the new vector to the graph

for (int ordinal = 0; ordinal < ravv.size(); ordinal++) {
    VectorFloat<?> v = vectors.get().getVector(ordinal);

    // Encode and add the vector to the working set of PQ vectors,
    // which allows the graph builder to access it through the BuildScoreProvder.
    pqVectors.encodeAndSet(ordinal, v);

    builder.addGraphNode(ordinal, v);
}

[!TIP] When you call builder.build(ravv), vectors from the RAVV are added to the graph in parallel. There's no parallelization if you add vectors one by one in the same thread. But you can parallelize manually by inserting from multiple threads at once, see the full example in LargerThanMemory.java.

Once we've added all the vectors we can write the graph structure to disk:

// Must be done manually for incrementally built graphs.
// Enforces maximum degree constraint among other things.
builder.cleanup();

// Serialize FP payloads and adjacency together after cleanup.
try (var writer = new OnDiskParallelGraphIndexWriter.Builder(builder.getGraph(), graphPath)
        .withParallelWorkerThreads(PhysicalCoreExecutor.getPhysicalCoreCount())
        .with(new InlineVectors(dim))
        .withMapper(new OrdinalMapper.IdentityMapper(ravv.size() - 1))
        .build()) {
    writer.write(Feature.singleStateFactory(FeatureId.INLINE_VECTORS,
            ordinal -> new InlineVectors.State(vectors.get().getVector(ordinal))));
}
builder.close();

The parallel writer batches up to 64 complete records without changing V6. Callbacks run concurrently, so the per-worker source views above are important for borrowed vectors. For NVQ reranking, supply NVQ.State instead of InlineVectors.State; see Deferred batch serialization and NvqExample.java. The construction scorer and two-stage query algorithm are unchanged.

We should also save the PQ vectors we created since we'll need them later on when it's time to run searches:

// PQ codebooks and vectors also need to be saved somewhere! (we'll not concern ourselves with Fused PQ)
Path pqPath = Files.createTempFile("jvector-ltm-pq", null);
try (var pqOut = new BufferedRandomAccessWriter(pqPath)) {
    pqVectors.write(pqOut);
}

[!NOTE] JVector supports a Graph feature called "Fused PQ" using which you can embed the PQ vectors and codebooks in the on-disk graph, similar to how full-resolution vectors are embedded. This saves you from the need to store them separately, but we won't cover that in this tutorial.

docs.title: Searching with Two-Pass Approach
docs.text:
Now that we've built and saved the index and the PQ vectors, we're ready to start searching. The only things that need to be held in memory are the PQ Vectors and the upper layers of the graph (if the graph is hierarchial). The full-resolution vectors and the lower layer of the graph remains on-disk and are read on demand.

Searching is done in two phases: - The first phase searches the graph to identify a set of candidates (as many as rerankK). In-memory PQ vectors are used to compute scores. - In the second phase reranks the candidates and returns the top topK results. Exact scores are computed using full-resolution vectors from disk.

// nothing new here
ReaderSupplier graphSupplier = ReaderSupplierFactory.open(graphPath);
OnDiskGraphIndex graph = OnDiskGraphIndex.load(graphSupplier);
// except that we also need a reader for the PQ vectors
ReaderSupplier pqSupplier = ReaderSupplierFactory.open(pqPath);
RandomAccessReader pqReader = pqSupplier.get();
// don't forget to close all of the above! (or just use try-with-resources)

// we need to have the PQ vectors in memory
PQVectors pqVectorsSearch = PQVectors.load(pqReader);

int topK = 10;
float overqueryFactor = 32.0f;
int rerankK = (int) (topK * overqueryFactor);

// a friendly reminder that searchers need closing too
GraphSearcher searcher = new GraphSearcher(graph);
var graphRavv = (RandomAccessVectorValues) searcher.getView();
VectorFloat<?> query = dataset.getQueryVectors().get(0);

// Two-phase search:
// 1. ApproximateScoreFunction (ASF) uses compressed vectors for fast initial search
// 2. Reranker uses full-resolution vectors from disk for accurate final ranking
var asf = pqVectorsSearch.precomputedScoreFunctionFor(query, vsf);
var reranker = graphRavv.rerankerFor(query, vsf);
SearchScoreProvider ssp = new DefaultSearchScoreProvider(asf, reranker);

SearchResult sr = searcher.search(ssp, topK, rerankK, 0.0f, 0.0f, Bits.ALL);

docs.text:

mvn compile exec:exec@tutorial -Dtutorial=ltm -pl jvector-examples -am
